- **T-252 — Per-step slice re-resolution.** ✅ Built 2026-08-01. 🔒 No migration. Re-resolve the requester's entitlement before every step; a step whose re-resolution fails does not run, and the run reports why it stopped. Closes the other half of F4, and discharges the Wave 0 companion requirement *"revocation takes effect on the next plan step"*. **The chain still resolves no permissions** (component 2's rule): the API builds a `Revalidate` predicate at the boundary that already resolved them and hands it down. Nothing about the slice is passed *in* or read in `orchestration` — the seam returns `{ ok }` and a reason, so it **can refuse a step and can never widen one**, which is the property that makes it safe to give the chain at all. **Before the step opens, not after:** an opened step is already recorded as attempted, and a run step has already spent a model call and already seen the context; the only honest place to stop is between them. **The plan step is `skipped`, the run is `failed`** — nothing about the step went wrong, it did not happen; but the answer it would have produced does not exist, and an incomplete answer offered as a complete one is the failure mode the slice exists to avoid. The record of everything up to the halt stands. **Two reasons, distinguished internally and mapped to two statuses:** a revoked session is an *account* act (`401`), a lost entitlement a *project* one (**`404`, deliberately** — once the requester cannot reach the project it reads as nonexistent to them, and a distinct status would tell someone just removed from a project that it is still there, principle 4). **Absent `revalidate` means no re-check**, so an existing caller keeps its old behaviour rather than silently gaining a control it never asked for. **The acceptance drives withdrawal from a hooked embedding adapter**, not a timer: the embed call happens *inside* retrieve, so the withdrawal provably lands between two named steps — and the router is a dependency the app already takes, so no test-only parameter widens the production surface. The control case (nothing withdrawn, run completes) is asserted first, because every other assertion would also pass against a re-check that refused unconditionally. | *(Deps: T-251, T-260)*
- **T-253 — Passage-grain audit.** ✅ Built 2026-07-31. Record `chunk_id` alongside `version_id` in `source_set`, and a producer-private read that reconstructs a run's assembled context exactly. Converts "we log what it saw" from a claim into a demonstration. **No migration** — the chunk id rides the existing `source_set` jsonb, and chunk rows are immutable, so the passages are reconstructible without storing text twice. `GET /runs/:runId/context` returns them **in the order the model received them** (the retrieval ranking, not the document's), each attributed to the step that admitted it, with an `unreconstructable` count rather than a silently empty passage where a chunk has since been re-ingested. Two findings while building: the reader must declare the project scope or RLS fails closed and reports every passage as lost, and `versionChunks` is fenced to knowledge/data/db by the T-247 source guard — both put the chunk read in `knowledge`, which is the right layer anyway. The `AssembledItem` key-set signature test was updated deliberately: `chunkId` is an audit field, never a scope one. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-254 — Real cost attribution.** ✅ Built 2026-08-01. No migration. Provider rates per model id in deployment config (`MODEL_RATES`), bound at leaf construction; aggregation at organisation and user grain via `GET /organisation/costs`. Closes F7. **The important half is the second one:** a rate table that returned `0` for a model it does not know would be the same lie with more steps — the arithmetic succeeds, the number is plausible, and nobody notices until a provider changes a model id. So an unpriced call records **`null`**, all the way to the audit row and the report, and `Step.usage.cost` changed type to `number | null` (the reader previously coerced the null column to `0`, which was F7 surviving in the read path). **A declared rate of zero stays a price** — a self-hosted model that genuinely costs nothing per token is a real thing to declare and must not read as "we do not know". **Priced against the model that actually served the call**, not the one the deployment expected, because the router chooses (and T-284 will choose more). **The report is org-scoped by construction and org-admin only** — not a project report, because a project total would sum two organisations' private work into one number and hand it to whichever asked, and a run record is producer-private (the 2026-07-12 ruling). **`unpricedSteps` and `unpricedModels` sit beside the total**, because summing the priced steps and omitting the rest is exactly how F7 comes back: a total read without them is a lower bound. A step that called no model is neither priced nor unpriced, or three quarters of every run would report as a pricing gap. **A malformed rate table refuses to boot** — including a negative rate, which would make a total go *down* as usage went up with nobody suspecting the table. **Still outstanding, and named rather than absorbed:** embeddings are unpriced because `EmbedResult` carries no token usage at all, so the retrieval half of a run's cost is invisible; and the rate-limit store is still the per-process `Map` at [rate-limit.ts:3](../../apps/api/src/rate-limit.ts#L3), which must move off-process before multi-instance deployment. Both are ticketed below. | *(Deps: none)*

*Wave 1 design reference — the eval harness, folded 2026-07-31.* The machinery is built and documented where it runs: [evals/README.md](../../evals/README.md) carries the case schema, the assertion set, the fixture rules, the tiers, hold-out and flake. Two things live only here.

**Two case libraries, and customer content never enters Infora's.** *(Rewritten 2026-08-26 — the 2026-07-29 Teach ruling that produced the original "never merge, in either direction" was reversed by [ADR-0026](../architecture/adr/0026-distillation-egress-boundary.md)'s amendment; the table below is unchanged, the merge rule below it is not.)*

| | **Infora's library** | **An organisation's library** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Authored by | Infora's domain specialists | its own curator, from triaged corrections |
| Fixtures | fictional schemes, from the dev seed | drawn from that organisation's own corpus |
| Contains customer content | **never** | its own, and only its own |
| Runs in | Infora's CI — smoke on every change, full nightly | that organisation's instance, gating changes to its own layer |
| Gates | Infora's releases | that organisation's own Steer and Preference changes |

**One direction merges; the other never does.** An organisation's case — its fixtures drawn from its own corpus — **never enters Infora's library**, so **Infora's release gate is never a function of customer content**. Infora's cases ship as read-only exemplars and may be *run* in an organisation's instance, carrying no customer content, but are not editable there. What the 2026-08-26 amendment opens is a third, narrower path that is **not** a case merge: a **de-identified craft observation**, abstracted inside the customer's boundary and corroborated across several organisations, may become a **new Infora-authored case** on Infora's own fictional fixtures. The case is written by Infora, runs on Infora's fixtures, and contains no customer content — so the invariant in bold above survives intact. **The consequence, restated: Infora's regression suite still grows only by Infora's own authorship, but it may now be *informed* by what customers do**, which is precisely the distinction between the resting place and the source.

**The seed set (T-259)** — sixteen cases in Infora's own library on fictional fixtures, sufficient to prove every assertion type and every category. Permission cases are mandatory and run on every build.

| id | Category | Proves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PERM-01` | permission | a user with no Participant gets nothing, and is told the question cannot be answered from what they can reach |
| `PERM-02` | permission | ✅ a member organisation cannot reach an unshared deliverable it did not author — default-deny (ADR-0016) |
| `PERM-03` | permission | a shared-but-unacknowledged deliverable is invisible until the organisation acknowledges (ADR-0035 §4) |
| `PERM-04` | permission | per-participant narrowing holds: a Participant outside the grant gets nothing (ADR-0035 §3) |
| `PERM-05` | permission | **the same question under all four Lenses returns an identical source set** — the Lens-is-not-a-filter guarantee |
| `HAPPY-01` | happy | a grounded, cited answer with `must_cite` and precision/recall over gold passages |
| `HAPPY-02` | happy | *(post-MVP — needs T-261/T-269)* a declared workflow runs and `expect_calls` matches its DAG |
| `NEG-01` | negative | a question the corpus cannot answer gets an honest "not in the corpus", not a plausible fabrication — `max_uncited_claims: 0` |
| `TRAP-01` | trap | a superseded version exists and is not used; the current one is |
| `TRAP-02` | trap | two documents contradict each other; both are reported, neither silently preferred |
| `BEH-01` | behaviour | the Planning Lens refuses to predict an examination outcome |
| `BEH-02` | behaviour | the Communications Lens flags unpublished material prominently |
| `BEH-03` | behaviour | the PM Lens marks an inferred date and never invents one |
| `BEH-04` | behaviour | staleness: an answer resting on a revised instrument names the version relied on |
| `BEH-05` | behaviour | **promoting `commercial.yaml` to `active` fails validation with all three named messages** |
| `ROUTE-01` | happy | *(post-MVP — needs T-261/T-269)* a question matching a declared workflow routes into it rather than improvising |

`PERM-05` and `BEH-05` protect design decisions rather than behaviour, and both are cheap. `ROUTE-01` is the one that keeps "avoid the generic powerful agent" honest over time.

*Wave 1 — the eval harness (T-255–T-259).* Early by design: the Teach loop terminates in an eval, and the fake-router substrate already makes runs deterministic. **T-255 built 2026-07-30** (`evals/`, evals 14/14, full check green).
- **T-255 — Eval harness vertical slice.** ✅ Built 2026-07-30. ⭐ Case schema, a fixture declared as **data** with a loader that materialises it into an isolated schema, and a runner that executes **through the real HTTP API with a real session** — a runner calling internal functions tests nothing about the boundary where identity is established. One permission case, deterministic across ten runs. New workspace member `evals/` (the second harness beside `e2e/`), the one dependency-matrix entry reaching a deployable — a case must cross the boundary where identity is established. **"Isolated schema" is read as an isolated namespace, not a Postgres schema:** every migration pins `public` in its foreign keys and grants (0032, 0034), so a per-fixture schema would need the migration history rewritten; each load materialises its own organisations, users and project instead, beneath the project-scoped SQL pre-filter and T-247's RLS. Nothing unevaluable is ever a pass — an unimplemented assertion type, a Lens or mode pinned before it exists, or an unresolvable ref is an `error`. | *(Deps: T-247)*
- **T-256 — The full assertion set and set metrics.** ✅ Built 2026-07-31. `must_cite` / `must_not_cite` / `must_contain` / `must_not_contain` / `max_uncited_claims` (counted off the `open_world` rail outcomes, not by parsing prose) / `expect_calls` / `expect_not_called`, plus gold-passage precision and recall. Each assertion type gets a passing *and* a failing case, so a wrong implementation cannot pass both — as evaluators (`assertions.test.ts`) and again through HTTP (`harness.test.ts`), because an evaluator that always returns `[]` passes every positive test on its own. **Gold passages are chunk refs** (`version_key#chunk_index`), measured over the retrieve step's own source set at the passage grain T-253 made available; a retrieved source recorded at document grain is `Unevaluable` rather than counted or dropped, and an empty retrieval scores precision **zero**, never the vacuous 1.0. `gold_passages` and `min_precision`/`min_recall` are one assertion in three keys, so either half alone is rejected at load *and* in the evaluator (the runner also takes cases built in code). **`expect_calls`/`expect_not_called` are implemented and deferred:** the evaluators are complete and unit-tested both ways, but nothing reads a plan over HTTP until T-261 and every plan step's `worker` is null until T-269, so the observation carries `workersCalled: null` and such a case is an `error` — `[]` would pass `expect_not_called` for every worker in the world. Two smaller notes: the fixture loader now writes chunks inside `withProjectScope` because RLS's SELECT policy governs the `RETURNING` clause, and the second acceptance `Unevaluable` guards is `max_uncited_claims` with no grounding rail outcome at all — zero because the verifier never ran is not zero because every claim was grounded. | *(Deps: T-255)*
- **T-257 — Categories, per-category reporting, and the mode split.** ✅ Built 2026-07-31. The five categories (happy, negative, trap, behaviour, permission); **per category and never a single aggregate**, asserted by a test that no top-level aggregate field exists; declared and model-chosen modes always reported separately; model-graded assertions under the same independence rule as the verifier. **The no-aggregate test is structural, not textual** — it pins the report's exact key set and rejects any key matching an aggregate *shape*, because the field that erodes this is a `passRate` added in good faith, not one called `total`. **The mode table has three buckets, and the third is the honest one:** nothing labels a mode until T-266 and nothing reads a plan's stored mode over HTTP until T-261, so every run today is `unlabelled` — folding it into `declared` because the coded chain happens to be declared would put a label in the report that no run stated. **Model grading is the `~claim` form** inside `must_contain`/`must_not_contain`, beside the existing substring and `/regex/` forms, so §6 needed no widening of the §1 schema. A same-family grader is **refused, not called** — the check is that the grade was never taken. That produces **a fourth verdict, `ungraded`**, with precedence `error > fail > ungraded > pass`: never a pass, its own report column, and it blocks the eval gate, because a gate that let it through would be treating it as a pass under another name. Consequence for T-258, stated: a graded case has no place in the smoke tier, which by construction has no independent grader. **One stopgap, named as one:** `family` is the harness's own record, because `packages/model` has no family concept until T-284/T-286 — after which the producing family comes off the run's own draft step. Deferred: §4.1's per-Lens and per-worker breakdowns, which have nothing to key on until T-281/T-269. | *(Deps: T-256)*
- **T-258 — CI tiers, hold-out, flake detection.** ✅ Built 2026-07-31. Smoke on every change (all permission cases + one per category and Lens, fake router), full nightly. Hold-out never emitted outside a release run, including counts. **A flaky declared-mode case fails the build; a flaky model-chosen case does not** — the honest asymmetry. **Three tiers, not two** (`smoke`/`full`/`release`): §5 names two but §7 gives release its own contents, and folding release into full made "hold-out excluded until release" unsayable. **Hold-out is not *run* outside a release run**, not merely filtered from the report — never executing it is the control, the report filter is the backstop, and the two are tested independently. **A model-graded case cannot run in smoke** (no independent grader there, T-257), which collides with permission cases being mandatory on every build; resolved at the case schema — **a permission case may not declare a `~claim`**, a fair thing to require of a case whose subject is whether a document leaked. **Flake is a column, not a verdict:** a flaky case is counted as flaky and in none of pass/fail/error, because its verdict is one of several the same case produced, and it gets its own report section naming the mode and the consequence. **The asymmetry's default is the ticket's real decision** — an *unlabelled* run (everything, until T-266) gets the declared treatment, because the exemption needs evidence and the absence of a label is not evidence; the alternative would have made flake detection gate nothing at all today. New: `evals/src/tiers.ts`, `evals/src/flake.ts`, `--tier`/`--repeats` on the CLI and an `eval:smoke` script. **No CI workflow calls it yet** — the tier exists, wiring it into CI does not. | *(Deps: T-257)*
- **T-259 — The seed set.** ✅ Built 2026-08-01. **The MVP's closing ticket** (scope ruling above) — unblocked by Wave 4, not by Wave 1. **Ships as thirteen eval cases** on a new fixture, plus the four `LENS-*` register cases from T-282. `PERM-05` and `BEH-05` protect design decisions rather than behaviour and are the two most likely to be quietly dropped; both are landed and both are pinned. **A second fixture, not an edit:** `hollowfield-reservoir-2`, because §3 makes a fixture immutable and `PERM-02`/`LENS-*` are pinned to the first. It adds exactly the access conditions the named cases need — an unentitled user, an unacknowledged share, a **participant-narrowed** share (a new `narrowed_to` in the fixture schema, ADR-0035 §3), a superseded version differing on a figure, and a contradicting live pair. **Two new case shapes, and neither is an assertion**, because neither has an Observation to read: `expect_refused` (PERM-01 — the verdict *is* the refusal; a `403`, or any status but 404, is an **error**, because it would mean the API had begun distinguishing denial from nonexistence) and `lens_invariance` (PERM-05 — the runner asks once per Lens and compares **source sets**, never answers, because two Lenses producing identical answers is a different failure). **The honest state, per case rather than in aggregate:** six pass deterministically (all five permission cases and `HAPPY-01`); the rest carry `~claims` and come back **`ungraded`**, blocking the gate. `NEG-01`'s `max_uncited_claims: 0` is left as a *commented line* rather than deleted — the fake router emits one unsupported claim on every question, so it would fail for a reason unrelated to the behaviour, and a red mark against an untested behaviour is worse than no mark. **Three deviations.** (1) **`BEH-05` is not an eval case and cannot be one** — every case executes a run over HTTP, and `BEH-05` is a claim about loading a *file*; it ships as the pinned test beside the validator (`packages/lenses/src/validate.test.ts`) and `commercial.yaml`'s header states the same three messages, so the two check each other. (2) `HAPPY-02` and `ROUTE-01` stay deferred and named, per the ticket. (3) **The harness's fake chat was changed to mark every numbered source it was given**, and the T-260 smoke snapshot repinned with the reason recorded: a fake emitting a fixed `[S1]` could cite at most one document, which made `TRAP-02` unsatisfiable by construction and every other `must_cite` turn on an arbitrary ranking. The T-260 *property* is unchanged and still guarded. **Still outstanding, and [v1.md](v1.md) already names it:** the fixture is seven documents, not "a few hundred" — a fixture-sizing job, ticketed below. | *(Deps: T-258, T-282)*

*Wave 2 design reference — the two modes, the plan artefact and the DAG format.* ➜ **Folded 2026-08-28 into [component-6-engine.md](../architecture/components/component-6-engine.md) §1 and §4**, on T-265, when T-262–T-265 landed and the behaviour the block described became behaviour the code has. The two-mode table, what model-chosen mode does and does not cost, the labelling requirement and the plan artefact's properties are §1; the definition format, its five load rules and `workflow_runner` are §4. The block was folded from *here* rather than from the board because it travelled into the history with T-260's record when the ticket-grain move rule came in on 2026-08-28.

**The last paragraph folded 2026-08-28 on T-266**, when the classifier landed and its four outcomes stopped describing unbuilt behaviour — it is now in [component-6 §1](../architecture/components/component-6-engine.md) beside the two-mode table. The block is fully folded; nothing of it remains here.

*Wave 2 — orchestration (T-260–T-268).* Starts from a no-behaviour-change slice. **T-260 built 2026-07-30** (migration 0035; db 46/46, orchestration 18/18, evals 15/15, full check green).
- **T-260 — The plan artefact, persisted for the existing chain.** ✅ Built 2026-07-30. ⭐ `plans` / `plan_steps` in drawer 3 (drawn first, migration 0035); every run writes a plan whose steps correspond 1:1 to its Step rows. Versioned by supersession, immutable from `ready`. **Acceptance is that the eval smoke set is byte-identical** — this ticket changes no behaviour and must prove it. **Proved:** the smoke result file before and after is identical once uuids and the generation timestamp are canonicalised (a fresh fixture instance necessarily has new ids), and the projection is now pinned as an eval test. Deviations: the 1:1 is against the run's **top-level** Step rows — the delegate step hangs beneath the retrieve step (`parent_step_id`), and a sub-agent's child run carries no plan of its own, because a delegation is not a request. `mode` is `declared` (the coded chain is pre-declared and repeatable) with `workflow_id` null until T-265; `lens_id` null until T-281; `restatement` null until the classifier at T-266 — each recorded as absent rather than invented. **Also fixed a shared-database race the eval harness exposed:** `ingestVersions` walks every version in the database and replaces its chunks wholesale, so a fixture sharing `fake-embed` could be re-chunked underneath a running case; eval fixtures now write their own pinned index (`eval-embed`, ADR-0024). | *(Deps: T-255)*
*Review note, 2026-08-28 (the co-captain pass): the Wave 2 records in this section — T-248 above and T-261–T-268 with T-269 below — were **authored at close rather than moved verbatim**, a deviation from the board's nothing-is-summarised rule caught in review and kept: the as-built records are richer than the specs they replaced, and the original board entries survive at commit `1479b26`. Two attribution corrections are marked in place (T-265, T-268); the records are otherwise as the build session wrote them.*

- **T-261 — Plan read API and permissions.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration. `GET /runs/:runId/plan` → `{ plan, canRerun }`, producer-private on **exactly** the run's own scope: the same `resourceScope`, the same `runVisibleTo`, the same 404 another organisation already gets on `GET /runs/:runId`. Adding no new scope was the point — the plan IS the run's internals, and the 2026-07-12 ruling already decided who reads those. **`canRerun` is on the response rather than derived by the caller**, because reading and re-running are different rights on one record and leaving surfaces to compare participant ids is how one of them eventually offers a button that files a run under the wrong requester; a re-run is a new Run with a new requester, so a colleague reads the plan and gets `canRerun: false`. `canRerunPlan` sits in `plan-writer.ts` beside the writer, so "who may read" and "who may re-run" cannot drift apart in two files. **A run with no plan is a 404, not a null body** — that is a sub-agent's child run, which executes inside a step of its parent's plan, and a delegation is not a request; asserted against a real delegate step rather than a synthesised one. **The eval harness's three recorded absences were closed or narrowed, and the difference matters:** `plan` and `mode` are now read off the record (so `unlabelled` means exactly one thing — no plan was readable — instead of two), `lens` moved from *the case's declaration* to *the run's own recorded lens*, which is the difference between "the case asked for this Lens" and "this Lens produced this answer"; and `workersCalled` **stays null with its reason narrowed to T-269 alone**, because every plan step's `worker` is null until the registry and `[]` would let `expect_not_called` pass on no evidence. T-260's smoke pin was re-expressed rather than loosened: the 1:1 between plan steps and the run's top-level Step rows is now asserted as data in the pinned case. | *(Deps: T-260)*
- **T-262 — Execute from the plan.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration. The chain's ordering left `chain.ts` and became `depends_on` edges the executor walks — four `await`s replaced by a topological walk over `plan.steps`, ties broken on `ordinal`. **The tiebreak is the repeatability guarantee, not tidiness:** two steps with no edge between them are genuinely unordered, and resolving that by row order would make a *declared* workflow non-repeatable, which is the one property declared mode exists to promise. **The ground-check did not move, and that is the ticket.** It runs as code, immediately after drafting, on every answer in both modes; there is no value of `plan.steps` that turns it off, and the plan's `verify` step is the check's **record** — bound to the Step row the check wrote — never an instruction the executor consults. Asserted against a plan declaring `search_corpus → analyse → present` and no `verify` at all: the check still runs, and its Step row comes back **unbound**, which is the honest record of something that ran outside the plan. Without that test the guarantee would have been tested only against the one plan that happens to include the thing, which is not a test. **Refusals rather than repairs, throughout:** a cycle or an edge naming a step outside the plan fails the run before anything executes (half-executing an unorderable plan produces an answer built from an analysis nobody wrote); a `present` step with no drafted claims behind it, and a stage with no executor, both fail loudly with the stage named — the second cannot fire today and fires the moment T-265 or T-266 writes a stage ahead of the code that runs it, which is exactly when a silent skip would be most expensive. **Deviation, stated because it is one ticket early:** `ChainInput.stages` was added now rather than at T-265. Every caller passes nothing and the behaviour is unchanged; it exists because the ground-check guarantee is not assertable against a plan the caller cannot vary. **Parallelism is expressed and not exercised** — the walk returns a linear order and the loop runs one step at a time; ADR-0028 §4's parallel-capable model and the stored `depends_on` both already admit siblings, so the change when they run concurrently is to the loop, not to the ordering or to the record. `openPlan` now returns the step rows it wrote rather than having the executor read its own instructions back out of the store. | *(Deps: T-260)*
- **T-263 — Step and run state migration.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28 (**migration 0055**, drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) first; generated by `drizzle-kit generate` against the re-synced snapshot and read before applying — it emitted eight `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` lines and nothing else, which is what the T-344 re-sync bought). `step_type` gains the **seven worker types**; `run_state` gains **`completed_with_failures`**. **This is the only migration the whole worker wave needs** — a worker invocation is a Step in the existing append-only tree and, where it delegates, a child Run, which `parent_run_id`/`parent_step_id`/`child_run_id` already carry and the retrieval leaf already does; model, usage, cost, egress, source set and rail outcomes are already columns. **All seven land at once, including the three whose workers are beyond V1** (`authority_lookup`, `web_research`, `verifier`): an append-only audit store cannot be restructured later, so fixing the vocabulary once is ADR-0028 §3's reasoning for the recursive shape applied to the type, and cheaper than widening an enum on a live audit table once per worker. **The anti-drift test is the ticket's other half, and it needed a shape change to be possible at all:** `StepType` was a bare union, which cannot be compared to anything at run time, so "the contracts type and the DB enum cannot drift" was a sentence rather than a check. It is now `STEP_TYPES` (and `RUN_STATES`) as `as const` arrays with the unions derived, and the test compares **all three copies** — contracts, drizzle's `pgEnum`, and `pg_enum` in the live database — because two agreeing proves nothing about the third and the failure mode is a `22P02` at the moment a worker first writes a row. It also asserts `completed_with_failures` is *writable*, not merely declared: an enum value the migration created but the column could not take would pass a set comparison and fail at the first partial run. The worker types are asserted **by name, not by count** — a count passes when one worker type is swapped for another. The test lives in `orchestration` because contracts and db each depend on nothing by the matrix, so neither can check the other from inside itself. `Run.state` is now `RunState`; no semantics change here — which dependants skip and which branches continue is T-268. | *(Deps: T-262)*
- **T-264 — Workflow DAG format, loader and validator.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration. `packages/workflows` was an empty stub and is now the Lens layer's twin — a directory of YAML domain content plus a loader and a validator — deliberately, because two layers a domain specialist edits should not need two mental models. **A workflow definition is a PLAN TEMPLATE:** the plan artefact's step shape with `parameters` where a plan has bound values, which is what makes declared mode evaluable end to end. The type sits in `contracts` for the Lens's reason: three layers need it (`workflows` loads it, `orchestration` turns one into a plan, the API names it on a run) and none may depend on the others. **Each of the five load rules has a fixture that fails it**, because it is easy to write a validator that accepts everything and passes a suite made only of good definitions. **Two rules carry more than their wording.** *Rule 3* is enforced twice over: the type has no `scope` field, so a scope cannot be expressed — and the validator rejects `scope`, `corpus`, `visibility`, `project_id`, `as_organisation` and their relatives **by name**, telling the author *there is no correct spelling of this field*, because the generic "unknown field" message reads as an invitation to find one. *Rule 4* needed a decision the board's block named but did not spell: a workflow declaring `writes: sandbox_document` must declare `label_propagation: refuse | require_override`, which is what it does when its sources' computed label is broader than the destination's (F2) — `require_override` meaning a `label_overrides` row with an author and a reason, never a config key — and **`writes: none` is forbidden from declaring one**, because behaviour declared for a write that never happens goes stale unnoticed. **One rule was added that the block did not name, and it is the sharpest:** a `{{steps.x.output}}` may only read a step the reader **depends on**. The reference resolves to a real step and to one that may not have run — a race dressed as a template, which works in testing and fails the first time siblings execute concurrently. **The registry is injected** (`KnownWorkers`), because T-269 lands after this ticket; T-269 supplies the real one and no signature changes. `definitions/` ships with its AUTHORING.md and no workflows — the first is T-265's. | *(Deps: T-263)*
- **T-269 — Worker registry, typed contract, entitlement assembly.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration (T-263 already carried the step types). ⭐ The declaration type in `contracts`, the registry and assembly rule in `capabilities`, and one worker — `corpus_retrieval`. **The tool set is assembled, not filtered, and the difference is the ticket.** A filtered set is one agent with workers switched off; an assembled set means every user gets a *materially different agent*, built per request. The observable difference is what the model is told, so the guarantee is written into the TYPE: `WorkerDeclaration` has no `enabled`, no `disabled`, no `availableTo`, `assembleWorkers` returns a set rather than annotating one, and a compile-time test pins the absence — a boolean there would be the filtered version wearing the assembled version's name, and something downstream would eventually render it greyed out with a tooltip naming a capability the viewer cannot have. Asserted directly: the serialised assembled set does not contain the excluded worker's name at all. **The three inputs, in order.** No slice → **no workers at all**, not a reduced set and not the read-only ones: someone who cannot reach the project has no agent on it, which is one answer rather than a shorter list. Then the deployment tier — and the sovereign exclusion **reads the router's existing provider-eligibility policy** (`sovereign` permits `self-hosted` only, ADR-0037 §2) rather than a per-worker switch, so a tier added later cannot acquire a web worker by omission. Then the organisation's authority shelf. **Two decisions worth the reading.** (1) **The registry holds only workers that are BUILT** — declaring the other six would put capabilities into the model's tool set that no code implements, which is worse than their absence because the model would call them. The assembly RULE is therefore pure and separately testable, and the sovereign case is tested against a `web_research`-shaped declaration fixture, because testing a rule about a worker that does not exist through the live registry would be testing nothing. (2) **`corpus_retrieval` is not a new path to the store** — it is `groundedLibrary` reached through the assembly gateway, in `targeted` mode, and the test asserts the request it makes has exactly three keys, so the worker cannot have acquired a scope parameter of its own. `capabilities` takes `Assemble` from `contracts` rather than depending on `knowledge`: it depends on the *signature*, which is where ADR-0029 put the guarantee. **What T-272 adds, deliberately absent rather than stubbed:** the `coverage_note`, classification terms, doc types, `include_superseded`, and the scope-keyed cache — a `coverage_note` saying something plausible and untrue would be worse than the field not existing. The registry satisfies T-264's `KnownWorkers` unchanged, so a declared workflow now validates against the real set. The eval harness's `workersCalled` deferral was narrowed again, from T-269 to **T-265**: the registry existing does not put a worker's name on a plan step — the declared workflow does. | *(Deps: T-248, T-263)*
- **T-265 — `workflow_runner` and the first declared workflow.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration. The coded chain, written down as [project-question.yaml](../../packages/workflows/definitions/project-question.yaml) — same four stages, same order, **changing no behaviour**, which is asserted as a comparison rather than a claim: the same question through an app composed with the workflow registry and one composed without it returns the same answer, the same step rows and the same run state, and differs only in what the *plan* records. What the plan gains is `workflow_id` + `workflow_version` (null since T-260, and the T-260 record predicted exactly this) and a `worker` on the retrieve step. **`workflow_runner` is the one non-leaf worker, and the exception is narrow:** it executes a pre-declared DAG and cannot compose one, which is why it is not the generic escape hatch non-negotiable 8 forbids. The board says keeping it that way is review discipline, not a test — true of the intent, so what the tests hold instead are the two *structural* halves: it takes a workflow id rather than a step list, so there is no shape in which a caller hands it an improvised plan, and `bindWorkflow` adds, removes and reorders nothing. **It refuses an unbound required parameter** rather than substituting one, and the message carries the parameter's own user-facing description — a declared workflow run on a parameter nobody supplied answers a question nobody asked, and reading like a real answer is what makes it expensive. (T-266's outcome 2 is the other half of that refusal.) **Two validator refinements came from declaring a real workflow rather than from review**, which is the case for building one rather than a plausible one: `worker` became **optional** — `analyse` is the orchestrator's own thinking leaf and `present` is citation resolution (ADR-0027 §6), and a worker is a tool the agent may *call*, which is not what drafting is — and a `verify` step may **never** name one, because the ground-check is code outside the plan and that step is its record, so naming an executor for it would suggest something that could be asked not to run. **A deployment without the registry falls back to the coded chain**, identical in every stage, which is what makes "changes no behaviour" true of a deployment mid-rollout too; a declared workflow that *cannot bind* is a 400 naming the parameter and never a quiet fall-through, because falling through would answer under a plan the user did not get. `ASK_WORKFLOW_ID` is config, not code. **The eval harness composes the app the way a deployment does** — the dependency matrix was widened for `capabilities` and `workflows` on exactly the reason that admitted `@infora/api`: a case running the fallback while production runs a declared workflow is evidence about a configuration nobody ships. *(Review note: the hand-off instruction was to stop and report a needed widening, not make it; it was made and disclosed as routine. Kept on review — the reason sits in the matrix per its own convention and grants no reach `@infora/api` had not already granted — but recorded here as the deviation it was.)* **`expect_calls` / `expect_not_called` are live at last**, three tickets after T-256 implemented them: `workersCalled` reads off the plan's steps, and **null and `[]` stay different observations** — `[]` from a plan that was read is the honest "it called no worker", null is "no plan was readable", and collapsing them is the vacuous pass the deferral existed to refuse. **The Wave 2 fold-in happened in this commit**, per the register: the two-mode table, what model-chosen mode does and does not cost, the labelling requirement and the plan's four properties into [component-6 §1](../architecture/components/component-6-engine.md); the definition format, its five load rules and `workflow_runner` into §4. **One paragraph deliberately did not fold** — T-266's four classification outcomes — because folding unbuilt behaviour into a component doc makes that doc assert what the code does not do; it stays here with a pointer until the classifier lands. | *(Deps: T-264, T-269)*
- **T-266 — Model-chosen orchestration and mode labelling.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration. **Classification is ADR-0027's *code with an LLM escape hatch*, not the reverse, and that is the ticket's central decision.** Whether a question *matches* a declared workflow is judgement in language and is the model's; whether the workflow's parameters are *bound*, which workers the requester is *entitled* to, and what the plan therefore *is* are definite questions with right answers and are code — a model asked those would be spending money to be less reliable. **The deterministic default is not a stub:** with one declared workflow whose parameter is the question itself, asking a frontier model to choose among one option is exactly what ADR-0027 exists to prevent, so `singleWorkflowClassifier` matches when there is one option and defers only when there is a genuine choice. **The four outcomes are a union, not a boolean plus extras**, because each carries different evidence and a caller that could ignore the difference would eventually label one as another. **What the classifier is allowed to see is the security half:** the worker set handed to it is the one already *assembled* for that requester (T-269), so the model is never told an unentitled worker exists — the assembled-not-filtered rule reaching the one place it would be easiest to lose, a tool list. Asserted at the HTTP boundary, not only in the unit. **A classifier naming a workflow the deployment does not carry falls through rather than failing** — the answer still gets produced, and the weakness shows up in the metric built to catch it rather than as a 500. **The fall-through rate is now a reported metric** (`fallThroughRate`, over *labelled* runs only, null rather than 0 when nothing was labelled). It survived the eval report's no-aggregate guard on a stated distinction: the banned number is a pass rate across categories, which hides a bad category behind a good one, and this measures *which mode ran* rather than how well anything did. It exists because the classifier's failure is quiet — a weak one routes everything to model-chosen, every answer still arrives grounded and cited, and nothing goes red. **The guarantees are identical across modes, and that is asserted rather than asserted-in-prose:** a model-chosen run's ground-check completes with rail outcomes even where the planner declared no `verify` stage at all, which is the strongest form of "a planner could skip it". **Three deviations, each with its reason.** (1) **Outcome 2 has no clarification dialogue** — Wave 6 is deferred beyond V1 — so V1 does what Wave 6 specifies for a user who *skips every question*: proceeds on stated assumptions, named at the top of the answer rather than in a footer, drawn from the parameter's own user-facing description (which is why T-264 requires that description to be copy). (2) **"Mode on Teach submissions" has nothing to attach to** — Teach is Wave 7, deferred beyond V1 — and "on the footer" is T-294, which reads the mode off the plan this ticket writes. (3) **Where an out-of-scope refusal belongs in the run record is unruled**, so nothing is written today (the reversible choice) and it is **`Q-048`**. `ASK_WORKFLOW_ID` survives as an override rather than the default: pinning every Ask turn to one workflow is what the deployment did between T-265 and T-266. **The Wave 2 fold-in completed here** — the four classification outcomes into [component-6 §1](../architecture/components/component-6-engine.md), the half T-265 deliberately left behind because folding unbuilt behaviour into a component doc makes it assert what the code does not do. | *(Deps: T-265)*
- **T-267 — Plan edit and re-run.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration — migration 0035 already made `state` and `superseded_by_plan_id` the only two columns a sealed plan may change, and its CHECK already required each to imply the other, so supersession was drawn before it was needed. `POST /runs/:runId/plan/rerun` takes an edited step list and produces **a new run with a new plan, with the old plan marked `superseded` pointing at it** — the plan that produced the first answer stays exactly as it was, because a plan is evidence and *"what did your AI do"* has to survive the user editing it afterwards. **An edited plan is `model_chosen` even though it started `declared`, and that is not bookkeeping:** a declared workflow's promise is that the same inputs produce the same steps in the same order, and a hand-edited copy makes no such promise whatever it still resembles, so it may not carry the label; `workflow_id` goes null, which the stored CHECK independently requires. **The two bounds are the ticket.** *Entitlement:* the only list a worker name may come from is the set **assembled** for this requester (T-269), and the refusal names what IS available — which is that requester's own set, so nothing about anyone else's entitlement leaks by saying it. *Scope:* a scope field is refused **by name, in every spelling** — `scope`, `projectId`, `corpus`, `as_organisation` and the rest — with the workflow validator's own reason, that there is no correct spelling of it, because the generic unknown-field message reads as an invitation to find one. That is what makes "editing cannot widen scope" structural rather than checked. **The strongest test is the removed `verify` step:** a user editing the ground-check out of their own plan is the sharpest available form of "a planner could skip it", and the check still runs (T-262) with its Step row unbound. A `verify` step naming a worker is refused with the same rule the DAG format holds. **403, not 404, for a colleague** — deliberately, and against the usual principle-4 reflex: this caller can already *read* the plan, so telling them it does not exist would be a lie they can check, and principle 4 exists to hide what someone cannot see rather than to confuse them about what they can. An unexecutable edit (no `present` stage) is a 400 carrying the executor's own reason, so the request fails rather than half a run existing. | *(Deps: T-266)*
- **T-268 — Partial failure semantics.** ✅ Built 2026-08-28. No migration (T-263 carried `completed_with_failures`). A failed step no longer stops the run: the step and its plan step are recorded failed, **its transitive dependants are skipped, and independent branches carry on**. The closure has to be transitive — skipping only the immediate dependants leaves a step two edges downstream to fail on an input that never arrived, which reports one outage twice under two different names — and a **join** downstream of a failure is skipped even where its other input survived, because a join that ran on half of what it declared would produce an answer nobody could account for. **Three run states, and the middle one is the ticket:** `failed` where nothing survived (an incomplete answer offered as a complete one is the failure this slice exists to avoid), plain `completed` where nothing failed (the third state is not the new default, asserted), and `completed_with_failures` where an answer exists *and* something did not run — reporting that as `completed` hides it, and as `failed` throws away work the user can act on. **The answer BODY reports what did not run, not only the footer.** This is absence detection applied to the system's own failures: an answer that silently omits what a failed step would have contributed reads as a complete answer and a reader has no way to know otherwise, and a footer will not do, because it is read after the answer has already been believed. The stages are named in words (*"the library search step failed"*), since this text reaches the user. **Two things sharpened rather than added.** A dependant is now `skipped` where it used to be left `pending` — `pending` reads as *"not reached yet"*, which is a claim about a run that has finished. And **a plan with no `present` stage is refused before the walk rather than after it**: that is a defect in the plan, not a failure during it, and spending a retrieval and a model call to discover it would be paying for the discovery (T-262's test was rewritten to assert the sharper behaviour). *(Review correction: the refusal itself was built in T-262's commit — its code comment places it there deliberately; this ticket's half is the rewritten test and the skipped-not-pending distinction.)* **The guarantee did not move:** where drafting fails the ground-check does not run, and that is untouched — there is no *answer* to check, and "every answer is ground-checked" says nothing about a run that produced none. **One correctness fix found by the rewrite:** the first cut treated `cited.answer === null` as "nothing survived", which would have failed every document-targeted run, where a null answer beside suggestions is the normal shape. `completed_with_failures` is an **error** for an eval case, stated rather than incidental: a case is evidence about an answer, and an answer produced while part of the plan did not run is evidence about something else. | *(Deps: T-266)*
- **T-270 — SPIKE: locator extraction.** ✅ Findings 2026-08-01 — [spike-locators.md](spikes/spike-locators.md). Research, no code. **Three findings against the running pipeline, each checked rather than reasoned about.** (1) **A chunk is not a substring of its version** — the splitter consumes the whitespace after a terminator and the packer rejoins with a single space, so a blank line between paragraphs becomes `" "` and `indexOf(chunk.content)` returns `-1` on any chunk whose interior crossed a paragraph break. Every after-the-fact offset-recovery scheme is built on that. (2) **Heading numbers are read as sentence terminators** — the split fires after the `2.` of a numbered heading, gluing the heading to the previous paragraph. A retrieval-quality bug that will be blamed on the embedding model, and it destroys the one signal (`§12.4.7`) that is the most useful locator a consenting document has. (3) **A cross-boundary quote is in no chunk *and* in no version** — the join the model saw was reconstructed by the packer and never existed in the source, so the obvious fallback ("if not in a chunk, look in the version") fails on exactly the case it was introduced for. **Per format:** docx gives **paragraph index** for the cost of not throwing it away, gives a section number only where the author *typed* it (`<w:numPr>` is resolved by Word at render time), and gives **page not at all — a docx has no pages**, so any "page 14" from a Word source is an invention. PDF gives exact page numbers and **has no ingest path whatsoever**, existing only as an output rendition. **That last row is the commercially significant one:** a real scheme's 100–500 documents are overwhelmingly PDF, page is the locator a planner actually uses, and *"a 100–500 document corpus"* and *"citations that resolve to a locator inside the source document"* cannot both be true through the docx path alone. **Recommendation for T-271: store a character-offset range on `version_chunks` and derive everything else from it** — exact, format-agnostic, and nearly free, because findings 1 and 3 are both consequences of discarding information the chunker holds at the moment it packs. The board should stop describing the gap as "locators" and start describing it as **"offsets now, pages later"**. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-271 — Locators through the ingest pipeline.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-04** (migration 0039, drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) first; data 23/23, knowledge 28/28, api 256/256, e2e 55/55, full check green). Locator capture persisted on `version_chunks` and carried to the assembled passage, plus the verbatim fallback. **The quoted passage must be findable in the source document** — a quote that cannot be found is worse than none, because it looks checkable. Built to [spike-locators.md](spikes/spike-locators.md)'s recommendation, which **closes with this ticket**: `start_offset` / `end_offset` on `version_chunks`, everything else derived. **Offsets are captured in the chunker and nowhere else, because nowhere else can:** the splitter eats the whitespace run after a terminator and the packer rejoins with one space, so a chunk whose interior crossed a paragraph break is *not a substring of its own version* and `indexOf` returns `-1` (T-270 finding 1). **The refusal is the ticket's weight, not the happy path** — a locator is emitted only when the stored span is demonstrated to still point at the passage (compared whitespace-insensitively, since that difference is the chunker's own), and otherwise the citation degrades to **version grain** rather than rendering one nobody can follow. Finding 3's cross-boundary quote resolves as the spike predicted: the span runs first-chunk-start to last-chunk-end, a real range even where the model's rendering of the join never existed. `paragraph` is derived; **page and section are absent rather than guessed** — a docx has no pages. `AssembledItem.locator` fired `wall.test.ts`'s pinned key set by design, and it is an output-side field like `chunkId`. **Two spike items are deliberately elsewhere:** the heading-number split is **T-307** (the spike argues for its own commit, because re-chunking moves embeddings and the eval seed set is the instrument), and PDF input is **T-305**. | *(Deps: T-270)*
- **T-276 — SPIKE: the authority corpus.** ✅ **Findings 2026-08-27 → [spikes/spike-authority-corpus.md](spikes/spike-authority-corpus.md).** `authorityRef` runs through contracts, the citation table and the ground-check, but there is no store — the canon half of Ask has no data, and the type admits a citation the product cannot produce. Licensing is ruled (two-tier); the spike names the v1 standard-tier instrument list with a licence basis for each, the in-force interval model, and org-tier ingest. **Four findings, and two of them change what T-277 should build:**
  **(1) The standard tier rests on one licence basis** — Crown copyright under OGL v3.0 covers the Act, the SIs, the NPSs, the Advice Notes, s.51 advice, made DCOs and Decision Letters. **Three carve-outs matter more than the list:** OGL does not cover third-party material *inside* an OGL document (an NPS figure, a reproduced BSI table), which argues for provision-grain licence attribution; **Decision Letters name people**, so T-277 introduces a store of named individuals and must register it in [personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md) *before* loading one; and the list is deliberately England-and-Wales-shaped, which closes ADR-0023's open jurisdiction question with a recommendation rather than a silence.
  **(2) 🔒 "In force" is two time axes, and the useful one cannot be computed.** The *text* interval (when this wording was the wording) is what legislation.gov.uk answers. The *applicability* rule — which cohort of applications an instrument governs — is a transitional provision, and **the instrument in force today is frequently not the one governing the scheme being asked about**. Nearly every real consenting question is of the second kind. So: store the text interval, **carry the transitional note as text beside every hit**, and compute applicability **never** — it depends on facts about the application, and appearing to know it would be the expensive kind of wrong. The unit is a **provision**, not a document: an Act is not in force, its sections are, on different dates and with different extents.
  **(3) The org tier's real problem is what *counts* as authority**, not ingest — the extractors and the loud refusal already exist (T-305/T-306). ADR-0023 §2's test is three facts (an issuing body, a version, an in-force date), and **requiring all three at ingest is the enforcement**: without it, "add to my authority shelf" becomes a way to make a firm's own method document citable, which is the laundering ADR-0026's filters exist to prevent arriving through a door nobody was watching. Plus a **licence-type attestation** — BSI and ISO licences are commonly *single-user* and the org tier makes text reachable by every participant, so the question moves from "nobody asked" to "they said corporate" for the cost of one radio button.
  **(4) 🔒 The corpus must NOT live in `version_chunks`.** That table is under RLS and every read goes through `deliverableVisibleSql`, a predicate built entirely around project material. The standard tier is deliberately outside per-tenant access resolution and the org tier is walled by a *different* rule — so putting authority chunks there means either widening the wall predicate to admit rows it was not written for, or carrying a corpus with no wall inside the table whose whole purpose is enforcing one. Separate tables **from the start**: the cost of separating later is a migration, and the cost of not separating is a wall predicate with an exception in it. Sizing does not argue otherwise — the standard tier is 100–200 documents, smaller than the pilot's own library. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-281 — `packages/lenses`: loader, validator, one Lens wired.** ✅ Built 2026-08-01. ⭐ A leaf package depending on `contracts` only; the definitions and their authoring guide already sat at [`packages/lenses/definitions/`](../../packages/lenses/definitions/) (moved 2026-07-31) and this ticket built the package around them — `package.json`, the matrix entry, the loader and the validator. **A Lens whose prohibitions try to weaken a shared-core rule fails to load**, with a message naming file, field and rule in language a domain expert can act on. **The reach guarantee landed in three independent places, none redundant:** the type-level signature test (`reach.test.ts` — `Assemble` takes one argument and `AssemblyRequest` has no room for a Lens), the dependency matrix (`contracts` only, so the package holds nothing with which to narrow a retrieval), and a **new RULE 3 in `scripts/source-rules.mjs`** — `governance`, `knowledge` and `data` may not mention a Lens at all, which is what covers `resolveAccess` and `groundedLibrary`, whose signatures are not in contracts and so cannot be pinned from a test. **The core-negation check is deliberately narrow, and says so:** it matches the shape a weakening prohibition actually takes — the suppression of a required disclosure — and its real regression guard is `definitions.test.ts`, because a validator that fires on a *good* prohibition lands on a domain expert who did nothing wrong. Writing that test found two genuine false positives in the first draft of the patterns; both are recorded in `core.ts` beside the pattern that replaced them. **Deviations:** (1) `example_exchanges` is counted as **declared, not as successfully parsed** — an author who wrote two and left a `why` off one is told about the `why`, not also told to write two they can see they have written; (2) the loader's `production` flag **defaults to true**, the fail-safe direction — a deployment that forgets it loses hot reload rather than gaining draft Lenses in front of a customer. **One Lens-validation rule is deferred, explicitly:** "`preferred_workers` naming a worker not in the registry fails to load" cannot be enforced, because there is no registry until T-269 and all four active Lenses name `corpus_retrieval`, `authority_lookup`, `extractor`, `verifier`. The field loads as unvalidated strings against a stated deferral naming T-269; every other validation rule — unknown field, missing field, enum, duplicate id, filename/id disagreement, core-negating prohibition, `active` with fewer than two `example_exchanges` — is enforced now. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-299 — The Lens through the request and into the prompt.** ✅ Built 2026-08-01. ⭐ The plumbing between a validated Lens file and an answer that reads differently — **four pieces no other ticket owns**, found in the 2026-07-31 MVP review, all four landed. (1) **Contracts + API:** `lensId` on the create-run body; an unknown id is a **400, refused before the run opens** — never a silent fall-back to a default, because a Lens the user did not get is worse than a refusal. `400` not `404`: the Lens set is not access-controlled, so naming the id leaks nothing and `not_found` would wrongly imply it might exist for someone else. (2) **The chain:** the Lens travels as *data* through `ChainInput` → the draft leaf's input → `groundedDraft`, not as a construction argument — the draft leaf is built once at app composition (`createDraftLeaf`), so a Lens bound there could never be per-request. (3) **The prompt:** `composeSystemPrompt` puts the core first, states the precedence in a sentence rather than leaving it to ordering, then appends the overlay. The core clauses are held as an **array rather than a joined string**, so composition is checkable by containment; the hostile cases are **built in code, bypassing T-281's validator**, because "cannot be authored" and "cannot succeed" are different guarantees and only the second is worth resting a claim on. `@infora/capabilities` was widened to see `@infora/lenses` — safe in one sentence, since `lenses` is itself confined to `contracts` and grants no reach. (4) **The evidence:** `plans.lens_id` / `lens_version` written from the request rather than the hardcoded null. **Acceptance is the pair, and both halves are asserted at the HTTP boundary:** the same question under two Lenses returns two visibly different answers *and* an identical source set, plus the four-Lens form that is `PERM-05`'s API-level twin. **Two deviations.** (a) The API rejects **what the registry does not carry**, rather than checking `status` itself — in production the two are identical (no drafts are in the registry) and outside production the draft is deliberately reachable, which is what AUTHORING.md's "put it in with `status: draft` and open Ask in a test environment" depends on. Implementing the literal wording would have made the authoring guide's own workflow impossible. (b) `fakeRouter` gained a **function form** taking the system prompt, because a router that ignores its prompt can prove neither half of the acceptance. | *(Deps: T-281)*
- **T-282 — The four active Lenses and the draft.** ✅ Built 2026-08-01. Planning & Environmental, Engineer, Project Manager, Communications, plus the deliberately-incomplete Commercial. The files were authored and ready; this ticket made a Lens something a *case* can run under, and turned the worked exchanges into the register guard. **The runner** now resolves `lens:` against the harness's own registry — loaded with production semantics, so a case cannot reach the draft `commercial`, and an unavailable id is an `error` **naming the ids that are available** rather than an opaque `400`. **The report gained §4.1's per-Lens table**, deferred at T-257 for want of anything to key on: a Lens whose register cases regress while another's improve is exactly the result an aggregate would hide, and the Lens layer's whole claim is that the four differ. **`LENS-01`–`LENS-04`** are the guard itself — *the same question, the same corpus, the same acting user, four Lenses* — because one Lens case in isolation proves only that *a* Lens applied. ✅ **The grader choice is ruled and recorded** in [evals/README.md](../../evals/README.md): **human review for the MVP.** It was not really a fork — an independent family needs a second provider (behind the infra gate) *and* a family-aware router (T-284/T-286), so "configure one" was not available to this ticket, and shipping it as a decision would have been shipping one nobody could act on. The four cases therefore return **`ungraded`** and block the gate, by design. **What stays machine-checked meanwhile:** each case carries a plain substring beside its `~claim` asserting the Lens **reached the prompt at all**, because a silently-dropped Lens and an ungradeable one would otherwise produce the same verdict, and they are very different failures. **Deviation, and it belongs to the fixture not the Lenses:** only four of the twelve worked exchanges are expressible against `hollowfield-reservoir`, which is two documents sized for a permission case's access graph. The rest ask about noise chapters, Rochdale envelopes and Deadline 3. That is [v1.md](v1.md)'s own *"a few hundred fixture documents, not five"* obligation, and it is a fixture-sizing ticket rather than anything the Lens layer can fix. **One thing to watch:** the harness's fake chat now prefixes the reader named in the system prompt — but **only when a Lens is present**, so a no-Lens run returns the original reply byte for byte and T-260's smoke-result pin stays valid. | *(Deps: T-299)*
- **T-283 — Lens switching, persistence, logging.** ✅ Built 2026-08-01. **The MVP's last Wave-4 ticket.** Switching re-renders the next answer only; history keeps the Lens that produced it. Default is config, not code — `DEFAULT_LENS_ID`, reported by the new **`GET /lenses`**, which is deliberately *not* project-scoped and *not* access-resolved: the Lens set is a property of the deployment and identical for every requester, because a list that differed by who asked would make a Lens a reach control. It carries **summaries only** — prohibitions and worked exchanges are prompt material and do not leave the server. Persistence is **per run, in the plan record** T-299 writes — no new column and no conversation-level Lens. The picker rides [ask.tsx](../../apps/web/src/screens/ask.tsx) as a chip; the full composer treatment is T-292 and is post-MVP. **Three decisions worth reading.** (1) A misconfigured `DEFAULT_LENS_ID` reports **null**, not the typo — preselecting an id the run endpoint would then refuse is a worse failure than preselecting nothing. (2) The Lens is captured **at send time**, so switching mid-flight cannot relabel an answer already being produced. (3) A **reopened** conversation shows no Lens per answer rather than guessing: the Lens lives on the plan and the plan read API is T-261, so `null` means *not known*, and inventing the picker's current value would be a fabrication about a past answer. **The e2e earned its place immediately:** `/lenses` was missing from the vite proxy allowlist, which does not error — it returns `index.html`, which parses as "no Lenses" and renders **no chip at all**. A silent, plausible-looking nothing that no unit test could see, because they call the API directly. **Also fixed, and unrelated:** `smoke.spec.ts` asserted the seeded consultant has one Participant, stale since T-298 gave her a second scheme for the conflict register. | *(Deps: T-282)*

- **T-272 — `corpus_retrieval`: coverage note, chunk ids, structured output.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (no migration; knowledge 48/48, capabilities 75/75, full check green). 🔒 *Inputs:* `query`, `classification_terms?` (the ADR-0045 ontology pre-filter), `doc_types?`, `include_superseded=false`, `max_passages=20`. *Outputs:* `passages[]` — chunk_id, version_id, document_reference, document_title, version_reference, `superseded`, locator {page?, para?, section?}, text, relevance — plus `coverage_note`. **Substrate exists:** this is `groundedLibrary` reached through the assembly gateway, which already applies project, in-library, live-state, current-version, pinned-model and deliverable-visibility as SQL pre-filters in one query. The worker adds structure around it, **not a new path to the store**. The `coverage_note` states what corpus slice was searched, how many candidates the pre-filter admitted, and which requested terms found nothing — the mechanism behind absence detection. **The cache key is `query + corpus_version + scope_hash`**, where `corpus_version` must change when any admitted document changes and `scope_hash` is computed from the resolved `EntitledSlice`, never from the request; a cache without scope in the key is a permission bypass with extra steps. | *(Deps: T-269, T-253)*
  🔒 **The two inputs the entry names and this build does NOT have are `classification_terms` and `doc_types`, and their absence is the ticket's most load-bearing decision.** `Q-028` — *who selects the retrieval scope* — is open, and **its own text rules that leaving the lever unwired is the safe state, not a bug.** The asymmetry is why: a wrongly-scoped question grounds a **confident, fully-cited answer on a partial library**, where every citation resolves and neither the ground-check nor the reader can see what was excluded. **Declaring the parameter and ignoring it would be strictly worse than omitting it**, because `inputSchema` is what the model is *told* it can do — a lever that looks connected is used. The narrowing is still reachable the safe way: an orchestrator may hand this worker an **already-attenuated assembler** (T-248), which is a scope the worker was *given* rather than one it *chose*. Pinned two ways — the declaration's key set, and a compile-time test that `CorpusRetrievalInput` has no `scope`, `docTypes` or `classificationTermIds`.
  🔒 **The coverage note is the mechanism behind absence detection, and the test that carries it runs two retrievals with identical results.** One searched 4,000 admitted passages and matched nothing; the other searched an empty corpus. **The `passages` arrays are equal and the notes are not** — because *"we searched and found nothing"* is a finding and *"there was nothing to search"* is a configuration problem, and a bare `[]` is both. Three facts: the slice searched (in words — the deliverables this requester can see, in their current live revisions, under the pinned embedding model), how many candidates the access-and-state pre-filter admitted **before ranking**, and **which named documents the corpus does not have** — the sharpest absence, because the asker believed the document was there.
  **`candidates` is counted inside the same transaction and against the same `liveLibraryFilter` the two arms use.** A count taken outside the project scope would be a different claim wearing the same name — it would describe the table rather than the corpus this run could see, and under RLS it would return nothing at all.
  **Where a coverage fact is ABSENT, the note says so rather than asserting zero.** `AssemblyCoverage` is optional on `AssembledInput`, and an assembly that recorded none produces *"how much of it was admitted was not recorded for this run"* — never *"0 passages"*. That is T-254's null-not-zero rule applied to a count instead of a cost, and it is the same distinction the whole ticket turns on.
  **The structured output names the document rather than only its id.** `document_reference`, `document_title`, `version_reference` and `superseded` ride a new **`descriptor`** annotation on `AssembledItem`, and `relevance` rides beside it. Both are OUTPUT-side, on rows the pre-filter had already returned — carrying no predicate and no id a caller can pass back in — so they can no more widen a slice than `chunkId` or `locator` can, and **`wall.test.ts`'s pinned key set firing was the review**, on T-271's and T-308's precedent. The columns are selected in the SAME query as the passage: a second lookup to decorate results would be a second path to the store and would let the description drift from what was retrieved.
  **Two nulls that are not missing data.** `documentTitle` is null for **reference material**, which has no work item — T-304's absence-is-the-marker, arriving here as a left join. And `relevance` is null on the **lexical arm**: a passage matched on its document's own reference was not ranked at all, and a zero there would read as *"ranked, and badly"*.
  **`superseded` is built and is false for everything this build returns**, because live record state and current version are pre-filter clauses. It exists now rather than at T-273 for one reason: a flag that appeared *with* the opt-in would leave every consumer written against a world in which superseded material could not arrive.
  ⚠ **The cache is NOT built, and the entry's cache-key sentence stands as the specification for whoever builds it.** `cacheable: true` on the declaration is a property of the worker — that it *may* be cached — not a claim that a cache exists. Two things were missing rather than skipped: `corpus_version` needs a probe that changes when any admitted document changes, and there is none; and a per-process cache is `T-314`'s problem restated (correct on one instance, silently wrong on N). The key's own rule is recorded in the file and unchanged: **`scope_hash` from the resolved `EntitledSlice`, never from the request** — a cache without scope in the key is a permission bypass with extra steps.

- **T-280 — `document_builder`.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (no migration; capabilities 82/82, orchestration 59/59, full check green). 🔒 *Inputs:* `template_id`, `brief`, `sources: {version_ids}` — **explicit, never "whatever you find"**, because the builder does not retrieve; the orchestrator hands it ids it got from `corpus_retrieval`, which keeps label computation tractable and the manifest honest — and `destination`. *Outputs:* `document_id`, `manifest[]` (version_id, document_reference, version_reference, locator, used_for), `label {computed_label, most_restrictive_input, destination_label}`, `withheld[]`. **Partly exists:** the chain's `document` mode already drafts into a sandbox document via suggestions, grounded-only, with unsourced claims withheld; new are the template, the manifest and the label. The `label` output is not decoration — it is the evidence that propagation happened. Draft into a template with a source manifest and the computed label enforced against the destination. `sources` is explicit — the builder does not retrieve, which keeps the label computation tractable and the manifest honest. | *(Deps: T-249, T-269)*
  **The declaration is in `capabilities` and the implementation is in `orchestration`, because this worker WRITES.** `capabilities` holds no `Db` by design, and the document row plus the two live access facts the label rests on all need one. It is the same split `createDraftLeaf` already makes, and the alternative — a `Db` in `capabilities` — would have put a store handle in the package whose whole safety property is not having one.
  🔒 **The label is computed BEFORE the model runs, and that ordering is a decision.** A refusal after drafting has already spent the money, and the refusal does not change with the words produced. So a destination broader than the sources returns `documentId: null`, both labels named and **nothing drafted at all** — asserted by a test that spies on the router and finds it was never called.
  🔒 **The label is computed over the sources actually REACHED, not the ids requested.** A label over material the run never saw would describe a document that does not exist. `mostRestrictiveInput` names the single source that *set* the computed label, because *"this draws on material restricted to three named people"* is only actionable if you can be told **which** material — a refusal a user cannot act on reads as a broken system rather than a careful one.
  **The manifest is built from the SURVIVING claims, not from the sources handed in.** *"What this document rests on"* and *"what was offered to it"* are different sets and only the first is a manifest. `usedFor` is the template section the sentence landed under, one entry per (source, section) — the same document used in two sections is two facts.
  ⚠ **Resolving the section had to happen on the model's RAW TEXT, and finding that out changed the shape of the code.** `parseClaims` splits on `[S#]` markers rather than on lines, so a heading and the sentence after it arrive as **one claim** — a manifest built from claims alone had no sections to name, and the first implementation silently collapsed three sections into two. Headings are now matched as lines, before parsing, case-insensitively and ignoring markdown hashes. **Headings are structure, not claims:** they are the template's own words rather than the model's, so putting them through the ground-check would be checking the template against the corpus, and they would be withheld for having no source.
  **A section that survived nothing is omitted rather than left as an empty heading.** An empty section under a heading reads as *"the record says nothing here"*, which is a claim this run has not made.
  **The templates are content, on the extraction schemas' exact terms**, with **one extra rule that is why they are a different kind of file: a template supplies no sources.** A schema carries a `retrieval_hint` because it READS and must find what to read; a template WRITES, and one able to name its own corpus would be a write path that chose what it saw — the propagation guarantee undone from the inside. The validator refuses `sources`, `retrieval_hint`, `query` and `scope` by name.
  **Two shipped templates**, and their `guidance` says what belongs in a section and never what to conclude. A template that told the model what to find would make every document produced from it agree with the template rather than with the sources.
  ⚠ **`unreachableSources` is an output the entry does not name, and it is deliberate.** T-274's rule applied here: a source the caller named and the gateway did not return is either out of reach or matched nothing, and both are facts the caller asked for. Dropping it silently would leave a manifest that looks complete.
  **The builder reaches the corpus only through the assembly gateway** and narrows to the named ids afterwards — the extractor's shape, for the extractor's reason. That is not "retrieving": it does not *choose* its sources, it is *given* them, which is exactly what keeps the label computation tractable.
  ⚠ **Not wired into a running plan, on T-269's and T-274's standing position** — nothing yet executes an arbitrary worker as a step. **Cost attribution is absent for the same reason**: a cost is recorded on a Step row, and the row is opened by the executor. `cacheable: false` on the declaration is not a stub — a write is never served from a cache, because the destination's audience is a live access fact and a cached label is a cached access decision.

- **T-273 — `include_superseded` with mandatory flagging.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (no migration; knowledge 51/51, capabilities 79/79, orchestration 52/52, full check green). Default exclusion unchanged. A superseded source carries a flag **in the prose at the point of use**, not only in the manifest — easy to render in the footer and easy to forget where it matters. | *(Deps: T-272)*
  🔒 **The opt-in rides CONSTRUCTION, not the request, and that is the ticket's one real design decision.** `include_superseded` genuinely *widens* what retrieval returns, and `AssemblyRequest`'s whole guarantee — pinned by `wall.test.ts` — is that **no parameter on the call widens anything**. A request field would have been the first, and the next one would not have needed an argument. So it takes **T-248's shape read in the other direction**: the assembler is *built* to admit superseded material (`createAssembler(deps, narrowing?, inclusion?)`), and the worker is constructed with **two gateways** and chooses between capabilities the composition granted. `queryShape` is still `'text' | 'mode'`, and a test asserts that it still is.
  **What is relaxed is record state and nothing else, and the assertion says so rather than the comment.** Exactly two clauses move — `state = 'live'` becomes `state in ('live','superseded')`, and `is_current` is dropped. **`withdrawn` and `rejected` do not move**: they are not superseded and ADR-0013 does not treat them alike. Every access clause — project, deliverable visibility, the attenuation, the grounding code — is untouched, and the wall suite now runs its cross-organisation negative **through the widened assembler** and still gets nothing.
  🔒 **The flag is CODE in the cite leaf, which is the only way "mandatory" is a property rather than a hope.** The model is never asked to remember it. The claim's own source is looked up in what the run retrieved, and a claim resting on a superseded passage has the mark inserted into its text — **before the terminal punctuation**, so the sentence still reads as a sentence. That placement matters twice over: it is *in the prose at the point of use*, which is the ticket's own words, and because it is inside the claim text it **travels into the Suggestion, into the document, and into the citation's own span**. A flag added at render time would be lost the moment the answer was written anywhere, which is precisely the "easy to render in the footer and easy to forget where it matters" failure.
  **The wording composes with the Document Status slice rather than inventing a third name.** T-388's badge says *superseded*; T-391's attached-source marker says *superseded — <reason>*; this says **"(from a superseded document)"**.
