A reader who has learned the badge and the marker must not have to learn a third vocabulary for one state. The mark is also **idempotent** and is left off a current source entirely — a mark on every sentence makes the mark invisible, which is T-391's "a grounding deliverable gets no marker at all" applied to prose.
  **The coverage note carries the half the prose cannot.** The point-of-use flag can only appear where superseded material was *used*; the **default exclusion is invisible by construction**, so the note states it — *"Superseded documents were excluded, as they are by default"* — and, when they were included, how many of the returned passages are from one. **A deployment that constructed no widened gateway says so** rather than returning the default silently, because a silent default reads as *"there are no superseded sources"*, which is a different and false claim.
  **`descriptor.superseded`, built at T-272 and false for everything, is now the field that can be true** — which is why it was built one ticket early: every consumer was already written against a world where superseded material could arrive.

- **T-274 — `extractor` and the named schemas.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (no migration; capabilities 69/69, full check green). *Inputs:* `schema_name` (commitments | consultee_responses | mitigation_measures | exa_questions | deadlines | parameters), `scope` as `{version_ids}` or `{query}`, `strict=true`. *Outputs:* `records[]` each with source + locator, `failures[]` (reason, source, locator, partial_record), `extraction_note`. Structured output only — no narrative. The named schemas are **versioned domain content beside the Lens files**, owned by the same specialists: adding a schema is a content change and the extractor's code does not change. `strict` defaults true and `failures` is a first-class output — **a silently coerced commitment is worse than no record**, because the whole value of a commitments register is that it is complete and checkable; failures feed absence detection. Non-negotiable 1 applies to structured output exactly as to prose: **every record carries source and locator**. | *(Deps: T-269)*
  🔒 **"Adding a schema is a content change and the extractor's code does not change" is the whole design, and it is what the file layout is for.** Six YAML files in `packages/capabilities/schemas/` with an `AUTHORING.md`, read and validated at startup on the Lens loader's exact terms — production reads once and the set is immutable for the process lifetime, non-production re-reads so an author sees the effect without a restart, and the `production` flag **defaults to true**, the fail-safe direction. A domain specialist adds `programme_risks.yaml` and the worker extracts against it: no registry entry, no code change, no ticket. A test proves exactly that, by loading a directory containing a schema nobody wrote code for.
  ⚠ **Placement deviation, stated rather than discovered.** The entry says the schemas are *"beside the Lens files"*. They are **not** in `packages/lenses` — that package's name and its whole documented purpose are the Lens, and putting a second kind of content in it would make the name a lie for the sake of a literal reading. They sit beside the worker that reads them, on the same *terms* as the Lens files, which is what the sentence is about: domain content, versioned in the repo, authored by the same specialists, validated at load, extended without a code change.
  **Validation failures are build failures, and every message names the file, the field and the rule.** Three rules are not stylistic. **The filename must equal the `name`** — the name is the address a caller asks for, and a disagreement means two names for one schema with one of them wrong. **`source` and `locator` are reserved field names and a schema declaring either is refused** — the extractor attaches them from the passage a row came from, so a schema *cannot forget them and cannot forge them*; this is non-negotiable 1 made unauthorable rather than merely required. **At least one field must be `required`** — a schema no row can fail cannot report absence, and absence detection is what a register is for.
  🔒 **`failures` is the output that carries the ticket, and nothing is coerced into shape.** A row missing a required value comes back as a failure with the **partial record** and a reason in words, because the difference between *"the model found nothing"* and *"the model found a commitment with no date"* is the difference between a gap in the corpus and a gap in the document — and only one of those is anybody's to fix. `strict` defaults true; `strict: false` permits exactly one coercion, a numeric string to a number, and **never** invents a missing required value or drops one it cannot read, since both produce a row that conforms and lies. **A date is refused rather than normalised** — `03/04/2026` is two different days depending on who wrote it.
  **A row citing a passage the extraction never saw is refused, in code.** The model returns a `[S#]` marker per row; a marker that does not resolve to a passage this run actually admitted produces a failure, not a record. That is non-negotiable 1 enforced at the boundary rather than asked of the model, and it is the same technique the draft leaf's claim markers use.
  **An unreadable answer is a failure, never an empty register.** They look identical downstream and mean opposite things — "there are no commitments in this corpus" and "the model wrote prose" cannot be allowed to render the same.
  ⚠ **The scope constraint the ticket's shape implies, made explicit: the extractor does not read documents.** It reaches the corpus **only through the assembly gateway**, on `corpus_retrieval`'s terms — a worker with a second path to the store bypasses the wall, which is the one thing a worker may never have. A `{query}` scope is that question; a **`{version_ids}` scope searches on the schema's own `retrieval_hint` and is narrowed to the named versions afterwards**, and a named document that produced no passage comes back as a **failure**, not a silence: it is either out of reach or nothing in it matched, and the caller asked about it. `extraction_note` therefore reports what was *admitted and read*, not how many rows were found — a count of a list somebody can count is not a coverage statement.
  **`extract` is now a real caller of T-284's task-class routing** — the first, and the reason the class exists: high volume, low judgement, verifiable against the schema, and a `mid` tier rather than a frontier one (the Wave 3 table's own row).
  **Two existing tests were updated for a changed fact, not a changed claim.** *"The registry holds only workers that are BUILT"* and *"the classifier is handed the ASSEMBLED worker set"* both enumerated one worker; the set is now two. The property each protects is untouched, and `extractor` joined `BUILT_WORKERS` at the moment it acquired an implementation, not before.
  ⚠ **Not wired into a running plan, deliberately, and on T-269's precedent.** `corpus_retrieval` has been built and unreachable-as-a-step since T-269 — the chain maps `search_corpus` to the retrieve leaf, and nothing yet executes an arbitrary worker step. This ticket builds the worker and its schemas; the executor that runs one is not its to invent. Consequently the schema registry is **not loaded at app composition** either — the fail-fast property it would buy is already held by the definitions suite in `pnpm run check`, and a boot load with no consumer would be a second place to keep in step. *(Review note: the schemas ride a new runtime dependency, `yaml@^2.8.0` in `packages/capabilities` — unmentioned here; in-matrix and consistent with the evals precedent, recorded for completeness.)*

*Wave 5 design reference — task-class routing.* ➜ **Folded 2026-08-28 into [component-1-foundation.md](../architecture/components/component-1-foundation.md)**, on T-285, when T-284 and T-285 landed and the second axis became behaviour the code has. The two-axis order, the task-class table, the configuration shape and the fallback chain's rules are all in that section; the fine-tune corollary travelled with them. The block was folded from *here* rather than from the board because it travelled into the history with the Slice Ask records when the ticket-grain move rule came in on 2026-08-28. **T-286's verify-independence constraint did not fold** — it is → beyond V1 and the code does not have it.

*Wave 5 — model routing (T-284–T-286).*

- **T-284 — Task-class routing.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (no migration; model 23/23, full check green). `Router.chat(task, …)` accepts a task argument and currently ignores it — the seam exists, the routing does not. **Tier conformance applies before task selection**, unchanged; the ordering is easy to invert when adding the second axis. | *(Deps: T-263)*
  **As built: the ordering is enforced by the shape of the code, not by a comment saying which comes first.** `selectRoute` did both jobs in one function — filter, then take `[0]` — so "tier before task" was true by there being no task step to get wrong. The filter is now `conformingRoutes` in [tiers.ts](../../packages/model/src/tiers.ts) and the ranking is `routesForTask` in a **separate file** ([tasks.ts](../../packages/model/src/tasks.ts)) that takes no policy, no classification and no attributes — so the second axis has nothing with which to re-open the first. Inverting the two would require handing task selection a `TierPolicy`, which is a reviewable one-line diff rather than a subtle reordering. `selectRoute` survives as the no-task form and is what the **embedding** path still uses: an embedding call has no task axis, and giving it one would have been inventing a second vocabulary to keep the signatures symmetrical.
  🔒 **Two layers — activity → tier → route — and the reason is where the judgement lives.** A caller names an ACTIVITY (`draft`); `TASK_TIERS` says what class of model that activity wants; a route declares which tiers the deployment configured it for. The alternative — callers naming a model tier — scatters the model-capability judgement over every call site, so re-tiering an activity becomes a sweep instead of a line. The tier vocabulary is contracts' existing **`WorkerModelTier`** (`triage | mid | frontier`), which the Wave 3 table already assigns to every worker: minting a second name for the same three values is how a system ends up with two answers to *"what class of model does this want"*.
  **The whole task-class table is in code, including classes with no caller — and this is the one place the "declare only what is built" rule is deliberately not applied.** The two things are not alike. A declared **worker** is a capability the *model* is told it can call, so declaring an unbuilt one makes the model call something that does not exist (T-269's own reasoning). A **task class** is a key a *deployment* configures routes against; it reaches no model and no user. Publishing half the table would mean a deployment cannot pre-configure the route a capability will want on the day it lands, and the table is the design's own vocabulary rather than this ticket's invention. `verify` is present with its tier and **without T-286's independence constraint**, which is correct: that constraint is a dispatch-time rule about a particular run's producing family, not a property of the class, and T-286 is → beyond V1.
  ⚠ **`draft` is still the only call site, and the structure agent was left on it rather than reclassified.** [structure-agent.ts](../../apps/api/src/structure-agent.ts) proposes a folder structure from an ask — judgement-heavy, user-visible, frontier-tier, and not any of the table's nine descriptions. Forcing it into `orchestrate` ("classification, intent, workflow selection") would have made the class name a lie to save a comment; it routes correctly as `draft` because both are frontier. The remaining classes arrive with their capabilities — `extract` at T-274, `triage` when retrieval filtering becomes a model call.
  **Nothing about the running deployment changed, by construction.** A route with no `serves` declaration serves every task, and every deployment and every test still passes a bare adapter, so the one-endpoint configuration behaves exactly as before — asserted by a test that runs three task classes through an undeclared route and gets the same model each time. `routesForTask` **ranks rather than filters**, returning the whole conforming set with the tier's declared routes first: a task whose tier no route serves still runs, because an optimisation that can make a call impossible has stopped being one. That ordered list is also what T-285 walks as the fallback chain, which is why it returns a list rather than a choice.
  **One new refusal:** a `Router` constructed with an empty route array throws immediately, and deliberately **not** as `SecurityPolicyError` — an empty chain is a misconfiguration and a non-conforming route is a policy refusal, and an operator reading the error needs to know which of those two problems they have.
  **`@infora/model` gained `@infora/contracts`** for `WorkerModelTier`. The matrix already allowed it (`'@infora/model': ['@infora/contracts']`); no dependency rule was widened.

- **T-285 — Fallback chains.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (no migration; model 33/33, orchestration 49/49, api 529/529, full check green). Per tier, documented, for provider outage or rate limiting. A fallback is attempted only if it also conforms to the deployment tier; **availability is never traded for conformance** — already the router's behaviour, and adding fallbacks must not weaken it. An exhausted chain fails the step with a stated reason and the run continues per T-268. Every attempt, including failures, writes a Step audit row with egress facts, so a fallback that fired is visible in the record. | *(Deps: T-284)*
  🔒 **"Availability is never traded for conformance" is true by there being nothing to trade with.** The chain is `routesForTask` over the set `conformingRoutes` already returned, so every link in it is a route that conforms to the deployment tier *by construction* — the walk has no access to a wider set and no branch that reaches for one. That matters because a fallback path is written for the bad day, and the bad day is exactly when "just this once, use the US endpoint" gets added. The test that proves it puts a **working non-conforming route second in the declared list** and asserts the chain exhausts without calling it.
  🔒 **A route that ANSWERED is never retried, and this is the half most likely to be got wrong.** A fallback exists for a route being *unavailable* — an outage, a rate limit, a timeout. A model that **refused**, a malformed request, a response with no text: those are answers, and retrying them on the next model is **shopping for a model that complies**. It would turn a safety behaviour into a latency problem and it would succeed *silently*. So `isRouteUnavailable` is a deliberate **allow-list** — transient HTTP statuses and transport error codes, read structurally rather than by instanceof-ing one vendor's SDK classes — and everything unrecognised is treated as an answer. The default direction of an unknown error is therefore *stop*, which is the direction that cannot launder a refusal.
  **Every attempt reaches the audit trail, as a child Step row.** A route that was tried **egressed** — the data left — so a record naming only the endpoint that eventually answered has omitted an egress event, which is precisely the fact ADR-0037 §6 exists to make provable per call. Failed attempts are written under the draft step via `parent_step_id`, which the append-only tree already models. **The successful attempt is not duplicated:** it *is* the draft step, whose egress columns already name it, and writing it twice would make every one-route call read as two model calls in every cost report. The rows are written **after** the fact rather than as each attempt starts, because a Step row is opened and finished exactly once (the T-008 trigger) and an attempt's outcome is not known until it is over.
  ⚠ **The writing had to happen in `orchestration`, not `capabilities`, and that is a layering fact rather than a preference.** `@infora/capabilities` holds no `Db` by design, so `groundedDraft` carries the attempts through untouched and `createDraftLeaf` — which has `ctx.db` — writes them. The leaf therefore has a `try/catch` it did not have before: an **exhausted** chain is the case where the record of what was tried is worth most, so the attempts are written before the error is re-thrown into T-268's failed-step handling. The router attaches them to whatever the last route threw rather than wrapping it, so a model refusal still surfaces as a refusal rather than as a routing failure; `attemptsOf` is how the leaf reads them back without every call site knowing that.
  **The configuration is `MODEL_CHAT_ROUTES`, and the one decision inside it is that nothing is inherited.** Each route declares its own credential (`apiKeyEnv` — a second procurement is a second key), its own endpoint and **its own four egress attributes**; none falls back to the `MODEL_*` deployment defaults, because inheritance is how a second procurement quietly adopts the first one's compliance claims — ADR-0037 §3's unattributed default arriving through a convenience. `endpoint` is **both** the audited egress fact and the client's base URL, deliberately: two fields would let a deployment record a host the call never touched, and an egress record naming the wrong host is worse than none. Parsed at boot and refusing on a typo, for T-254's reason — a malformed route silently never conforms, and the symptom would be a deployment failing closed on every call with no clue why.
  **The design block's `defaults {fallback_attempts, timeout_ms}` are both built**, as `MODEL_FALLBACK_ATTEMPTS` and `MODEL_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_MS`. The timeout is real rather than a race: the router's `AbortSignal` is **passed to the adapter** as well as raced, so a provider client that supports cancellation actually stops instead of running on and being billed behind an answer nobody is waiting for. That widened `ChatRequest` by one router-set field and `AnthropicLike` by an optional options argument.
  ⚠ **Deviation from the block's configuration shape, stated rather than discovered.** The design writes the table as *one entry per task class* with `primary {family, model}` and `fallback[]`. What was built keys the chain on the **route** — an ordered list, each route naming the tiers it serves — because task→tier is *design* (the table, now in the component doc) and route→tier is what a firm actually *procures*. A per-task-class object would repeat the same two endpoints nine times and, worse, would let a deployment silently disagree with the design table about what tier `triage` wants. `family` is not modelled at all: its only consumer is T-286's independence constraint, which is → beyond V1.
  **Nothing changed for a one-route deployment**, which is every deployment today: `MODEL_CHAT_ROUTES` unset means the single route the `MODEL_*` variables describe, the chain is one long, and `attempts` comes back with one entry. It is populated even then, deliberately — *"no fallback fired"* and *"the field was not written"* must not read the same to whoever writes the audit rows.
  ➜ **The Wave 5 design reference block folded into [component-1-foundation.md](../architecture/components/component-1-foundation.md)** in this commit, and the fold-in register row is closed. T-286 is the wave's third ticket and is → beyond V1, so the fold carries the table and the chain's rules and **not** the independence constraint — folding behaviour the code does not have is the thing the register exists to prevent.

*Wave 8 — interface (T-292–T-296).* The wave's design reference stays on the board; only this ticket has landed.

- **T-293 — The progress rail.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (no migration; ui 37/37, full check green). Driven by plan step states, **never a client-side timer** — a timer-driven rail looks right most of the time, which is what makes it a trust problem rather than a bug. A stage that did not run is never shown as having run. | *(Deps: T-268)*
  🔒 **The signature is where the ticket is won: `steps` is `PlanStep[] | null`, and `null` is not an empty rail.** A run in flight has no readable plan — `POST /runs` returns on completion — so the honest rendering of *"we are waiting"* is a **stated absence of record**, not the first stage lit up. A rail that lit `Understanding your question` on send would be a client-side timer with the timer hidden, and it would be right often enough that nobody would look. The empty-plan case renders differently again: *"this run's plan declared no steps"* is a fact about a plan, and *"no plan has been recorded yet"* is the absence of one.
  **All four of the design reference's rules are kept structurally rather than by care.** (1) A stage that did not run is never shown as having run — state is read from `step.state` and from nothing else, and `pending` renders *not started* in words. (2) A conditional stage that was not needed is absent — the rail renders the **plan's** steps, so a stage the plan never declared has no row at all, while one the walk skipped renders as skipped. (3) Failed and skipped show as failed and skipped, in those words; there is no state that renders as a tick without being complete. (4) Transitions come from the plan's step states, and the component holds **no state, no effect and no clock**.
  **That last one is pinned by a guard rather than a rendering test**, in this repo's own idiom: a test reads `progress-rail.tsx` and fails if it contains `setInterval`, `setTimeout`, `requestAnimationFrame` or `Date.now`. A timer would break the rail's whole claim *silently* and would still look right, which is precisely the class of defect a rendering assertion cannot see.
  **The stage vocabulary is a `Record` over the closed `PlanStage` union**, so a stage added to `PLAN_STAGES` without a user-facing phrase is a **compile error** — where a lookup with a fallback would put a raw enum value, or a blank line, on the one surface whose job is saying what happened. Ordering is off `ordinal`, not array position: the rail must not reorder what the plan declared.
  **In the kit, not beside its caller**, for the AgentReceipt reason — the Wave 8 layout puts a rail on the left of Ask and the same rail will serve the editor's chat; a component written next to the first caller becomes that caller's.
  **The wiring is one read, after the fact.** `GET /runs/:runId/plan` (T-261) gained a client method, and Ask calls it **after** the run reports, clearing the rail to `null` on send so the previous answer's stages cannot stand and read as this run's progress. A reopened conversation loads the **last** run's plan — one read, not one per run in the history. The plan is producer-private and inherits the run's read scope exactly, so a refusal is an ordinary outcome and the rail stays honest by staying empty rather than by inventing stages.
  ⚠ **What is NOT built, so it is not mistaken for done.** There is no live progress: the run is synchronous, so the rail is a post-hoc rendering of what ran, and it says so while waiting. Streaming is the Wave 8 block's own named non-scope and the rail is its natural home when it arrives. The rest of the Wave 8 layout — the composer chips (T-292), the completion footer (T-294) and four-register rendering (T-296) — is untouched.
  📸 **No walkthrough capture was needed and none was run.** The rail sits on the Ask surface, and no photographed beat is an Ask screen — the 39 shots run schema → plan → sandbox → review → library, and Ask appears in none of them. *(Review note: this ticket also added `e2e/tests/progress-rail.spec.ts`, unmentioned here — and the omission mattered: the new spec visits Ask, which lazily creates the default `Sandbox` card, and turned a latent strict-mode fragility into a clean-seed e2e failure. The review hardened all seven selector sites and minted T-394 for the substrate fix.)*

- **T-292 — Composer chips.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-29.** Lens, Model, Data sources, Tools, Context. The Lens picker states in the picker that a Lens does not change what you can see. The Model chip lists only tier-conforming routes. **The Data sources chip warns when zero sources are in scope**, and refinement narrows only, intersected server-side. | *(Deps: T-283, T-284)*
  ⚖ **Four chips, and the Model chip deliberately not built — it is `Q-021`, and a ticket may not rule a question.** The entry asks the Model chip to *"list only tier-conforming routes"*, and the Wave 8 block adds a per-conversation pin. A chip that lists routes for the user to choose from **is** the user-facing model picker `Q-021` holds open, so building it would have answered an open question by shipping it, which is exactly what the Q/T boundary forbids. The display-only escape was considered and does not survive either: T-284 routes **per task class**, so a single model name in the composer would be a prediction about a run that has not happened, and *which* route actually served a step is on the Step row and belongs in **T-294's completion footer**, where it is a fact rather than a forecast. The chip therefore stays the placeholder T-100 left, with its tooltip retargeted from the Router seam to `Q-021` so whoever picks it up finds the ruling it waits on. `Q-021`'s Blocks field now names this half.
  **The Data sources chip is the ticket, and its warning state is why it exists.** A grounded answer over an empty scope is the single most misleading state Ask can be in: the answer arrives, it is fluent, and nothing on the screen says it rested on nothing. So zero renders as *"No sources in scope"* in a warning tone — `Chip` gained a `tone` for this one statement, because the disabled grey is what would make it invisible — and the zero case is a **statement, not a menu**: there is nothing to refine, and a dropdown over an empty list reads as a loading failure rather than a fact.
  🔒 **It could not be built from the library list, and finding that out is half the ticket.** The two look like the same question and are not: since the ADR-0011 rider a **live deliverable whose acceptance code does not ground** is on the library list and out of the AI's reach, and a document with **no chunks under the deployment's pinned embedding model** is indexed for nobody. `GET /projects/:id/grounding-scope` therefore runs `liveLibraryFilter` itself — the same predicate **both arms of the gateway call** use — so the chip cannot name a document the answer could not have used, and cannot omit one it could: the two statements are one piece of SQL. Both failure modes carry a test, and the unindexed one asserts the document **is** on the library list first, so the test states the divergence rather than assuming it.
  ⚠ **`groundingSources` declares its project scope, and the bug it would otherwise have shipped is the interesting one.** `version_chunks` is under row-level security and the policy fails **closed** (T-247), so an unscoped read returns nothing — which would have rendered as *"No sources in scope"* for every user on every project. The warning state would have been firing on the policy rather than on the corpus: the one wrong answer this chip must never give, arriving as a green build. Caught by the first run of the new suite.
  **Refinement narrows through T-248 and cannot widen.** `sourceContainerIds` is the one request field in this API that names documents, and it is admissible beside principle 2 because the ids are handed to `attenuate` and intersected **into** the grounded pre-filter's own `and()` rather than applied around it — so a narrowing is never evaluated on rows the wall already excluded. **Nothing validates the ids, deliberately:** checking them would mean answering *"does this container exist"*, which deny-as-404 exists to refuse, and it is unnecessary because an unreachable id **removes** exactly as a reachable one does. A test proves it — a run narrowed to another organisation's unshared deliverable retrieves nothing rather than reaching it.
  **The narrowed retrieve leaf is a factory, not a mutable field**, for the reason T-248 put the narrowing in the constructor: `attenuate` is monotonic and `createAssembler`'s narrowing is a construction argument, so there is no route from the narrowed assembler back to the wider one and a later step cannot quietly undo the user's refinement. The refinement is captured **at send time**, like the Lens, so narrowing while a run is in flight cannot relabel what that answer was built on. The surface never sends an empty array: absent means *not narrowed* and empty means *narrowed to nothing*, and T-248's `absent ≠ empty` is a distinction a UI is very easy to lose.
  ⚠ **The Context chip says less than the design sketch, and says so.** The sketch reads *"budget consumed against the assembly budget"*. The budget is a real deployment fact and is reported. **Consumption is not on the record** — `AssembledInput.budget` reaches no Step row, so no answer can be asked what it spent — and computing a plausible figure client-side from something that is not it is the failure the coverage note and the null-cost rule were both written against. The chip states the budget and says the rest is not recorded; putting consumption on the Step row is a contract-and-migration change nobody has asked for yet.
  **The Tools chip is a pointer, never a launcher**, per `Q-030`'s owner steer: the V1 tool set lives in the rail's Tools section, and pinning a codified workflow from the composer is **T-334**, queued behind T-309's executor ruling. The chip names where tools live and does not pretend to start one.
  **The Lens chip is T-283's and was not rebuilt** — it already carries the sentence the entry names, in the panel rather than a tooltip. It now sits in a five-chip row rather than alone.
  📸 **No walkthrough capture, and it was checked rather than assumed:** every chip here is on the Ask composer, and no photographed beat is an Ask screen (the 39 shots run schema → plan → sandbox → review → library).

- **T-294 — The completion footer and plan view.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-29.** The orchestration mode stated **in words**, always visible; the Lens and version; Details exposing the plan, workers, per-step cost with pins marked, and the citation manifest. | *(Deps: T-267, T-293)*
  **Composition, as the entry says — with one read path that had to move.** The mode, the Lens and its version, the plan's steps and their states all come off `GET /runs/:runId/plan` (T-261); the counts off the ground-check step's `railOutcomes`; the per-step model and cost off the Step rows T-254 and T-313 built; the manifest off the cite leaf's citations. Nothing new is computed and nothing is stored.
  🔒 **The mode is read from `plan.mode` and never derived from `workflowId`, and T-267 is why that is the ticket rather than a detail.** An **edited** plan is `model_chosen` even though it began declared and still carries a workflow-shaped history — so a footer inferring the label from the workflow id would print *"Ran a declared workflow"* over a plan that had been hand-edited, which is precisely the promise (same inputs, same steps, same order) that editing breaks. A test pins it: `mode: 'model_chosen'` with `workflowId` still set must read *"Composed for this question"* and must not read the declared phrase.
  **The mode is outside the Details affordance and a test pins that too** — it appears before the toggle in the markup. The entry calls it *"a hard requirement rather than a nicety"*, and a mode a user has to open a disclosure to find is a mode most users never read.
  **A plan that could not be read is a stated absence.** `plan` is `Plan | null` for the progress rail's reason (T-293): a refusal is an ordinary outcome — the plan inherits the run's read scope exactly — so the footer says *"orchestration mode not recorded for this answer"* rather than falling back to a label. The same rule one level down: **no ground-check outcomes at all is not "nothing was withheld"**, so an empty rail-outcome list renders as *"no ground-check outcomes were recorded"* and never as a clean bill.
  ⚠ **"Where verification could not be taken independently, say so" is on EVERY answer this build produces, and that is correct rather than pessimistic.** The deterministic ground-check always runs and is code; the independent-family verifier is T-275 and its enforcement T-286, both → beyond V1. So the footer says the check was taken against the sources the run actually admitted and that **no independent model verification was taken** — a sentence that becomes conditional when the verifier lands and would otherwise have been an assumption nobody stated.
  ⚠ **There is no "pinned model" marker, deliberately.** The Wave 8 block's pin is per-conversation and belongs to the **Model chip**, which T-292 stopped on `Q-021`. Nothing in this build can pin a model, so a pin column would be a marker that can never be true — T-269's rule (*a value the schema carries and no code can set is a claim the schema makes falsely*) applied to a surface. Each step's model instead says **router-chosen**, which is what actually happened.
  ⚠ **The manifest carries document reference and register, and says what it does not carry.** `Citation.source` holds a version id and a document reference, or an authority ref; the **version reference and the locator** live on the assembled item and reach no persisted row, so the entry's *"version, locator"* cannot be honoured from the record. The manifest states that rather than rendering a plausible stand-in, and points the reader at the source panel where the passage itself is.
  ⚠ **The plan renders read-only; editing and re-running are not built here.** The board entry's Details list — *"the plan, workers, per-step cost with pins marked, and the citation manifest"* — does not include editing, and the design block's *"editable and re-runnable"* is a surface of its own rather than a line in a footer. **T-267's `POST /runs/:runId/plan/rerun` therefore still has no caller**, which is worth saying out loud: it is a built endpoint with no surface, and `canRerun` comes back on the plan read unused.
  **Two duplications were removed rather than left.** The Lens and the withheld count had been on the audit-trail summary line (T-283/T-088); they are the footer's now, because two places to read one fact are two places for it to go stale. `formatStepCost` is exported and tested directly — the per-step costs sit behind Details, which static markup does not render, and T-254's **null is not zero** rule is far too easy to lose to leave untested for that reason. A declared rate of **zero stays a price**, asserted beside it.
  **T-293's own recorded gap closes here as a side effect.** A reopened conversation could not recover which Lens produced a past answer, because the Lens is on the plan and the rail read only the last run's. The footer states the mode under **every** answer, so every run's plan is read — and the Lens comes back with it. The rail still shows one plan; it is now the same read rather than a second one.
  📸 **No walkthrough capture, checked rather than assumed:** the footer is on the Ask surface, and no photographed beat is an Ask screen.

- **T-295 — The output destination selector.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-29.** 🔒 A destination broader than the source material warns naming both labels and is blocked by default. Cannot ship before T-249 — a selector without propagation implies a guarantee the backend does not make. | *(Deps: T-249, T-280)*
  🔒 **The selector makes no judgement of its own, and that is the ticket rather than an implementation note.** Both labels and the verdict come from `GET /runs/:runId/destination-check`, which calls the **same** `checkPropagation` over the **same** freshly-computed audiences that `POST /runs/:runId/sandbox-document` calls — `propagationVerdict` is now one function with two callers. That is **T-373's rule from the promotion window, one slice along**: *a preflight computed separately from the act it previews is a preflight that will eventually lie*, and the shape of that lie here would be a selector saying "fine" over a write that then refuses. Every preflight test pairs the preview with the act and asserts they agree, because a preview asserted alone is decorative.
  **T-249 did the hard half a month ago; this ticket is the surface it was owed.** The refusal, the both-labels sentence, the explicit override with its mandatory reason and the append-only `label_overrides` row all already existed and are untouched. What did not exist was any way to *choose* a destination or to learn the answer before clicking — so the refusal could only ever be discovered at the point of action, which is the worst moment to meet it.
  **The two rules, and why the second one matters as much as the first.** A destination broader than the sources is **blocked** and names both labels — *"This answer draws on material restricted to named people. The selected destination is shared across organisations."* — with the override offered inline and refused until a reason is typed. **Narrower is allowed with no warning at all**, deliberately: writing restricted material somewhere more restricted is the safe direction, and a warning there is how people are trained to click through the one that matters.
  ⚠ **The verdict is rendered per ANSWER, not per conversation, and the reason is not cosmetic.** The source label is computed from *that run's own source set*, so one destination can be legal for one answer in a conversation and refused for the next as the grounding changes. Nothing is cached across runs, and a check that could not be taken renders nothing — leaving the write to refuse, which it still does. **A check that failed is never read as an allowance.**
  **The destinations offered are resolved server-side.** `GET /projects/:id/sandboxes` is grant-based (ADR-0036) and takes no scope parameter, so the list is the sandboxes the requester can actually reach and cannot be widened from the client. `null` — no destination named — stays the organisation's default working area, which is what the server already picks (T-171).
  **The preview inherits the write's refusals exactly, and both are tested.** A colleague who may *read* a run may not carry it anywhere, so they may not ask where it could go either — the answer would be a fact about a document they cannot make. A destination the requester cannot reach answers `404`, because a preview that distinguished "exists but is refused" from "does not exist" would be a disclosure channel the write itself closes.
  **One test-ordering note worth recording**, because it caught a real confusion: the T-295 block is declared **before** the T-249 write-back suite, whose last case deliberately **revokes the narrowing** to prove the label is computed rather than stored. Declared after it, these cases read `multi_organisation` where the fixture means `participant_narrowed` — the suite proving the label is live is the same suite that moves it.
  📸 **No walkthrough recapture, and it was verified rather than assumed** (T-293's record did the same): `grep -i ask` over `capture.mjs` returns three prose hits and no navigation, and `build.mjs` names no Ask screen among its 39 beats. The selector, the chips and the footer are all on Ask, so nothing photographed moved.

### Raised during the build

- **T-298 — Seed the conflict-register scenario; deterministic participant order.** ✅ Built 2026-07-30. A second client and scheme, so an exclusion has two projects to pair; `readMe` ordered by `created_at` because twelve e2e specs index `participants[0]`. **Fixed a T-247 regression:** under RLS a DELETE must first *find* its rows through the SELECT policy, so ingest's replace-wholesale step deleted nothing and re-insert collided — ingest had become silently non-idempotent. The existing test would have caught it, but turbo had **cached** `@infora/data`'s result from before the migration; turbo keys on file hashes and cannot see database state. | *(Deps: T-245, T-247)*

*Where the design documents went (2026-07-31):* the Ask specification is **folded into this board and deleted**. Its design content lives in the wave reference blocks and the ticket entries above; the Lens definitions and their authoring guide moved verbatim to [packages/lenses/definitions/](../../packages/lenses/definitions/); the eval harness's machinery is documented beside the code it describes at [evals/README.md](../../evals/README.md). Decisions stay in the ADRs and vocabulary in CONTEXT.md, as they always did — those were never the specification's to hold. As each area is *built*, its reference block condenses into the built ticket's own entry, the same way T-255–T-258 already have.

### Waypoint A — the pilot floor

- **T-300 — The three-organisation seed.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-04** (no migration; e2e 55/55 with a new `three-organisations.spec.ts`, full check green). **Org C is Redgate Ecology**, a new organisation rather than a promotion of **Halvern Associates** — Halvern's documented meaning is *"an organisation with no Membership at all"* (T-022's wall subject), and reusing it would delete a test subject in order to create one. Seeded with its own org admin (Nadia Okonjo), Participant (elevated, as Org B's lead author is), a single-org sandbox with a working document, and **`WA-ECO-PEA-001`, produced and shared with nobody** — the missing `deliverable_shares` row *is* the negative. **The spec asserts the positives too:** Trentmoor sees the deliverable because it owns the library (producer | project owner | live share, ADR-0016 as data), so the test cannot pass against a broken project — only the share is absent. Org B's half of the negative is created **at runtime rather than seeded**, so it is live work rather than a fixture. `SEEDED.thirdOrg` was left alone and commented: it means Halvern, *outside* the project, and the new persona is `SEEDED.secondConsultant`. The dev seed carries an owner and two members on one project so the wall is **demonstrable in the customer's own tenant** — a screen the buyer can look at, not a property they take on trust. Mirrors the Session B design story exactly (Org A owner, Org B consultant, Org C brought in to probe cross-organisation sharing), and **B↔C invisibility is the thing a consultancy will actually poke at**. Seed the third organisation with its own user, Participant, sandbox and at least one deliverable it produced and did **not** share, so the negative is demonstrable rather than merely absent. **Two of the three are operator-held or fictional** ([v1.md](v1.md)) — this is a demonstration, not a commercial proof, and the entry must say so where an operator will read it. **Do not extend the e2e specs that index `participants[0]`** without re-reading T-298: the order is deterministic by `created_at` and a dozen specs depend on it. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-301 — The elevated tier: close-as-rejected and owner supersede/withdraw.** ✅ **Ruled 2026-07-31** (recorded against the tracker's existing 2026-07-18 QA-themes entry): the destructive actions are gated on **`Participant.elevated`**, audited, with **org admin deliberately not extended** — being able to manage an organisation's people is not the same authority as being able to end a deliverable. Surface the affordance as **absent rather than disabled** for an unelevated Participant — the same principle as an unentitled worker (T-269) and a non-conforming model route (T-292). ⚠ **Re-cut 2026-08-04 — the ticket's premise was stale and two thirds of it is already built.** It says *"what does not exist is any path that checks it"*; **T-174 and T-176 built those paths.** `close-rejected` checks `slice.elevated` ([cycle.ts:1076](../../apps/api/src/cycle.ts#L1076)) and withdraw/restore check `canEditPlan` ([plan.ts:343](../../apps/api/src/plan.ts#L343)), and both surfaces already hide rather than disable ([cycle.tsx:177](../../apps/web/src/screens/cycle.tsx#L177), [plan.tsx:516](../../apps/web/src/screens/plan.tsx#L516)). **What is genuinely outstanding is two things, and they part company:** (a) **the refusal audit** — ✅ **built 2026-08-04**, migration 0038, drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) Drawer 2 first. `elevated_refusals` is append-only on the T-008 trigger, because a refusal record a super-user could quietly delete is worth nothing and the people who hold this tier are exactly the people who would want to. Participant grain, not User — the tier is a *project* capability. `required_tier` is stored although one value is possible today, so a row still means what it meant once a second tier exists. **`container_restore` is recorded although it is recovery rather than destruction** — the record answers *"who attempted an act this tier holds and was refused"*, and one direction of the same gate going unrecorded leaves it incomplete while looking complete; plan-metadata editing rides the same predicate and is deliberately out. **A cross-organisation attempt is not recorded** — it is answered `404` above the tier check, and logging it would record an act against a container the requester was never shown. No read endpoint: the record exists so the question *can* be answered, and what surface answers it is not this ticket's to decide. (b) **Supersede, which does not exist at all** — nothing in the codebase sets `containers.state = 'superseded'`, and building it means creating **the first cross-organisation container write**, which is 🌫 **fog until `Q-036` is ruled**, per the Q/T boundary rule. `supersede` is deliberately absent from the `elevated_action` enum for the same reason: a value the schema carries and no code can set is a claim the schema makes falsely. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-302 — Incremental ingest: a version id, not a full-table walk.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-03.** 🔒 **The single highest-leverage fix in this slice, and it is small.** `ingestVersions` walked **every version in the database** on each call, chunking and embedding in a serial in-process loop, and ran on library admission. At the skeleton's few dozen rows that is invisible; at 500 documents the per-admission path is roughly **125,000 version re-ingests**, and even one call at the end leaves every subsequent admission re-ingesting all 500. **This was not theoretical:** on 2026-08-01 the shared dev database reached ~1,050 versions and the api suite began failing on 5-second timeouts in the cycle tests — always the ones that admit a version to grounding. **Two entry points, not one** ([contracts.md](contracts.md)): `ingestVersion(db, router, versionId)` on every product path, and the sweep surviving as `ingestAllVersions` under a name that says what it does — reachable from the ingest CLI and the e2e substrate, which index a seeded database from nothing, and from nothing on a request path. An unknown id **throws** rather than indexing nothing quietly. **A version is indexed when it comes into existence, not when it starts grounding** — ingest excludes nothing, exclusion being retrieval's job (ADR-0022, T-033) — so all three version-creating acts ingest: the sandbox freeze, promotion, and the contractual revision an accepting verdict issues. **That closed a real gap the sweep was masking, and it is the reason this ticket is three call sites rather than one:** a promotion onto a container already in the library makes a new version current, and its chunks previously arrived only at the *next* acceptance anywhere in the project — between the two, the deliverable's current version had no chunks and it **silently dropped out of retrieval**. `cycle.test.ts` now pins that case. Each call sits after its transaction commits; an outbound embedding call holds no transaction open. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-303 — The bulk-load path.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (no migration; api 374/374, full check green). A corpus load is an **operator action, not an interactive one**, and must not run through the per-admission path at all.
  **A CLI, not an endpoint** — `pnpm --filter @infora/api run bulk-load -- --project … --organisation … --directory …`. Nothing that is allowed to take hours belongs on a request path, and there should be no endpoint until someone can say what the surface does while it runs. Each document is one `ingestVersion` (T-302), so a 500-document load is 500 targeted ingests and steady state is one.
  **Resumability is the part that is easy to get wrong by doing less.** The obvious check — *"does a container with this reference exist"* — is wrong, and wrong in the direction that hides the failure: a document whose container committed and whose embedding call then died is **in the library, listed, and answering nothing**, which is worse than absent because the list says it is there. So the resume check is *"is this document's current version indexed under the pinned model"*, and a re-run reports three distinct outcomes — `present`, `reindexed` (it finished a half-landed document), `loaded`. **`isVersionIndexed` lives in `@infora/data`**, not here: `scripts/source-rules.mjs` RULE 1 caught the first draft reading `version_chunks` from `apps/api`, correctly. It scopes its read, because the index is under RLS and the policy **fails closed** — an unscoped read answers "never indexed" for everything and re-embeds the whole corpus on every resume.
  **What it admits is T-304's ruling, built:** a library-scope container, `in_library`, `live`, one genesis version `R01` — and **no work item**, which is the entire distinguishing fact. No new state, no new table, no marker column. `producing_organisation_id` is *whose material this is*, so the wall reads received material on the existing predicate with **no carve-out** — a carve-out here would be a hole in the one predicate grounding, the library list and citation resolution all share.
  **The reference is the file name, and that is a decision.** The project's naming scheme composes codes for *planned deliverables*; generating a scheme-conforming code for a consultee response would dress received material up as a deliverable, which is the laundering T-304 exists to prevent. The file name is also what makes the load resumable at all — it is the only identifier stable across re-runs.
  **Refusals are per document and named twice:** in the line as it happens, and again in a closing block that says plainly *"these documents are NOT in the corpus"*, because a 500-line log with forty refusals scattered through it is a log nobody reads to the top of. **A non-zero exit** is the difference between "the corpus is loaded" and "the corpus is loaded except for the forty nobody was told about". A duplicate reference *within one run* is refused rather than silently resolved — it is a different fault from a re-run and deserves a different answer. | *(Deps: T-302)*

  *What the ticket asked for, kept as the standard it was built to:* admit N documents as reference-material containers (the 2026-07-31 ruling) in one pass, ingesting each **once**; [operating-envelope.md](../architecture/operating-envelope.md) measures this separately from interactive ingest and **allows it hours**; what it may not do is block an accepting action or leave the corpus half-indexed on failure — a partial load must be resumable and must say what it did not load.
- **T-304 — Reference-material containers, and the marker that keeps them distinguishable.** 🔒 ✅ **Ruled 2026-07-31 (Claude's call, owner-delegated):** a legacy corpus is *received* material, not *produced* material, and V1 must not invent a lifecycle to admit it. It enters as **reference-material containers** — admitted to the library with a single genesis Version at `live`, so it grounds (ADR-0011) and rides every existing access and state pre-filter unchanged, but carries **no work item**. The ADR-0032 addendum already establishes that reference-material containers have none and that surfaces must never assume the link, so **the distinguishing fact is an *absence***, exactly as ADR-0038 made `container_id` the sole distinguishing fact for a bound sandbox document. No new state, no new table, no parallel lifecycle. **One consequence is build work, not a note:** a loaded reference document must be **visibly** distinguishable in the Documents view from an accepted deliverable, or the corpus quietly launders itself into the produced record. That marker is part of this ticket, not later polish. | *(Deps: T-303)*
  ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (no migration; api 377/377, e2e 63/63, walkthrough recaptured, full check green).
  **`LibraryItem.kind` is derived and nothing is stored** — the left join to `work_items` answering null *is* the marker, so there is no flag a writer can forget to set and no second definition to drift. The test pins that the two rows differ in the work item **and in nothing else**, `metadata` included.
  **Two tables, not a badge in one.** The ruling's failure mode is laundering, and a badge inside a table headed *Live deliverables* still lists a consultee response as a live deliverable. So reference material has its own section, and its **columns differ because the facts differ**: no Suitability and no Discipline (received material carries neither), no Transmit (this project did not produce it and has no standing to issue it), and *Held by* rather than *Producer* — the organisation named holds the document, it did not write it. The section is absent entirely on a project that has loaded none.
  ⚠ **The seeded library turns out to be reference material, all of it** — the seed's own comment has said so since it was written (*"the seed library is owner-added reference material (ADR-0011)"*), and the Documents view has been listing it under *Live deliverables* the whole time. Nothing changed except that the screen now says what the data always meant. The recaptured walkthrough shows the two genuinely produced deliverables above five received documents, which is the first time that page has been honest about the difference.
  **The premise checked, because it is only sound in one direction.** The ruling reads the absence of a work item as "reference material", which holds only if every *produced* library deliverable has one. In the built flow it does — a plan row creates the container and its work item together, and promotion promotes a planned container — so the marker is sound. Worth stating rather than assuming: nothing *enforces* it, and a future path that admits a deliverable without a plan row would mislabel it. If that path is ever wanted, it needs a constraint, not a second marker.

*The corpus's format reach (T-305–T-307).* [v1.md](v1.md) rules format coverage **narrow — text-extractable only, an unsupported document failing loudly and per-document** — and [spike-locators.md](spikes/spike-locators.md) found what that currently means in practice.
- **T-305 — PDF text extraction on the ingest path.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (migration 0048, drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) Drawer 2 first; api 372/372, data 15/15, e2e 63/63, full check green). 🔒 **The commercially significant gap T-270 found.** PDF existed in the codebase only as an **output rendition** (`textToPdf`); there was no PDF *input* path at all. A real scheme's 100–500 documents are overwhelmingly PDF — issued deliverables, Advice Notes, Decision Letters, consultee responses — and **page is the locator a planner actually uses**, and the only format that has one (a docx has no pages: pagination is computed by the viewer, so any "page 14" from a Word source is an invention). *"A 100–500 document corpus"* and *"citations that resolve to a locator inside the source document"* cannot both be true through the docx path alone. Text-extractable PDFs only; a scanned one **fails loudly, per document**, per the ruling — OCR stays out of V1.
  **The page locator needed no column, and that is T-271's rule paying off rather than a shortcut.** [`pdfToText`](../../apps/api/src/pdf-text.ts) terminates every page with a **form feed inside the extracted text**, so page is *"count the separators before the span, plus one"* — the same derivation as paragraph, over `chr(12)` instead of `E'\n'`, computed in the same query. *Store the position, compute the view* meant the second locator dimension cost one SQL expression. A version with no form feed anywhere reports **no page**, which is every docx and always will be: absent still means absent.
  **Where extraction sits was the ticket's one real decision.** It is at **upload**, not in the ingest sweep, and the reason is structural rather than preference: `versions` is append-only (T-008) and `versions.content` is both what the chunker indexes and what every locator is an offset *into*, so extraction must precede the version that carries it — the sweep cannot write one. A PDF also has no conversion path to extract it later, deliberately (ADR-0004 — the PDF is the record rendition, never an editing surface), so it is text at upload or never. What T-302 kept off the request path is the corpus-wide walk; this is one bounded document. **The bulk-load path (T-303) calls the same extractor** and inherits the same refusals.
  **The extractor is hand-written, and that is a deliberate divergence from the spike**, which called a PDF extractor *"a real dependency, not a refactor"*. [`upload.ts`](../../apps/api/src/upload.ts)'s zip reader and [`xlsx.ts`](../../apps/api/src/xlsx.ts)'s workbook reader made the same call twice already, and what is needed here is text and page boundaries out of the text-extractable subset — not rendering, not layout — which does not justify taking a rendering engine into a deployable meant to run in a sovereign tier. It sweeps the file for objects rather than following the cross-reference table (real exports arrive with broken ones), expands object streams, decodes Flate and the three ASCII filters, and reads text through `/ToUnicode` CMaps and font encodings. **Glyph advance widths turned out to be load-bearing, not polish:** a browser positions each glyph individually, and without the widths the extracted text reads *"t h e a s s e s s m e n t"* — the pen position alone cannot tell a space from kerning.
  **Every failure is the whole document, by name.** `pdf_no_text` (the ruling's scan), `pdf_encrypted`, `pdf_unreadable`, `pdf_unsupported_filter` — and a content stream that will not decode refuses the **document**, never the page, because a corpus that answers confidently out of the pages it happened to read is exactly the failure the loud-and-per-document rule exists to prevent. The sandbox's multi-file upload was changed to match: it **runs to the end and reports each file by name**, where before the first refusal aborted the batch and named nothing. A refused document is written nowhere — no opaque blob parked in the sandbox for someone to miss. The test suite proves this against a **real browser-printed PDF** committed as a fixture, not only against our own writer's output, because reading back what `textToPdf` wrote proves the reader agrees with the writer and nothing about a client's corpus. | *(Deps: none; wanted by T-271)*
- **T-306 — xlsx and pptx text extraction, and the loud per-document refusal.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (no migration; api 391/391, full check green). Both upload today and neither converts (`unsupported_conversion`), so they sit in the sandbox as opaque blobs and never ground. Extract text — sheet-and-cell for xlsx, slide-and-placeholder for pptx — which also gives each its natural locator. **The refusal path is half the ticket:** [v1.md](v1.md) requires an unsupported document to fail **loudly and per-document**, and a bulk load of 500 that silently indexes 460 is the failure mode — the corpus then answers confidently from a library missing the forty nobody was told about. | *(Deps: T-303)*
  **The natural locator turned out to be the one that already existed.** A sheet and a slide are each a *paginated unit* — the thing a reader names when they say where something is — so both render **one per page** with T-305's form feed between, and the page locator T-271's stored span already derives addresses them unchanged. **Four formats, one locator mechanism, no new field and no migration.** A slide is the cleanest case of all: `page` *is* the slide number, with nothing lost in translation.
  **A row is a row, not a list of cells.** `A1: Reference / B1: Respondent` embeds as coordinates rather than as meaning, and nobody cites a spreadsheet by cell — a planner cites *"the consultation register, the Environment Agency's row"*, which is that row's own text. So the row is the passage and the verbatim is a line a reader recognises. **Cell-grain addressing is not delivered and deliberately not half-delivered:** it needs a locator that is a coordinate rather than a count, which is a different mechanism and should be asked for before it is built.
  **Slide order comes from `presentation.xml`, not from the file names** — a reordered deck still stores its slides in creation order, and slide number *is* the locator, so it is the one thing that must not be guessed. **Speaker notes are not read:** they are the presenter's script, not the document, and indexing them would put words in the corpus that nobody in the room ever saw.
  **Two refusals worth naming.** A workbook of charts and formulas is refused `xlsx_no_text` — and the gate counts **rows, not characters**, because every workbook has tab names and "is there any non-whitespace" passes a chart-only file on the strength of the word *"Chart"*. A deck of images is `pptx_no_text`, the pptx form of the scanned PDF the ruling names.
  ⚠ **One asymmetry, deliberate and stated:** a **docx still keeps `''` at upload** while the other three extract. It is the only uploaded format with a conversion path, and that path makes its text *canonical* rather than merely grounding — extracting at upload too would give `content` two meanings for one format. The bulk load has no such exception and reads every format, docx included, because reference material never converts.
  **Found while consolidating:** the zip reader had been copied into `upload.ts` and `xlsx.ts`, and **the copies had drifted** — the xlsx one inflates with a bounded output length and a try/catch, so a crafted entry cannot balloon kilobytes into gigabytes, and the docx one did not. Both read untrusted uploads. A third copy for decks would have been a third chance to be the unhardened one, so there is now one reader (`zip.ts`) and it is the hardened one. `parseXlsx` also generalised from *the first tab* to *every tab, named* — corpus extraction wants all of them, and two walks of the same relationship graph would be two chances to disagree about which tab is which.
- **T-307 — Chunker: stop reading a heading number as a sentence terminator.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (no migration; data 25/25, full check green; eval seed set run either side — see the caveat below). [spike-locators.md](spikes/spike-locators.md) Finding 2.
  **The spike's proposed fix was narrowed, deliberately.** It asks for *"a digit, then whitespace, then a capitalised word"* — but that also matches every ordinary sentence ending in a number, so *"The predicted level is 54. The barrier is three metres."* would stop splitting: one retrieval bug traded for a commoner one. **What separates a heading from a sentence is not the digit — it is that the number starts its line**, so the test is anchored there: a run of digits and dots, at the head of a line (indentation allowed, prose not), ending in the dot in question. A form feed counts as a line start too, so a chapter opening a PDF page is covered — T-305's page separator earning its keep a second time.
  ⚠ **The instrument was weaker than the spike assumed, and saying so is the point.** The seed set was run before and after and is **unchanged — 6 pass, 0 fail, 0 error**. But **11 of its 17 cases are `ungraded`**: they need a model grader and none is configured, so what was actually compared is the deterministic half — one happy case and the five permission cases. Those five are about *reach*, which re-chunking cannot move, and HAPPY-01 asserts **recall only** (T-312 records why). So this run proves *no regression in access or retrievability*, and it does **not** measure retrieval quality, which is the thing the change was made to improve. The measurement the spike wanted needs **T-312**'s larger fixture and a configured grader; until both land, "run the evals either side" buys less than it sounds like. | *(Deps: none)* `SENTENCE_BREAK` fires after the `2.` of a numbered heading, so a heading is severed from its own section and glued to the tail of the previous paragraph — *"…the NPS. 2. Method"* becomes one chunk. **A retrieval-quality bug that will be blamed on the embedding model**, and it destroys the one signal (`§12.4.7`) that is the most useful locator a consenting document has. The fix is a lookahead. **It changes chunk boundaries, therefore embeddings, therefore what retrieval returns** — so run the eval seed set (T-259) before and after, and do it in its own commit rather than folded into T-271's offsets. Explicitly out of scope: resolving Word's `<w:numPr>` list numbering, which means implementing Word's numbering algebra and is its own ticket if it is ever wanted. | *(Deps: none)*

### Waypoint C — the product surface

- **T-308 — The rulebook's home.** ✅ **Unblocked 2026-08-01 → [ADR-0048](../architecture/adr/0048-the-checker-findings-not-prose.md).** The rulebook is **guiding-channel material in org context, in its entirety** — a house drafting manual is the firm's own preference document, not a published external instrument, so it fails the 2026-07-29 ruling's operative test on its own terms. Build the loader and the org-context binding. **The part that is not obvious:** a finding may quote it **verbatim without citing it**, so the loader must preserve enough structure to quote *a clause* (§4.2, not "page 11") — a rulebook chunked for steer alone would make the ruling unimplementable at the surface. | *(Deps: none)*
  ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (migration 0051, **drawer 7 — Context**, the first store any of component 4's three scoped stores has ever had). Until this landed `guiding` in the assembly gateway returned an empty array *because there was nothing to return*: the ticket reads as one binding and was in fact the whole channel's first data.
  🔒 **The not-obvious part is the design, not a caveat on it.** The stored unit is the **clause**, not the chunk — [rulebook.ts](../../packages/data/src/rulebook.ts) sits beside `chunker.ts` and deliberately is not it. `chunkText` trims sentences and rejoins them with a single space, so a chunk is **not a substring of its own source** (T-270 finding 1) and carries no clause address at all; quoting from one would produce a rule the manual does not literally contain. A test asserts exactly that difference. Splitting is anchored to the **line**, which is T-307's lesson borrowed from the other side: what separates a heading from a sentence is not the digit but that a heading number starts its line — a "digit, dot, capital" rule would carve a rulebook at every measurement in it. A clause with no number is stored with **none rather than a guessed one**: it still steers, it simply cannot be quoted with a reference, and the load reports how many *can* be, so an org admin learns their manual is unquotable at upload rather than from a finding that reads oddly six weeks later.
  **The org-context binding is one key: the organisation.** No project, no share, no acknowledgement, no wall predicate — *portable to every project the organisation touches* (ADR-0020) **is** the query. Asserted both ways: the same firm's people reach it on a second project, and a rival on the **shared** project reaches none of it (ADR-0048 §6 — a competitor's drafting standards are the ethical-wall breach nobody thinks of as crossing the wall). These rows are **not in `version_chunks`**, applying [the authority-corpus spike](spikes/spike-authority-corpus.md)'s Finding 4 a store early.
  ⚙ **One contract change, and it is the ADR made structural.** `AssembledItem.source` is now **optional**, absent meaning *not citable* — `source` is what a citation resolves to, and guiding material never is (ADR-0021, ADR-0048 §5); previously every guiding item was forced to carry a source identity it had no business having. The clause address lives in a new `rule` field instead, pairing with T-328's `RulebookEvidence`, deliberately outside `source` so it cannot resolve like a source chip. `wall.test.ts`'s pinned item shape fired on both, which is the review that pin exists to force.
  ⚠ **`Q-046` raised, and it constrains T-310 rather than this.** The rulebook rides the channel *in its entirety* and is not retrieved against the question, so the token budget is the only thing that narrows it — and `mergeChannels` drops guiding before grounded. For an Ask answer that degrades tone; for a **checker**, whose silence is a claim, *"no findings against your drafting manual"* after reading three-quarters of it is indistinguishable from compliance.
  **Scope calls:** an org-admin door exists (`POST`/`GET`/`DELETE /organisation/rulebooks`, the `/organisation/users` tier, multipart through the same extractor and the same vocabulary of refusal the corpus path uses) but **no UI** — there is no org-administration screen in the product, and inventing one is not this ticket. Retire, never delete: a finding written against a rule the firm has since withdrawn must still resolve to the words it quoted. The original bytes are **not kept** — what steers is the clause text, and a blob nothing reads is a deletion obligation nothing needs.
- **T-328 — The finding schema.** The type both the checker DAG and the findings surface stand on, in `contracts`, minted **ahead of** them because they cannot be specified without it. A finding carries: the **input it arose from** (corpus / attached / rulebook, which decides its citation treatment), an **anchor** at the locator grain T-271 establishes, a **severity**, its **evidence**, and an **optional proposed revision** expressed as a Suggestion rather than as free text — the ADR-0048 constraint that keeps the checker from acquiring its own write path. **Severity's vocabulary is this ticket's call** (ADR-0048 leaves it open deliberately: it is a naming question, not a design fork) — pick the smallest set that a reviewer can triage by, and resist per-organisation configurability until someone asks. | *(Deps: T-271)*
  ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** — [packages/contracts/src/finding.ts](../../packages/contracts/src/finding.ts), types only, no migration and no endpoint.
  **Severity is `required` / `advisory`, and the argument for two is that a third has no work to do.** The reviewer's triage question is single — *must this change before the draft goes out, or may I reasonably decline it?* — and a middle level answers neither and becomes the drawer everything ambiguous is filed in. **Neither word is a verdict**, which is what ruled out `critical / major / minor`: those grade the *document*, and a finding states a defect and never a verdict. And **`required` is deliberately not `blocking`** — ADR-0049 §7 blocks promotion on an **open** finding of any severity, so naming one level "blocking" would imply the other is not, which is the exact confusion §7 exists to prevent. One vocabulary for everyone; per-organisation configurability refused.
  🔒 **ADR-0048 §7 is carried as a TYPE, not as a rule to remember.** `evidence` is a union discriminated by the input the finding arose from, so a rulebook finding has **nowhere to put a `Citation`** — the dishonest object does not compile, and the test file's `@ts-expect-error` lines are the acceptance. That is §5's quotable-but-never-cited ruling made structural rather than documented. The same union gives the clause quote a home (`clause` + `quote`), **which is the field T-308's loader has to be able to fill**: a rulebook chunked for steer alone would leave it empty and the ruling would survive in the model and die on the screen.
  **`FindingStatus` is `SandboxComment['status']` word for word**, pinned by a test rather than by a comment — ADR-0049 §7 counts findings and threads identically, and two words for one state is how "why does this list stop me and that one not" starts needing an answer. `OpenFindingCount` is the query obligation §7 handed back, with the breakdown beside the gate and gating nothing.
  **Types only, no zod, and that is a scope call:** what the checker's model call must return is a parse boundary belonging to **T-310**, and specifying it here would design that ticket ahead of itself.

### Slice V1-S

- **T-337 — Schema import: a spreadsheet becomes candidate fields.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (no migration; api 404/404, full check green). Every consultancy already has its schema in a spreadsheet, and [schema.tsx](../../apps/web/src/screens/schema.tsx)'s `OptionsEditor` — a code and a description typed per row, built to scale to "the long routewide code lists" — makes retyping it the highest-friction moment in the product, landing in the pilot's *first hour* before the firm has seen a single benefit. **Deterministic-first, ADR-0027 §2 pattern 1** (code with an LLM escape hatch): a CSV or XLSX whose headers are recognisable maps to `NamingSchemeField` with **no model call at all**, and only unrecognised columns escalate to `extractor` (T-274) rather than growing a second extraction path. The deterministic half is useful alone, which is what keeps this off Waypoint B's critical path. **No migration** — the upload is parsed in-request and the result is written through the existing naming-scheme `PUT`. Three hard constraints: (1) the file is **never admitted to the library**, never chunked, never retrievable — it is not corpus and must not touch the ingest path; (2) **the run request must not echo the file body**, because `runs.request` is persisted and an existing schema routinely carries **named people** in its author and reviewer columns, so echoing the upload would silently create a personal-data store ([personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md)); (3) an unparseable file **fails loudly and names the row**, matching V1's per-document ingest ruling. | *(Deps: none)*
  **All three constraints are structural rather than remembered.** (1) [schema-import.ts](../../apps/api/src/schema-import.ts) holds no `Db` and imports nothing that does, and the route parses in-request and keeps nothing — there is no code path from an upload to the ingest path to forget to close. (2) The deterministic path makes **no model call, therefore no Run**, so there is nothing for `runs.request` to echo; that is the strongest available form of the guarantee, stronger than remembering to strip a field. (3) `skipped` carries **the row number Excel shows**, so "row 47" is a row a person can go and look at.
  **Candidate is the load-bearing word, and the endpoint's main test is that it writes nothing.** An import that saved the scheme by arriving would let a mistyped upload rewrite a project's numbering, and numbering is what every reference in the record is built on. The owner reviews the codes in the options editor — where the friction was — and the existing `PUT` is still what commits.
  **Two sheet shapes, because these files come in two shapes:** *Code / Description* (the options editor's own shape) and *Field / Code / Description* (a routewide schedule, several lists in one sheet, grouped by the field column). The header row is **found by scanning** rather than assumed to be row 1, because these sheets routinely open with a title and a blank line.
  **The synonym list is deliberately small.** A list that guesses wrongly is worse than one that refuses, because a wrong guess writes a plausible code list nobody checks. An unrecognised sheet is refused with **the column names it actually found** — "rename the column" is a ten-second fix, and it is why this path does not reach for a model when a header is unfamiliar. **A duplicate code is reported, never collapsed:** in a code list it means two meanings competing for one code, which is the firm's to resolve and not this import's to pick a side in.
  **`ApiError` gained `hint`** — the specific half of a refusal. `detail` is a machine code the surface maps to a sentence; a hint is request-derived text no map could hold ("the columns are Widget, Sprocket"). Both are usually needed for a refusal a person can act on, and folding the second into the first would make `detail` unmappable.

### Slice V1-S — continued

- **T-338 — The schema surface accepts an import and stages it for review.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (no migration — surface and one contract helper). Upload on the deliverable-schema screen; the parsed fields land **in the editing table, unsaved**, for the owner to check row by row before `Save schema`. **Nothing is auto-applied, and the guarantee comes free** — the owner already holds the write and the table is already an editor, so the import gains **no write path the owner did not already have**, which is ADR-0048 §3's principle arriving without new machinery. **A diff, never a silent replace:** the table states what the import would add, change and drop, because `Reset to Infora default` already sits beside it and an import that quietly wiped a schema in progress is the same accident with a worse cause. **Scoped to `canEdit` (the owner super-user) in V1** — a guest super-user's import would have to become `NamingProposal` rows, whose `body` is free text and cannot carry a field list. That is a deliberate scope cut, recorded so it is not later read as an oversight. | *(Deps: T-337)*
  **As built, and the merge is where the danger actually was.** The ticket's stated accident is a wipe, so the obvious build — replace the field list and show a preview — is the wrong one: T-337's parse produces fields with **labels and option lists** and nothing else, because that is all a spreadsheet of codes can express. A replace would therefore have cleared `inCode`, `required`, `role`, `isOriginator`, `isSerial` and `width` on every matched field, **silently unmaking the coded reference** — the same accident arriving through a merge instead of a replace, and wearing a safer-looking control. So a matched field keeps all six, the panel says so on screen, and a test pins each one.
  **Drops are reported and opt-in, default off.** A sheet not mentioning a field is weak evidence that the field should go — most sheets cover one part of a schema — so removing them is a second, deliberate tick with the fields named in the label. That is the difference between a diff and a replace with a preview.
  🔒 **The diff lives in `packages/contracts`, and that placement is the ticket's one real decision.** It is the function that decides whether an owner's schema survives, and `apps/web` has **no test runner** — the dependency matrix leaves a surface only `contracts` and `ui` to reach for, and a kit component is the wrong home for schema logic. `diffNamingSchemeFields` / `applyNamingSchemeImport` therefore sit beside `defaultDeliverableSchema` and `isCodeField` as pure functions over `NamingSchemeField`, with eight tests. The screen renders the result and owns nothing about it but the words on the page. **The matrix was not widened and nothing new was imported** — this is the existing rule used as intended.
