  **Matching is on `key`, with a label fallback**, because the parse derives a key from the sheet's own field name: a firm that renamed a label without renaming the key would otherwise see its own field as new and end up with two of it. **Adds arrive at the end**, because field order is what orders the coded reference's segments and a sheet has no view on that. **The scope cut holds by construction:** the control sits inside the screen's `canEdit` block, so a guest super-user never sees it — their path is still a `NamingProposal`, whose free-text body cannot carry a field list.
  ⚠ **No e2e.** `apps/web` carries no unit tests by design and a file-upload journey through the browser was not built here; the parse is covered by T-337's `schema-import.test.ts` and the diff by the contracts suite, which between them cover both halves of the act. What is not covered end to end is the click path. *(Review note: the diff renders in a panel above the editing table rather than "in the table" as the entry words it — substantively equivalent, recorded here so the deviation is disclosed rather than discovered.)*

### Slice V1-P

- **T-370 — Agent actor identity, and the receipt-with-undo substrate.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (migration 0059). The ADR-0027 agent-act amendment's administrative lane (S10, owner-ruled 2026-08-09) licenses an embedded agent to execute menial acts directly — and no build may adopt that lane until two substrates exist, because both are what makes direct execution *reviewable after the fact* rather than merely permitted: (1) **the act attributed to the agent run** — today every write is attributed to the invoking participant alone; the run is recorded, but the act itself never says an agent performed it — an acting-run reference on audited acts, surfaced wherever the act is shown; (2) **the "what the agent did" receipt with undo**, designed once and reused by every administrative agent (reversible or additive acts only — the amendment's own boundary). Until this lands, T-337 and T-364 stay preview-confirm, which the amendment reads as interaction design, not doctrine. personal-data.md check rides along (no new named-person data expected — the run already carries its requester). | *(Deps: none)*
  **As built: one table, not a column per audited act, and the reason is not economy.** The ticket says *"an acting-run reference on audited acts"*, which reads like a column — and a column would have said the wrong thing. The amendment's own premise is that the agent acts **within the invoker's own permissions**, so the subject row's existing attribution is *correct*: the participant really is who the act is attributable to. Agent performance is an **additional** fact about the same act, and a column beside `created_by_participant_id` reads as replacing it. `agent_acts` also carries `undone_at`, which is not a fact about the folder or the plan row at all, and it admits a new act kind with no DDL — Drawer 8's guard applied for the same reason, with the same consequence that `subject_id` is not a foreign key. **"Surfaced wherever the act is shown" is a lookup by subject**, which the `(subject_kind, subject_id)` index serves.
  🔒 **The vocabulary is empty on purpose, and that is the substrate working rather than missing.** Nothing performs an administrative act yet, so `act` is `text` with **no union in contracts and no enum in the store**: a closed set here would be T-301's rule broken twice over — values the schema carries that no code can set. The undo **registry** is likewise empty in every deployment, bound at composition beside `workers` and `lenses`, and an act kind with no handler is refused `not_undoable` rather than quietly stamped. A test pins exactly that, because "the empty case behaves" is the only property a substrate with no consumer can actually be held to.
  ⚠ **A precondition the ticket did not name, and it is not free.** Actor identity is a **run** reference, so an agent adopting the direct lane **must record a Run** — and T-364's structure agent writes none today, which is its own recorded residual. The first adopter closes that before it can use this.
  **Two fields were deliberately not built.** No `undoable` flag: whether an act can *still* be undone is a runtime question — an added folder that has since filled with documents is additive and no longer safely removable — so the handler answers at the moment of asking and returns its **own reason**, passed through rather than unified, because *"the folder now holds documents"* and *"the plan row has been promoted"* are different answers a receipt should distinguish. And no `undone_by_participant_id`: the receipt belongs to the run, the run already names its requester, and **only that requester may undo**, so the actor is fixed by construction. That is what makes the ticket's own prediction true — **this table introduces no new named-person data**, and the register records the check rather than a new row.
  **The receipt is in `packages/ui`, and the placement is the point of "designed once".** A component written beside its first caller becomes that caller's receipt; the second agent copies it and the two drift in the direction of whatever each was doing. It has no caller today — the amendment's sequencing — and is covered by the kit's static-markup tests instead. Three properties it enforces: it **lists acts line by line** rather than summarising them (*"the agent tidied your folders"* is not a receipt), **undo is per act** because the amendment's boundary is per act, and an **undone act stays on the list, struck** — a receipt that emptied itself would leave a person unable to answer *"what did it do that I then reversed"*.
  ⚠ **The amendment's absolute boundary is written into the module and enforced nowhere, on purpose.** *No agent act ever crosses the wall or fires a gate* — promotion, issue, acceptance, transmittal, reviewer confirmation, purge and library removal are human acts, always. `recordAgentAct` is deliberately **not** a wrapper that performs acts: it is called *beside* the ordinary write, because the governance the amendment relies on is the endpoint's ordinary guards, and a helper that wrote on an agent's behalf would be the second write path the amendment exists to refuse. A ticket recording an `agent_act` for a promotion would be breaking the amendment, not using it. *(Review note: clause (1)’s second half — "surfaced wherever the act is shown" — is NOT yet met: the (subject_kind, subject_id) index makes it possible, and no surface queries it; the no-caller fact recorded above for the receipt applies to the attribution surfacing too. It ships with the first act that adopts the substrate, and the board should read this ticket as substrate-complete, surface-pending.)*

- **T-356 — Lead-reviewer moderation on the cycle screen.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (no migration; a client method, an affordance, and the walkthrough gap card it closes). ADR-0007's "moderate in the open" — edit or amend a reviewer's comment and its code, resolve duplicates — exists as `PATCH /review-comments/:id` with no client method and no control anywhere. Add the client method and a lead-only edit affordance on the open round's DRR rows; moderation stays within the open round (the issued record is a snapshot, ADR-0009). | *(Deps: none)*
  **As built, and the endpoint had never been exercised.** It shipped in Slice A with no caller, so no test touched it either — the suite now proves the affordance and the rule agree rather than only that the screen renders: the lead amends body and code, `null` on `acceptanceCodeId` **takes a code off** (where `undefined` means leave it alone, which is the distinction a lead needs to strip a code that should not be there), and the authoring side is `403` — it cannot even see the open round's comments (ADR-0014).
  🔒 **"In the open" is made true by two absences.** There is **no delete** — a duplicate is amended to say so, never quietly emptied — and there is **no shadow original**: the amended comment IS the record, because a moderated record with the pre-moderation text hidden underneath it would be two accounts of one review. The window is the open round only; issue freezes the snapshot (ADR-0009) and the server refuses regardless, so the affordance is gated on exactly what the API is gated on and the surface never offers something that will be turned down.
  **Two small surface decisions.** The editor's textarea starts **full** — the existing comment is already in it — so it is taller than the comment composer beside it: a moderator who can see only the last two lines of what they are amending is being asked to edit blind. And the draft is held in the row's own state, so *Cancel* means *never happened* rather than *saved and reverted*.
  📸 **The walkthrough's "Moderation — endpoint without a surface" gap card is now a beat with a real capture** (`18a-moderation`, Act IV). ⚠ **The whole walkthrough was recaptured, not just the new beat**, and it had to be: T-331 put a **Notifications item in the rail**, which is in every screenshot on the page, so a single-shot update would have left 38 photographs showing a rail the product no longer has. The recapture also picks up two of this session's other changes honestly — `00-schema` now shows T-338's import control beside *Reset to Infora default*, and `27-accepted-status` carries T-392's **On acceptance** row reading *"Contractual — the C revision was issued from the accepted content"*. **The capture ran** on a fresh seed with the API restarted after it, in that order.
  ⚠ **The 1479b26 trap was hit and worked around explicitly**, and the workaround is a different one from the acceptance-codes beat's. There the fix was `el.scrollIntoView({ block: 'start' })` on the section heading; here the DRR column **scrolls independently of the page**, so scrolling the column did nothing useful — the shot came back with the editor's Save and Cancel below the fold and the textarea scrolled to its own tail, photographing an edit whose subject was invisible. The capture now drives the scroll from the **textarea**, setting `scrollTop = 0` and `scrollIntoView({ block: 'center' })`. Both shots were checked by eye, and `18a` was checksummed against `18-round-open` to prove it is not the byte-identical duplicate that failure mode produces.
  **[user-stories.md](../architecture/user-stories.md)'s moderation aside loses its "(the control is T-356)" caveat** and gains the two constraints in the lead reviewer's own voice — no delete, and open-round only — because the story now describes something a person can do.

- **T-357 — Retire the review screen's parallel plan form.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (no migration; a deletion and a link). `review.tsx` still carries a pre-Plan-screen "+ Plan a deliverable" inline form: it bypasses the naming scheme, lacks the elevated-tier gate `plan.tsx` enforces, and maps every failure — including the API's `403 super_user_required` — to "That document reference already exists on this project." One creation path (the Plan screen's modal); the review schedule links there instead. | *(Deps: none)*
  **As built: the button stays and does something else.** Removing it outright would have been the smaller diff and the worse surface — *"plan a deliverable"* is a reasonable thing to want from the schedule, and a screen that offers no route to it teaches people to go looking. So the control now navigates to the Plan screen, where the reference is **generated** from the scheme (ADR-0008: generated, never typed), the elevated tier is enforced, and a refusal says which refusal it was.
  **The third defect was the quiet one.** Bypassing the scheme and skipping the tier gate both fail visibly at the API; mapping *every* failure to *"that document reference already exists"* fails **invisibly and confidently** — a super user without the elevated tier was told their reference was a duplicate, which is a wrong answer stated as a fact, and the next thing they would do is invent a different reference. Nothing else in the app maps a status to a message it did not come from; this was the last one.
  Three imports and a form's worth of state went with it (`FormEvent`, `Card`, `TextInput`, and the reference/title/error/adding state). Nothing referenced the form in the e2e suite or the walkthrough, so there was nothing to re-point.

- **T-341 — Library removal: withdraw, then the owner organisation removes.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-27** (no migration — it reuses T-340's `purge_events` and its append-only carve-out; api 418/418, full check green). ADR-0050 §7, and the answer to the realistic V1 incident — the first real corpus load is also the first real test, so a document belonging to a *different client* going in is the failure to design for. **Two steps, and the first is already built:** `containers.state = 'live'` is a pre-filter *inside* the retrieval query ([retrieval.ts:90](../../packages/knowledge/src/retrieval.ts#L90)), so **withdraw already stops grounding** in the same statement as the wall — no work. This ticket is the second step: the **owner organisation** removes a **withdrawn** container from the library, **on request from the producing organisation**. **The authority is the point** — the lever sits with the party whose library it is (ADR-0016; ADR-0026 Filter 1), and putting it in the producing firm's hand would let a consultancy erase six months of corpus ahead of a dispute, leaving every citation in every accepted deliverable resolving to nothing. **Removal means erased, not delisted** — same derived-store reach as T-340. **Refused on a container that is not withdrawn**, so the two steps cannot be collapsed into one click. | *(Deps: T-340)*
  ✅ **This closes T-340's third Done-when clause**, and it was verified **before** the act was built rather than assumed: a probe test cites a version, erases its chunks, and reads the run's context back. `unreconstructable` fires, `content` and `locator` come back null. The reason it works is worth recording — **a run's evidence lives in `steps.source_set`, which is jsonb and carries no foreign key**, so erasing a version cannot touch it. `citations` rows *do* go, because their FK to `versions` compels it and the CHECK forbids nulling the column; harmless, because ADR-0050 §7's guarantee rests on the step record rather than on that table.
  ⚠ **Refused on a container carrying a work item or a review cycle, and this is where §7 and §8 pull against each other.** §7 says removal erases; §8 says the owner **retains the deliverables and the review-cycle metadata, named individuals included**. Erasing a deliverable that has been through a cycle would destroy a signed-off record to solve a problem that record does not have. The ticket's own stated incident settles it — *"a document belonging to a different client going in"* is **loaded reference material**, which has no work item and no cycle (T-304) — so removal is scoped to exactly that, and removing a produced deliverable is left **unruled rather than decided by an implementation**. A `has_review_record` refusal says so by name.
  **The refusals carry the ticket; the erasure is T-340's machinery reused** — the same `infora.purge` carve-out, `deleteChunksForVersions`, `deleteBlob`, and the same `purge_events` register with `subject_kind: 'library_container'`. One register rather than two: both are acts of erasure with a name against them, and one place to look beats two. The typed confirmation is the **deliverable reference**, checked server-side.
  **A shape worth noticing:** removal's tier is *not* purge's. Purge reaches an organisation's **own** material, so an org admin holds it; removal reaches the **owner's library**, so the check is against the project's owning organisation rather than against the caller's claim.
- **T-342 — The conflict register's `reason`: narrow its purpose on screen.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-04** (no migration, no contract change — the guidance beside the field in the T-246 declaration panel: placeholder *"Why — the fact, not the client"* plus a hint naming a worked example, *"bid team conflict" rather than naming the other side*, and stating that it is kept for whoever reviews the wall later, which is why the field survives at all). ADR-0050 §3's minimisation half, and the cheapest real reduction available. `conflict_exclusions.reason` is nullable free text ([drawer1-parties.ts:196](../../packages/db/src/schema/drawer1-parties.ts#L196)) and is the **single field that turns "a person and two project ids" into a client roster** — which matters because ADR-0046 §7 puts the register on the ADR-0018 private floor while a break-glass operator reads it regardless, and encryption was rejected on a finding (the operator controls the deployment and therefore the key). **The field stays** — a compliance partner reviewing a two-year-old wall needs the why. What changes is the guidance beside it in the T-246 declaration panel: **record the fact, not the client.** Small, and it is the difference between a useful note and a disclosure. | *(Deps: none)*

**Review Surface follow-ups** *(owner feedback on the built screens, 2026-08-06 — the slice closed and the owner drove it; these are the residue with numbers. T-351–T-353.)* Also in the same feedback, without numbers: the mockup-diff display fixes (org under every name, badge noise, revision context, the days-left countdown, the "for organisation" clause on the acknowledgement) and the elevation ruling — **cards keep the design system's nested-card treatment; the pane-elevation experiment was tried and reverted the same day.**
- **T-351 — Acknowledge widens to confirmed reviewers.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-06** (ADR-0051 addendum, owner-ruled: the review group is who receives the submission into review; a project whose lead reviewer is not owner-side must not park every round behind the owner's inbox). Guard: owner organisation **or live confirmed reviewer** — proposal confers nothing (ADR-0033). The surface states on whose behalf the receipt was fired. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-352 — The lead reviewer manages the review group from the status page.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-06** (ADR-0033 addendum). The Plan screen's appointment drawer stays; this page gained the same acts where the coordination actually happens. **The wall shaped the split:** a live confirmed **lead reviewer** proposes from the visible roster (non-confirming unless owner-side — confirmation stays the owner's act, ADR-0015/0033 unchanged) and revokes (narrowing is always wall-safe). Build note: the two handlers stepped off `scoped()`/`planVisible`, whose owner/producer pair the lead may sit outside — the lead's own confirmed grant is their sight. **Residual, deliberately not built:** a *third-org* reviewer's status page still shows no plan row (plan visibility is owner/producer by design, ADR-0008) — widening that is a wall question, not a UI fix. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-353 — Per-reviewer completion.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-06** ([ADR-0052](../architecture/adr/0052-per-reviewer-completion-signal.md), migration 0041). *"Has each reviewer finished?"* became storable: `review_completions`, one row per (round, participant), marked and withdrawn by the reviewer **only while the round is open** — the set freezes at issue with no trigger, and no count of completions gates the lead's issue (the ADR-0005 no-gate rule held). **Walled like the open round's comments (ADR-0014)**, phased server-side in the cycle read. The Reviewers card shows live state to the group and owner, standing completions after issue, and the viewer-reviewer's own mark/resume act. Register row extended. | *(Deps: T-351)*

**Code-review findings** *(the 2026-08-09 component-5 review and T-368's verification, both run for the user-story narrative — the residue with numbers.)*
- **T-354 — The response's change link, actually sendable.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-09.** ADR-0004's rule — *point at the change in vN+1, or say explicitly that none was made* — was in the contract and unreachable from both response forms, which hard-defaulted a `noChangeReason`; every response on record claimed "no change made". **The sequencing was the real bug:** vN+1 does not exist while the respond phase runs (promotion is gated on the responses), so a respond-time `nextVersionId` was never obtainable. The link is now **declared as the revised passage** (`nextVersionAnchor.quote`, the contract's XOR moved off the version id) and **promotion stamps `nextVersionId`** on the change-declared responses when it creates the version they point into; both forms gained the two-way choice, and the DRR renders the pointer ("Changed in P02 — *quote*"). **Residual, named:** the interactive jump from a response to its highlighted change in the vN+1 PDF is not built. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-355 — The internal QA cycle gets its surface, and the QA gate becomes policy.** *(Grown in place 2026-08-09 by the DMS walkthrough session's S9 — same number, wider spec.)* The org-private freeze → QA round → QA-accepted promotion path is **API-complete and e2e-proven** (`slice-a.spec.ts` runs it end to end) and unreachable from any screen: the cycle screen resolves its deliverable via `GET /plan`, which filters `scope='library'`, so a sandbox-scope QA container renders "not on a plan you can see" — and no surface appoints an internal reviewer either. Admit the freeze container to the cycle read for its own organisation (the wall is untouched — the container is org-private by scope; a dedicated sandbox-side row read is the clean cut — widening `GET /plan` would make `documentReference` nullable for every consumer), and surface staffing and the QA round from the sandbox / status side (the roster UI at [deliverable-status.tsx](../../apps/web/src/screens/deliverable-status.tsx) already speaks the grant endpoints, which auto-confirm at sandbox scope, [plan.ts:455](../../apps/api/src/plan.ts#L455)). **Plus S9's gate (ADR-0032 addendum):** `sandboxes` gains *promotion requires QA acceptance* — **default ON for project sandboxes, off for personal ones** — beside the folder toggle in the settings modal (with T-365's mode, the settings are now folder mode ×3 + the QA gate). With the gate on, the live-head promotion source at [cycle.ts:701](../../apps/api/src/cycle.ts#L701) is **refused** (`409 qa_acceptance_required`) unless the latest freeze cycle is `accepted`; `PromotionResult` states **which source promoted**, and the promote surface carries the drift notice — what promotes is the QA-accepted frozen version, never the head as it has drifted since QA. ✅ **Built 2026-08-09** (migration 0045). **Three holes the adversarial review found and closed, each worth recording:** the gate reads the *drafting* sandbox, and nothing binds a plan row's draft to the team's area — so create-in-personal-workspace → bind → promote walked around it with no elevation and no visible act; the gate is therefore **on for every sandbox**, personal included (scratch work is unbound and cannot promote, so the exemption bought nothing). **One promotion per QA acceptance:** re-promoting after a rejecting round silently re-issued the *same* frozen content while the responses claimed changes — now `409 qa_acceptance_stale` until a fresh freeze and pass. And an internal **"revise" verdict was a dead end** — the freeze container carries reviewers but no authors, so nobody could answer the comments (403 `authors_only`), the head could never be re-frozen and never promoted; a sandbox-scope cycle now takes its authoring side from the deliverable's own library row. **Residual, named:** "this acceptance was spent" is *inferred* from a timestamp comparison (newest issued version vs the QA cycle's `closedAt`) rather than recorded — it fails closed and is correct for every sequential flow, but a `versions.source_round_id` would make it a fact and let the surface name which revision spent it. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-376 — `null` means two things on the plan screen, and one of them reopens invented references.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22.** *(Found 2026-08-22 by the Slice Walkthrough 2 capture — an e2e flake was the symptom, and the cause is in the product.)* [plan.tsx:648](../../apps/web/src/screens/plan.tsx#L648) holds the naming scheme as `NamingScheme | null` filled by an async read, and the New-deliverable modal branches on it: `scheme ? coded dropdowns : a manual reference field`. So **`null` carries "this project has no scheme" and "the scheme has not arrived yet" in one value**, and the UI renders the same thing for both. Two consequences. **The manual branch has no reachable state:** `GET /naming-scheme` never returns null — `loadSchemeOrDefault` serves the Infora default when nothing is saved (T-188) — so it is an unlabelled *loading* state wearing the costume of a configuration, and opening the modal fast gives you a reference field you can type into which is then swapped out under you. **And a failed read degrades to hand-typing:** there is no `.catch` on that effect, so a rejection leaves `scheme` null forever and the modal presents manual reference entry as though it were the project's setting — quietly reopening the thing ADR-0008 exists to close (*the reference is generated, never invented*). **The contract let the ambiguity in:** `GetNamingSchemeResponse` is `NamingScheme | null` and is never null. Make the type honest, give the screen a real three-state (loading / ready / failed) with creation **refused** rather than degraded when the scheme cannot be read, and delete the dead branch. The e2e flake at [slice-a2-ui.spec.ts:42](../../e2e/tests/slice-a2-ui.spec.ts#L42) — which branches on the same race — then needs no test-side fix at all, which is the tell that the repair is in the right place. **What it uncovered is worth as much as what it fixed:** the manual branch was an accidental escape hatch, and deleting it made two flakes hiding behind it deterministic — both **T-369**, fixed alongside. The lesson generalises past this screen: an optional type is a claim that the absent case is *reachable and meaningful*, and where it is neither, some surface eventually invents a meaning for it. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-369 — The plan-seed test asserts on a position it does not own.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22**, alongside T-376, which turned it from intermittent into deterministic and so forced it. *(Found 2026-08-09 verifying T-368 — it failed once, then passed on three consecutive runs, which is the tell.)* `sandbox-structure.spec.ts:61` creates one plan row with `discipline: 'ECV'` and then asserts the builder's **first** proposed folder name matches `/ECV/` — but the T-363 seed derives one candidate per **distinct discipline on the whole organisation's plan**, ordered, so `first()` is only ECV while nothing sorts before it. `slice-a2-ui.spec.ts:45` drives the New-deliverable modal by selecting `{ index: 1 }` on every combobox, and index 1 of the discipline field is **`CCA`** — the first entry in the default scheme's discipline list, and alphabetically ahead of ECV. Both suites share the seeded database and `fullyParallel: false` only serialises *within* a file, so whether the CCA row exists yet is a matter of which file a worker picked up first. **The assertion is the defect, not the ordering:** the test should match its own row's candidate wherever it sits (filter the inputs by value, or assert the row it created is present among them) rather than assume position — pinning the execution order would hide the same fragility in the next test that seeds a discipline. Worth a sweep for the sibling pattern: any `.first()` assertion over a list the shared seed can grow. **As built, and the sweep found the bigger half:** the assertion now polls the candidate inputs' live values for its own row wherever it sits, rather than reading `.first()`. But the diagnosis above named the real defect and stopped short of acting on it — *"`fullyParallel: false` only serialises within a file"* — and that is a **configuration** claiming a guarantee it does not give: the comment beside it said *"suites share the seeded database"* while the files were being handed to five workers. The sharper case is not ordering at all: `slice-a2` **replaces the project-wide coding scheme** mid-suite while `slice-a2-ui` is driving the New-deliverable modal against it, so the modal's selections stop matching the scheme between render and click and creation is refused. No assertion can be written around that — it is two tests owning one piece of mutable global state. `workers: 1` is the honest version of the intent the comment already had; the whole suite runs in under thirty seconds, so the parallelism was never paying for the flakes it bought. **Second pass, 2026-08-23 (the audit's finding):** the sweep had missed a file and half the mutation — `ontology.spec.ts` read `plan.items[0]`/`library.items[0]` off reference-ordered lists that three sibling suites plant earlier-sorting rows into (passing purely by file order, which `workers: 1` hides rather than fixes), and `slice-a2` replaced the project-wide coding scheme with **no restore**, so a second local run of any suite met the WA/BB-CC/GEO-ENV scheme instead of the seeded default — serialisation orders mutations, it does not undo them. Both closed: the reads are named, and `slice-a2` puts the Infora default back in `afterAll`. | *(Deps: none)*

### Slice Walkthrough 2 audit findings

- **T-377 — The lead swap could not be performed, and in one configuration destroyed the appointment.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22.** The promotion window fired the swap as revoke-then-grant, and both halves were wrong. **The revoke:** a producing-side caller may only retract an *unconfirmed* proposal ([plan.ts](../../apps/api/src/plan.ts) revocation guard), so the mockup's State B — the scenario the window exists for — aborted at its first act with a bare "not found", after permanently applying any staged removals of unconfirmed reviewers ("Undo means never happened" was false the moment Promote was clicked). **The gate:** `resolvePromotion` demanded a *confirmed* lead, while ADR-0033 §1 says *"replacing the lead stalls that round"* — the submission exists and waits — and the approved mockup drew Promote clickable with the new lead badged Proposed; where the promoting author happened also to be the confirmed lead reviewer, the revoke *succeeded*, the grant landed unconfirmed, the promotion refused 409, and the deliverable was left with no live lead and nothing rolled back (reproduced live). **As built:** promotion accepts a **named** lead — proposed is enough; the confirmed-and-accepted gates stay on the acknowledgement where ADR-0051 put them — and the swap is **one transactional act**, `POST /containers/:id/lead-reviewer`, revoking the standing lead and writing the new proposal together, because the one-live-lead invariant makes the pair inseparable. The revocation endpoint additionally admits the producing side's row-editors (ADR-0008 addendum: the lead author *"may amend the review group"*; revocation only narrows access, so the wall is untouched). The window fires the swap as that one act, enables Promote when the only blocker is the very lead the staged swap creates, and refuses client-side when a lead is staged-removed with no replacement named. E2e now drives State B end to end — the half no run ever drove, which is how it shipped broken. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-378 — A failed scheme read could wipe the project's coding scheme.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22.** T-376 fixed "loading wearing the costume of configuration" on the plan screen and missed the same shape one screen over, where it writes: [schema.tsx](../../apps/web/src/screens/schema.tsx) loaded the scheme with no `.catch`, a failed read left the editor showing an empty field table, and Save would have written that emptiness back over the real scheme. The editor now holds the plan screen's three-state (loading / ready / failed) and **saving is refused, not degraded**, until the real scheme has arrived; the failed state says so beside the disabled button. The sandbox screen's cosmetic read gains its missing `.catch`. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-379 — The wall is one discipline, not one screen's.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22.** T-375 walled the record screen and the audit found two siblings still asserting the absence the wall denies: the cycle screen rendered *"No comments yet — the round is open to the review group"* to the walled side — the exact sentence the record's e2e forbids, one click from the record via its own "Open the round" button — and the status page drew a "Reviewing" badge for every confirmed reviewer off a withheld-empty completions list, asserting "nobody has finished" from data the server refused to send. The cycle screen now states the withheld notice; the contract gains `Round.completionsWithheld` beside `commentsWithheld` (an empty array alone cannot tell "none" from "not yours to know"), computed in the same server-side phasing, and the badge stands down when it is set. E2e now visits the cycle screen as the walled side. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-380 — The refused promotion window contradicted itself on screen.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22.** A preflight that refuses carries no real source decision — the API fills `source: 'head'` as a placeholder — so the very window showing the QA-gate refusal also asserted *"The QA gate is off for this sandbox… Nothing has assured this revision internally"*, flatly false, and photographed into the walkthrough's beat 10. The window now renders the source claims and the "What promotes" card only when the preflight succeeds; a refused preflight states the refusal and nothing the refusal makes unknowable. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-381 — The target date the user was shown was not the date the server stored.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22.** [addWorkingDays](../../apps/api/src/review-period.ts) counts working days in UTC; the window's Target preview counted them in the browser's local time, so whenever the local clock and UTC sat on different calendar days at the click — evenings in the Americas — the preview and the stored target disagreed by a day, with the round going overdue a day before the date the window promised (US Pacific, Friday 18:00, one working day: preview Monday, stored target renders Sunday — computed, not speculated). The preview now walks the same UTC arithmetic as the server, so the two cannot disagree. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-382 — The window's "what promotes" promise, made honest under concurrency.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22.** The preflight and the act run the same decision function, so the *gates* could never drift — but the *statements* could: a fresh QA acceptance landing between the window opening and Promote being clicked would silently promote different content than the version the window named, with no re-confirmation. The promotion body now carries `expectedSourceVersionReference` — the source the caller was shown, null for the head — and the POST refuses `409 promotion_state_changed` when the answer has changed; omitted, no check, so bare callers and tests are untouched. | *(Deps: T-373)*

### Slice Walkthrough 2

- **T-371 — The review period gains an owner.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22** (migration 0046). ADR-0005 gave a round *"a configurable review period"* and never said who configures it or when, and the build shows the cost: `rounds.review_period_target` shipped ([drawer5-review.ts:125](../../packages/db/src/schema/drawer5-review.ts#L125)), the contract exposes it ([endpoints.ts:822](../../packages/contracts/src/endpoints.ts#L822)), the status bar renders a target date **and an overdue state** ([cycle-status-bar.tsx:98](../../apps/web/src/cycle-status-bar.tsx#L98)) — and nothing anywhere sets the value. Chrome ready and permanently idle. Migration: a project-level default of **ten working days**, set on [schema.tsx](../../apps/web/src/screens/schema.tsx) as its **own settings section and deliberately not a schema attribute field** — the schema's fields are the header row of the fillable deliverables template (T-337/T-359), so a review period modelled as one would arrive as a column nobody should be filling in. Round creation computes the target from the promotion timestamp; **working days are Monday to Friday with no holiday calendar** — none is modelled anywhere and a per-jurisdiction one is a separate job, not an implementation guess. The period's *power* is unchanged: it chases and flags overdue, and only the lead reviewer closes a round — which is exactly why the producing side may set it (a guide carries no access consequence, unlike the review group sitting in the same window). The reminders that chase the date stay with Slice V1-N. **As built:** the default is `projects.review_period_default_days`, its own settings section on the schema screen and its own endpoint pair — never a `NamingSchemeField`, so it cannot reach the deliverables template as a column. The target is computed at **every** round creation, the internal QA round included (ADR-0032's one workflow at two scopes renders the same status bar, so exempting it would have left the same idle chrome one scope down). The per-submission override landed with T-373. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-372 — The lead reviewer accepts the appointment, or declines it.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22** (migration 0047). Appointment has until now been something two organisations do *about* a person — proposed by one side, confirmed by the other — with **no act anywhere in which the named person says yes**. A lead reviewer holds the deliverable's contractual verdict, and nobody can give that undertaking on someone else's behalf. Migration: `deliverable_reviewers` gains an acceptance timestamp and a decline reason. **Two consequences fall out of rules already in place rather than new ones:** where the appointee is owner-side, **acceptance *is* the confirmation** — a proposal is non-confirming *"unless the proposer is owner-side"* (ADR-0033, 2026-08-06) and they are — so appointment and access collapse into one click; where they sit **outside** the owner organisation, which a lead reviewer may ([plan.ts:740](../../apps/api/src/plan.ts#L740)), the owner confirms first because that is where ADR-0015's share-first invariant runs, and the appointee then accepts for themselves. The `no_lead_reviewer` precondition that already refused to open a round without a *confirmed* lead ([cycle.ts:668](../../apps/api/src/cycle.ts#L668)) now reads *accepted*. A declined or unanswered appointment stalls the submission **visibly and indefinitely** — no clock, in keeping with ADR-0005 — and the way out is **re-appointment, never an override**, because an override here would be one person giving an undertaking in another's name. Surface on [deliverable-status.tsx](../../apps/web/src/screens/deliverable-status.tsx): your own row reads differently from everyone else's, an undertaking card states the duty in four lines, Accept / Decline with a reason. **Closes T-355's named staffing residual too** — no screen appoints the first *internal QA* lead reviewer either, and it is the same act at the other scope. Personal data: the decline reason is a named person's stated refusal and is registered ([personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md)). **As built, and one correction to the spec above:** the acceptance gate landed on the **acknowledgement**, not on promotion. The line reference above points at the promotion guard, but ADR-0033's own words are that the precondition *"refused to open a round"* — and since ADR-0051 what opens a round is the receipt. Both approved mockups show P01 promoting and then sitting unacknowledged while the appointment is unanswered, and ADR-0051's addendum of the same session says it outright (*"until a lead reviewer has accepted, nobody may acknowledge"*). Promotion still needs a **confirmed** lead; refusing it would have erased the stalled state the surface exists to show. A **decline does not revoke**: the interval stays open and the refusal stands on the record, while the one-live-lead index (and its application-side twin) excludes it, so a refusal never blocks the replacement it exists to ask for. **Residual, named:** the internal QA *second freeze* — the one that opens the round once a lead stands — is still an API act; the Editor cannot offer it while the head is locked. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-373 — The promotion window.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22.** Promotion was one click and no form at all ([sandbox.tsx:992](../../apps/web/src/screens/sandbox.tsx#L992)) — which was ADR-0008's deliberate design, because a form filled in the moment is a form filled wrong. The walk kept the principle and added the surface: a window that **reconfirms** rather than composes. Read-only: the plan-owned identity metadata (ADR-0038 §2) and **which version is promoting** — the QA-accepted frozen one, with who accepted it (T-355). Editable: authoring metadata, the review group **including which reviewer is lead** (new — no rule previously let the producing side touch `is_lead`), and the review period from T-371. The click-through risk ADR-0008 named does not return, because the risky fields are locked and a thoughtless confirm produces exactly the plan's state. **Every reviewer control writes a proposal** — confirmation stays owner-side, so a producing organisation still cannot open the wall from this window. It reopens at **every** promotion, which earns its place at round two more than round one: six months and a staffing change later, the alternative is silently inheriting a review group named at planning and never looked at since. States the consequence of a lead swap *before* it is committed — the round waits until the new lead accepts (T-372). **As built:** `PromotionPreflight` is served from `resolvePromotion`, the one function the POST also runs, because a preflight computed apart from the act eventually lies about the act; its `blocker` is data rather than a status, so the window renders the refusal beside a disabled Promote. Reviewer edits are **staged**, which is what lets the lead-swap consequence be stated before it is committed and makes Undo mean *never happened*; they apply revoke-before-grant so a swap clears the one-live-lead invariant. Wired at **all three** entrances — the sandbox row, the Editor and the cycle screen's next-version act. The promotion body itself takes only `reviewPeriodDays`: the reviewer and metadata edits stay their own audited acts, so the window sequences acts rather than becoming a composite write. | *(Deps: T-371, T-372)*
- **T-374 — Acknowledgement narrows to the lead reviewer.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22.** ⚠ **This supersedes T-351, which is not a bug — read it first.** The guard at [cycle.ts:150](../../apps/api/src/cycle.ts#L150) is `owner_organisation_or_reviewer_only`, and that is exactly what T-351 deliberately built on 2026-08-06: gating on the owner organisation alone would park every round behind a firm with no stake in its pace. The owner narrowed it on 2026-08-22 to **the lead reviewer alone, or the owner organisation's super user when the lead is away** — the single accountable receiver ADR-0051 §3 explicitly parked (*"deliberately not built until asked for"*), role-derived rather than ADR-0035's named controller. The earlier argument is **answered rather than discarded**: this does not gate on the owner organisation — it gates on the lead reviewer, who may sit outside it and who fires the receipt in the ordinary case. What goes is a non-lead reviewer signing for a submission they do not run, and an owner participant who is not elevated. **Also gated on an accepted appointment** (T-372): until a lead has accepted, *nobody* may acknowledge — the super user included — because the override covers the **receipt**, never the **undertaking**; a super user facing an absent lead re-appoints. Narrative fix rides along: the walkthrough's acknowledge beat describes the pre-narrowing rule. **As built:** the detail code went with the ruling — `owner_organisation_or_reviewer_only` → `lead_reviewer_or_owner_super_user_only` — because a client still naming the owner organisation would describe a gate that no longer consults it. **No elevated refusal is recorded** on a rejected attempt: that register (T-301) holds destructive lifecycle acts, and a receipt is not one. The who-gate is checked *before* the acceptance gate, so a bystander is told the act is not theirs rather than handed the state of an appointment they have no part in. The cycle suite's round-2 acknowledgement — which existed to prove T-351's widening — now proves its supersession from the same fixture, with the earlier reasoning carried inline. | *(Deps: T-372)*
- **T-375 — The review record as one appended table.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-22.** No ADR changes — [component-5](../architecture/components/component-5-document-management.md) has named *"the DRR table interface"* as this surface since it was written, and the build drew round cards instead: [cycle.tsx](../../apps/web/src/screens/cycle.tsx) renders comments as a div grid with each round's deliverable code as a badge in its header. **This is a drift that exists today regardless of the walk**, which is why it depends on nothing. One continuous table either side can open — every comment in order with its location, code, author and response, each round closed off by the deliverable code it concluded with, appended to as rounds open, so the chapter's whole review history reads in one scroll rather than a sheet per round (the thing ADR-0009 refused to materialise). `packages/ui/src/table.tsx` exists. **The wall is a different record, not a hidden column:** for the authoring side the open round's rows are *absent*, not greyed, under a stated withheld notice — silence would read as absence, which is a different and wrong fact — enforced in the server's read as ADR-0014 already is. **No export control anywhere on the screen**, deliberately: ADR-0009 dropped the DRN and a download button here would quietly reinstate it — and the e2e run asserts the absence, because a negative nobody tests is a negative that comes back. **As built:** the wall needed a contract field — `Round.commentsWithheld`, because `comments: []` cannot tell *none were written* from *not yours to read yet* — computed in the same server-side phasing that already drops the comments, with the surface's counts taken off what arrived rather than the whole record. **The mockup's one open fork is not settled:** it left *pane or tab* marked *needs your yes/no*, and the record was built as its own pane because that is the form the mockup **drew**; the confirmation it asked for is carried as **`Q-041`**. The cycle screen keeps the round under review as the working surface (PDF beside composer, the anchored hover intact); its collapsible per-round sheets — the rendering being replaced — give way to a pointer at the record. | *(Deps: none)*

### Slice Document Status

*Ruled 2026-08-27 by the document-status session (amendments to ADR-0013, ADR-0003, ADR-0041, ADR-0045, the ADR-0011 rider and ADR-0049; closing `Q-036`), built from 2026-08-28. Records move here ticket by ticket as they close.*

- **T-383 — Migration 0048: the grounding rule and who withdrew.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** — **as migration 0052, not 0048.** `acceptance_codes` gains `is_contractual` and `grounds`; `containers` gains `withdrawn_by_participant_id`. Seed the default scheme from the **2021** NA — ⚠ **not the 2018 table**, which most free material still reproduces and in which `S5` meant *withdrawn*, `S6`/`S7` and `CR` existed and `A2` implied a RIBA stage. `container_state` is **unchanged** — all four values shipped from the start. Drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md); hand-written, journal appended by hand, atlas regenerated. **As built, and three things the spec did not settle** *(and one correction, added in review: "hand-written, journal appended by hand" above described the pre-T-344 convention — as built the migration is drizzle-kit **generated** on the re-synced snapshot, with the `grounds` backfill hand-added and the journal entry generated with it)*. (1) **The migration number in the title and the drawing was already taken** — `0048_pdf-document-format` is T-305's, landed the same day the drawing was made. This is **0052**, and the drawing's label is corrected in this commit, where the drawn block also reduces to narrative + pointer under [data-model.md](data-model.md)'s state rule. (2) **The seeded scheme is `S0`–`S5` and `A1` only**, in [acceptance-code-seed.ts](../../packages/db/src/acceptance-code-seed.ts) — a copy-at-creation module beside `ontology-seed.ts`, replacing the four hand-written `A/B/C/D` rows in the seed. `A1` is the sole Published code because the NA rules that *the reason for each `An` code must be written into the project's information standard*: a default that invented meanings for `A2`–`A5` would be asserting exactly what the standard refuses to fix, and T-390's editor is what lets a firm add its own. `B1`/`Bn` is deprecated and therefore not seeded, though a project may still add it. Every code stays `level: 'both'`, as the previous default was — the NA has no comment-grain verdict codes and inventing a split was not this ticket's to make. (3) **The migration backfills rather than defaulting.** Both columns default `false`, which is the restrictive and therefore visible direction for new rows; but for rows written *before* the migration, acceptance **was** admission **was** grounding, so a bare default would have silently stopped every already-accepted deliverable grounding in any existing database. The hand-added backfill sets both from `is_accepting`, reproducing the pre-migration rule exactly for data written under it. E2e's two hard-coded assertions on the old `A — Accepted` code move to `A1`; every other test picks its code by `isAccepting` and needed no change. | *(Deps: none)*
- **T-384 — The withdrawal guard follows the publication boundary.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28.** Producer-only pre-publication (T-189's existing guard, correct and kept), owner-only once the container is in the library, with a producer **propose** path. Records which side acted. **This is where `Q-036`'s ruling becomes code**, and the guard it replaces is unconditional. **As built:** the two acts that share the word *withdrawal* are separated by `containers.in_library` and nothing else — pre-publication the owner is answered **404**, not 403, because that is already what the plan tells one organisation about another's unpublished rows; published, the owner writes the state and the producer's identical `POST /containers/:id/withdrawal` **proposes** instead. **The proposal had nowhere drawn to live.** The slice's migration drew two columns and explicitly enumerated what it left undrawn (context state) without naming a proposal table, so a proposal rides **the same two columns as a withdrawal**, with record state telling them apart: reason + proposer recorded while `state` is still `live`. Nothing is in force — the deliverable is in the library and **still grounds** until the owner answers — and `withdrawnReason` is suppressed in the contract while a proposal stands, because one column meaning two things is tolerable in the store and not in a surface. The owner answers on `POST /containers/:id/withdrawal-proposal/resolution`: accepting withdraws it **under the proposer's own reason** (rewriting it in the owner's words would lose the only account of why), while **re-stamping `withdrawn_by` to the confirming owner participant** — §5 asks which side *withdrew* it, and once published the answer is the owner, which is exactly what T-385's restore rule then reads. **The elevated tier gates the proposal too**: T-362 lists withdraw among the acts a row's lead author does not hold, and asking a client to end a published deliverable is not a smaller act than removing an unpublished plan row. **Not built, and not in the ticket:** the producer cannot retract its own standing proposal — it asks the owner to decline. | *(Deps: T-383)*
- **T-386 — Confirming a `supersedes` edge sets record state, and the owner confirms.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28.** Today confirmation writes the edge and touches nothing else. Proposal stays open to either party; on a **library** container only the owner confirms ([ontology.ts](../../apps/api/src/ontology.ts) currently makes all relationship writes a producing-organisation act). **As built:** confirmation authority keys on the edge's **target**, not on its source, because the target is the container a confirmation writes to — a `supersedes` edge *into a library container* sets that container's record state, and a record in the owner's library is the owner's (ADR-0045 amendment §1/§2 read together with ADR-0013 §2). A target that is not yet published is unchanged: the producing organisation's own record, its own edge to confirm. Both endpoints must be **visible to the writer**, which was already true of proposal and was not of confirm/retire — the wall does not open because an edge points through it. **Only `live` is overwritten:** a target already `withdrawn` or `rejected` is in a state a person set for a reason, and since none of the three grounds there is nothing to gain by restating it and a reason to lose. **Retiring a confirmed `supersedes` edge returns the target to `live`** when no other confirmed, un-retired one still points at it — ADR-0045 §1 grants the consequence to a confirmed **and un-retired** edge, and this is the *only* way back from `superseded`: nothing withdrew the container, so T-385's restore rule has no act to read. | *(Deps: T-383)* **Follow-up in its own commit (e43a026), added in review: the ontology e2e now confirms the edge as the owner and asserts the producer’s confirm is refused with 404 — the suite had been confirming as the producer, the very act this ticket makes impossible.**
- **T-385 — Restoration stops being symmetric.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28.** Reads `withdrawn_by` to decide who may undo. As built either side could restore what the other withdrew with neither act recording the other; the comment justifying it (*"recovery is never a helpdesk ticket"*) was reasoning about a producer undoing its own mistake. **As built:** an owner-side withdrawal is the owner's to undo and the producer is **403**, not 404 — it can see the container, so denial-reads-as-nonexistence would be a lie here; a producer's withdrawal is undoable by the producer **and by the owner**, which is §5's own second clause and is coherent rather than lopsided, because the owner may un-break where it may not break (it has no withdrawal act on an unpublished row at all). **Two things fell out that the ticket did not name.** A withdrawal recorded **before migration 0052** carries no actor, so the publication boundary stands in for the missing row — pre-publication only the producer could have acted, in the library only the owner — which is exactly what the absent record would have said. And restoration now **refuses anything that is not `withdrawn`** (409 `not_withdrawn`), where it previously set `state = 'live'` from whatever it found: with T-386 landed that would have been a second, unguarded way back from `superseded`, bypassing the retire-the-edge path and leaving a container live while a confirmed edge still said it was superseded. The elevated tier and its refusal record are untouched, and are still checked **before** the authority rule, so an unelevated member is told the act is above their tier rather than handed the state of a withdrawal they have no part in. | *(Deps: T-384)*
- **T-387 — The grounding filter gains the code clause.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28.** ⚠ **The sensitive one:** it changes what the AI can answer from, and it fails **silently and asymmetrically** — too permissive is invisible (answers cite what they should not, and every citation still resolves), too restrictive is visible (answers thin, users complain). Weight the test effort toward the invisible direction. Retrieval joins the accepting round's code and checks `grounds`, beside the existing `state = 'live'` — which **is** genuinely in the retrieval SQL as a pre-filter, verified 2026-08-27 at [retrieval.ts:96](../../packages/knowledge/src/retrieval.ts#L96) with a `withdrawn` unit test, so there is no latent bug to fix first. **Four conditions, all of them the point of the ticket.** (1) **New eval cases, not just a re-run.** The seed set covers version-level supersession (TRAP-01) and container state is unit-tested, but **nothing asserts an absence for a non-grounding code** — so a broken-permissive build passes the whole suite unchanged. Write `must_not_cite` cases against a deliverable admitted under a non-grounding code (the harness supports the shape; PERM-02 uses it for the wall), **and keep them in this ticket** — a control split into its own ticket is a control that can be deferred away from the thing it controls. Run the suite either side regardless. (2) **The clause lands inside the assembly gateway, never in a caller** — ADR-0029 §4 puts baseline assembly and targeted sub-agent retrieval on one call precisely so guarantees hold in both modes, and this is the first new pre-filter clause since; in one path only, an agentic sub-agent reaches what the baseline excluded. (3) **Measure before optimising.** The join is container → accepting round → code, on a path that also carries the wall filter. That depth is an *inferred* risk, not a measured one — build the join, measure it against the seeded corpus, **denormalise the immutable half only if the number justifies it**, and record the number either way (ADR-0013 §6 permits caching *which* code admitted a container, and forbids caching the answer). (4) **The code's own `grounds` flag is read live**, because T-390's screen promises a count about the next query. | *(Deps: T-383)* **As built, and the numbers the ticket asked for.** The clause is one SQL scalar subquery inside `liveLibraryFilter` — the filter BOTH arms of the one gateway call share, so condition (2) holds by construction and the lexical arm is covered as well as the vector one (a case asserts it, because naming a code in the question is the path most likely to reach past a filter applied to similarity alone). **The null is load-bearing:** `is not false` admits a container with no accepting round at all, which is owner-added reference material (T-304 — no work item, no cycle, no code). A clause demanding a grounding code would have silently emptied the reference half of every project library, which the ticket's own framing predicts: that is the RESTRICTIVE failure, and it is the visible one. **Condition (3), measured and not inferred:** interleaved over the dev corpus (1,847 chunks, 1,749 candidate rows before the clause and 1,724 after) the join's median was **2.7 ms against 8.4 ms for the same query without it** — the clause is not a cost at this size at all, because pruning containers before the vector sort pays for the join several times over. **Nothing is denormalised**, and the number is why. The corpus is small against v1.md's 100–500 documents, so the honest claim is that no cost was found rather than that none exists at scale. **Condition (1):** `hollowfield-reservoir-4`, the fourth fixture — the first able to say HOW a deliverable was admitted (`acceptance_codes` + `admitted_by`, materialised as a closed cycle whose round carries the code, because retrieval reads that join and a fixture that only set `in_library` would declare a state the product cannot reach) — and `TRAP-04` on it, whose two documents disagree on a figure so a wrong reliance shows in the answer's own words. Verified BOTH ways: with the clause removed, `TRAP-04` fails on `must_not_cite` **and** on `must_not_contain`, and five of the six unit cases fail. **One thing the ticket did not settle:** `TRAP-04` sorts after `TRAP-01`, so the smoke tier's one-per-category rule leaves it to the nightly `full` run. The deterministic half of the control therefore lives in `packages/knowledge/src/retrieval.test.ts`, which `pnpm run check` runs on every commit — a control this quiet should not wait for a nightly tier to be exercised at all.
- **T-388 — Context state on the deliverable read, and the badge that names its reason.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28.** Derived, never stored — *not used for AI answers — superseded* · *— partial sign-off* · *— withdrawn*. A switch that set it independently of its inputs would give the platform two state machines that could disagree. **As built:** one derivation in [context-state.ts](../../apps/api/src/context-state.ts) with **no writer and no endpoint that sets it**, read by both the plan and the library, so the surface cannot re-infer it and become the second state machine itself. It lands on **both** reads because each shows a different half — the library list carries only the live corpus, so it is the only place a *live but out-of-reach* deliverable is visible at all, and the plan is where a `superseded`, `withdrawn` or `rejected` record is actually read. **The reason for a non-grounding code is that code's own description**, not a platform enum: the 2021 National Annex requires each Published code's meaning to be written into the project's information standard, so no phrase Infora could ship would be true of every project — a project whose `B1` reads *"partial sign-off"* gets the ticket's own wording, and one that wrote something else gets that. **A correction to a sentence on the Documents screen fell out of it:** *"Superseded and withdrawn documents leave this list and the grounded corpus together"* had been true and stopped being — since the ADR-0011 rider a deliverable can be **on the list and out of reach**, which is exactly the case the badge exists for. | *(Deps: T-387)*
- **T-389 — The owner's supersede and withdraw actions, and the producer's propose actions.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28.** The buttons that do not exist today, in Documents. Withdrawal takes a **mandatory reason**; its visibility follows the container, so the producing organisation reads it. **As built:** both sides press the **same** control and the publication boundary decides what it does — the owner's *Withdraw…* and the producer's *Propose withdrawal…* are one endpoint (T-384), so the surface cannot drift from the rule. The copy is where the two differ, and it is careful not to overstate: a proposal says *"it stays live and keeps grounding until the owner accepts"*, because it does. **Supersession needed a picker, not a button.** It is an edge and not a state (ADR-0013 §3) — the case it exists for is a *different document* becoming authoritative — so the modal names the replacement, and the owner's press runs **propose then confirm as two calls** rather than a third kind of write: the record then reads proposed-then-confirmed, which is what happened. **A standing proposal sits on its own row**, visible to both sides with the answer offered only to the owner, because a proposal leaves the deliverable live and listed, and the row already carries its reason, its producer and its state. **`LibraryItem` gained `producingOrganisationId`** — `producerName` had been enough while the screen only read, and the first writes on it are exactly the ones where which side you are on decides which act you hold. **The user story's one unbuilt beat is now marked as such:** *"I find out because Infora tells me"* is the notifications slice (T-329–T-332), and until it lands the fact reaches the producing organisation on the Documents screen and the plan rather than by a pointer that arrives. | *(Deps: T-384, T-386)*

- **T-390 — The acceptance-code editor, on the schema screen.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (migration 0053). Read and write API — there is **no write path today**, so a pilot firm cannot represent its own scheme at all, independently of anything AI. Label, `is_accepting`, `is_contractual`, `grounds`; retire-never-redefine enforced; **the blast-radius count per code** (*"this will exclude forty-one deliverables from AI answers"*), which is what makes the screen safe rather than dangerous; audited like a rails change. ⚠ **That count is a promise about the next query**, so this copy is only honest if T-387 reads the `grounds` flag live rather than caching the composite — the two tickets have to agree, and the surface is the one making the claim. | *(Deps: T-383)* **As built, and one migration the slice's drawing did not have.** *"Audited like a rails change"* has nothing to imitate — **rails as scoped records is still undrawn** — and every audit in this repo is instead a purpose-built append-only table, so this ticket drew and built one: `acceptance_code_changes`, one property per row with its old and new value and **the reason in free text**, because a code's history reads as a sequence of decisions rather than of states and the why is the half a diff cannot reconstruct. The changer is a named person and is registered. **Retire-and-replace bites on two properties and deliberately not on the third.** `is_accepting` and `is_contractual` are claims about what ALREADY HAPPENED under the code — that a cycle ended, that a C revision was issued — so once it has been used they are refused (409 `code_in_use_retire_and_replace`). **`grounds` is edited in place**, because it is not a claim about what the code meant but a policy about the next query, ADR-0003 gives it to the owner in as many words, and retire-and-replace could not deliver it anyway: retiring `A3` and adding a replacement would leave every deliverable already admitted under `A3` exactly where it was. What makes that edit safe is the blast radius beside it and the audit behind it, not immutability. **The blast radius counts deliverables, not rounds**, through the same `admittingCodes` derivation retrieval's clause and T-388's badge read — a code named on a round later re-accepted under another admitted nothing, and counting it would make the sentence on screen describe a set that is not the one the next query returns; a test pins that a withdrawn deliverable is not in the number. **`AcceptanceCodeRow` split off from `AcceptanceCode`** rather than widening it, so a round's own verdict does not carry a blast radius nobody asked for.
- **T-391 — The attached-source marker carries the withdrawal reason.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (migration 0054). Pinning an out-of-context document stays legal and deliberate (ADR-0022); the badge names *why* it is out, because that is what separates legitimate use from dangerous use. **As built, and the ticket could not be built as written until one gap was closed.** *"Stays legal"* was true of the rule and not of the build: `attached_source_kind` carried `sandbox | upload | web`, so **a library deliverable could not be pinned at all** — and ADR-0013's own consequences say a superseded or withdrawn document *"may still be pinned as an attached source to ask about it deliberately"*. The badge had no subject. Migration 0054 adds the one enum value, drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) first like every other. **The marker is resolved server-side** through the same `contextStateOf` derivation the plan and library reads use, so the badge on a pinned source and the badge on the deliverable itself cannot say different things, and **behind the same wall predicate**, so a pin whose container the requester can no longer see resolves to nothing rather than leaking a reference through its own marker. **It reads `withdrawn — the survey it rests on has been retracted`, not `withdrawn`:** a bare marker tells the reader that something is unusual and not what, and the reason's visibility already follows the container (ADR-0013 §4), so nobody learns anything they could not already read. **A grounding deliverable gets no marker at all** — the badge explains an exception, and one on every chip would make the exception invisible. Nothing about the channel changes: a library pin still never joins a corpus, never grounds and never cites. | *(Deps: T-388)*

### Slice Document Status — follow-ups

- **T-392 — The C revision issues only on a contractual code.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (no migration — T-383's `is_contractual` finally has a consumer). *(Minted 2026-08-28 by the slice's review — the slice stored the flag and flagged, honestly, that nothing consumes it.)* ADR-0003's amendment says an accepting code ends the cycle but **only a contractual one issues the `C` revision** (ADR-0041 — the 2021 NA's own `S4`/`S5` split), and T-383 stored `is_contractual`; [cycle.ts](../../apps/api/src/cycle.ts) still issues the C on **any** accepting code, gated on `isAccepting` alone. **Done when:** acceptance under an accepting, non-contractual code closes the cycle and admits per `grounds`, but issues **no C revision** — the accepted content keeps its reviewed `P` revision; a contractual code issues the C exactly as today; and the accepted-status surface states which of the two happened rather than implying C. | *(Deps: none)*
  **As built.** The acceptance block splits in two where it previously ran as one: `in_library` is set on **any** accepting code — admission is what `is_accepting` decides, and whether the deliverable then *grounds* is the code's own `grounds` flag read live by retrieval (T-387) — while the C issue, its renditions and its ingest are gated on `is_contractual`. Under a non-contractual code **nothing is issued at all**, and that is the correct shape rather than a gap: the reviewed P revision already carries its renditions and its chunks from the promotion that created it, so the accepted content is complete, current and reachable without a second version existing.
  ⚠ **The failure this fixes is one-way, which is why the negative case carries the tests.** `version_reference` is immutable (T-008/0013), so an over-issued contractual revision **cannot be taken back** — a project whose scheme says `B1` accepts without contracting would have been handed a `C01` it could only ever explain, never withdraw. `c-revision.test.ts` asserts the absence directly (`versions` is exactly `['P01']`, current is `P01`) rather than asserting a count, because a count passes on the wrong revision.
  **One existing fixture had to change, and it is the ticket in miniature.** `cycle.test.ts` seeded `{ code: 'A', isAccepting: true }` and asserted `C01` — `is_contractual` defaulted to `false`, so the suite had been asserting the exact behaviour this ticket removes. It is now explicitly contractual, which is also what the **seeded scheme** already does: `A1` is the only accepting code in [acceptance-code-seed.ts](../../packages/db/src/acceptance-code-seed.ts) and it is contractual, so the e2e suite and the dev database needed no change at all.
  **The surface change needed one contract field.** `PlanRow.deliverableCode` gains `isContractual`, because the only other way to tell was the current revision's prefix — inferring the outcome backwards from its side effect, and wrong in the direction that matters: an accepted deliverable whose current revision is still the round's `P` would have rendered as *"round 2 issued"*, which reads as still under review. The status page now says **"round N, retained on acceptance"** and adds an **On acceptance** row that states the fork in words: *contractual — the C revision was issued*, or *not contractual — no C revision, and the reviewed revision stands as the accepted content*.
  **A consequence worth naming:** with no C, the **P series is what continues**, so the next submission is `P02` rather than a `P02` sitting after a `C01` that never existed. Pinned by a test, because the revision sequence is the one thing every reference in the record is built on.

- **T-393 — The ingest sweep's test is scoped to its own fixtures.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-29.** *(Minted 2026-08-28 from Session C's report.)* `ingestAllVersions` is a full-table sweep and its test inherits the shared dev database's entire history — it timed out at ~740 and again at ~1,170 versions **on a clean tree**, and only a `docker compose down -v` reset makes `pnpm run check` meaningful again. CI never sees this (empty database), so the failure lands exactly where the check is supposed to be trusted: locally, on any dev machine old enough to have history. **Done when:** the test exercises the sweep against a bounded fixture set of its own and passes on a dev database of any age; a full reset stops being the workaround. | *(Deps: none)*
  **As built.** `SweepOptions` adds one field to the sweep — `projectId` — and
  the suite is the only caller that passes it. **It narrows and cannot widen:**
  ingest excludes nothing by policy (ADR-0022, T-033), so a scope on an ingest
  can only leave *less* indexed, never reach further, which is what makes it
  admissible at all next to principle 2's no-widening-parameter rule. The dev
  CLI and the e2e substrate both index a seeded database from nothing and pass
  none, so the sweep's default behaviour is unchanged and neither call site
  moved.
  🔒 **The bound is also the assertion, and that is the half that keeps the fix
  honest.** `summary.versions` is now `toBe(2)` — exactly the two fixtures
  `beforeAll` makes — where it was `toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1)`, a shape that
  passed identically whether the sweep walked two versions or eleven hundred.
  A sweep that reached past this project now **fails** the test rather than
  slowing it down, so the scope cannot be quietly dropped later and go
  unnoticed. Verified on a dev database already holding 116 versions from
  earlier runs: the sweep reports two.
  ⚠ **Raising the timeout was the available non-fix and is what the ticket
  forbids.** The test was not slow; it was measuring the wrong thing — the age
  of the developer's database — and a larger timeout would have made that
  measurement quieter without making it mean anything. `docker compose down -v`
  stops being the workaround because there is nothing left for the reset to fix.

- **T-394 — The e2e suite survives its own substrate: the lazy `Sandbox` card.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-29.** *(Minted 2026-08-28 in review, the day it stopped being latent.)* `ensureDefaultSandbox` (apps/api/src/sandbox.ts) lazily creates an org sandbox named **`Sandbox`** from the document-listing path — so any browser test that merely *visits Ask* creates a card whose accessible name collides with the toolbar's `Sandbox` button, and `getByRole('button', { name: 'Sandbox' })` becomes a strict-mode violation in every later sandbox spec. Adding `progress-rail.spec.ts` (T-293) turned this from a re-run fragility into a **clean-seed CI failure**; the review hardened all seven selector sites with `exact: true`, which treats the symptom. **Done when:** the suite passes **twice in a row on one seed** — rename the lazily-created default so no card shares the toolbar button's name, or stop the listing path creating state, and the selector hardening stops being load-bearing. | *(Deps: none)*
  **As built — the rename, not the selector.** `ensureDefaultSandbox` names the
  lazily-created default after the organisation that owns it, through an
  exported `sandboxDefaultName(organisationName)`; the seeded Redgate row
  mirrors it, since its own comment says it is *"provisioned exactly as the
  API's lazy path would"* and a demonstration dataset spelling the default
  differently would quietly disagree with the code that produces it. No
  migration and **no backfill**: `ensureDefaultSandbox` matches on
  (project, organisation, `single_org`) and never on the name, so an existing
  database's `Sandbox` row is still found and still used — the name is a
  display fact, and CI starts empty.
  🔒 **The name deliberately does NOT contain the word "sandbox", and that is
  the whole mechanism.** A non-exact `getByRole` name matches by **substring**,
  so the obvious rename — *"Calder & Hale — project sandbox"*, which is the
  phrase the editor's own location chip already uses twice — would have left
  `{ name: 'Sandbox' }` matching two controls exactly as before, while looking
  fixed. `— working area` is CONTEXT.md's opening word for a sandbox, it is the
  vocabulary the create dialog's own placeholder uses (*"e.g. Ecology working
  area"*), and it keeps the card from reading as its owner line printed twice.
  **The guarantee moved out of the browser suite and into a unit test.**
  `sandbox.test.ts` asserts the lazy path names the default after the
  organisation, and asserts directly that the name matches no `/sandbox/i` — so
  the collision cannot return silently. The seven `exact: true` sites **stay**:
  exactness is right regardless, and the point of the ticket was that it should
  stop being the only thing holding the suite up, not that it should be undone.
  `sandbox-freeze.spec.ts`'s comment, which described the collision in the
  present tense, now describes it in the past and names where the guarantee
  lives.
  📸 **The walkthrough was recaptured**, and it had to be: the default working
  area is the card `openOrgSandbox` clicks in five beats, its name is the
  sandbox screen's **breadcrumb root**, and 24 committed screenshots showed
  both reading `Sandbox`. The capture ran on a fresh seed with the API
  restarted after it, in that order.
  ✅ **Acceptance, run as the ticket words it:** `docker compose down -v` →
  migrate → seed → the suite twice in a row on that one seed, servers started
  fresh so the new API code was the code under test. **64 passed, then 64
  passed.** The pre-fix baseline is worth recording honestly: the suite already
  passed twice on one seed *before* this change, because the review's
  `exact: true` pass was doing the work — the collision was real and present in
  the database (a `Sandbox` card sat beside the `+ Sandbox` button on every run)
  and the hardening was what kept it from failing. That is exactly the state
  the ticket calls treating the symptom, and it is why the acceptance here is

### Slice V1-N

*Ruled 2026-08-01, design session 3 → [ADR-0049](../architecture/adr/0049-notifications-and-the-promotion-gate.md), closing `Q-012`; built from 2026-08-28. Records move here ticket by ticket as they close. **T-330 is not among them** — the emitter waits on T-323 (the SES transport) and therefore on external lead time, so the record, the surface and the gate ship first and the telling follows.*

- **T-329 — The notification record.** ✅ **Built 2026-08-28** (migration 0056, **drawer 8 — Notifications**, the first drawer the drawing-board rule was applied to end to end). An event-shaped table — recipient, event type, a reference to its subject (round, document, comment), created-at and a read state — plus the read/mark-read API. **Visibility follows the subject**, resolved through the same path as the thing the notification points at; a notification is never a channel by which a fact reaches someone who could not otherwise reach it (ADR-0018 applied to a surface nobody thinks of as a data surface). **Design guard from ADR-0049 §2: adding a third event type must not require a schema change** — build it so lock-flipped joins as a new event type and subject reference alone, and say so in the migration note. | *(Deps: none)*
  **As built, and the guard is what decided the shape.** §2's test — *adding a third event type must not require a schema change* — rules out a Postgres enum by construction, because `ALTER TYPE … ADD VALUE` **is** a migration. The obvious escape was to seed the deferred `lock-flipped` value now, and that fails the other rule instead: T-301 left `supersede` out of `elevated_action` because **a value the schema carries and no code can set is a claim the schema makes falsely**.
