The on-screen name of the corpus family becomes **"Accuracy"**. Presets (Quick/Full) survive and still set families and depth together, staying individually adjustable. **Done when:** per-check options unfold under their ticks; depth renders only under Accuracy and the global control is gone; style's tick shows the guide selection; the presets still work; the plan regenerates on any change with the launch keeping its state. | *(Deps: none)*

  **As built. *Plainly: each check in the QA checker now has its own tick-box, and ticking one opens that check's own settings underneath it — so "how hard to look" sits under Accuracy, where it belongs, instead of at the bottom of the card looking like it governed all five.*** The card is now **"Which checks to run"**: the two presets at the top as a starting point, then the five checks, each a tick, a name, a sentence saying what it looks for, and — when it is on — its own options unfolded beneath. **Nothing unfolds under an unticked check**, which is the honest form: a setting for a check that will not run is a control with no effect, and that is worse than an absent one because it looks like it has one.

  🔒 **THE GLOBAL CONTROL IS GONE, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE DEFECT.** The old card opened with **"How hard to look"** as its heading and closed with the depth select at its foot. The select was already conditional on the accuracy check being on, so the bug was never in what it did — it was in what the layout said, which is that this was a setting for the run. The owner read the photograph and caught it: *"I thought this was only for certain checks."* ADR-0053 §2 declares grain and options **per family**, precisely because the five are different enough that one setting cannot serve them, so the record was right and the screen was wrong. What matters as much as moving the control is that **there is no global block left for the next option to land on** — the shipped one had already collected this one that way.

  **The corpus family is called "Accuracy" on screen** (owner, 2026-09-01). The old label, *"Accuracy against the record"*, was the family's whole job written into its name, which left nothing for the options now unfolding under it — the scope it checks against, and how hard it looks — to say better. The `description` beneath still names the project library, so nothing about what it does is lost.

  **Ticking House style shows the rules that will be applied, and it is a STATEMENT rather than a picker.** The checker does not choose its style material: the project's guides and the firm's own manual bind the draft either way (ADR-0053 §3). So the unfold names the loaded project guides with their clause counts, names the firm's own manual as filling the gaps where they are silent, and states the precedence. Its **three states are `StyleGuidePicker`'s three, for the same reason**: "none loaded" and "could not be read" are different facts about a project, and a check that conflated them would let a project nobody had set up read exactly like one deliberately left plain. A screen listing only the project's guides would also read as though the firm's manual did not apply, and it always does.

  **What deliberately did not change.** The presets still set families and depth together and stay individually adjustable — a preset is a starting point, not a mode. `change()` still discards the plan and keeps every other answer, so the launch keeps its state (ADR-0053 §1) through the re-layout. **No plan-side code was touched at all**, so the determinism tests are untouched and pass unchanged. **Two new pure components** — `CheckFamilyRow` and `StyleSourcesNote` — so both can be pinned in the render suite; a sentence that cannot be rendered in a test is a sentence nobody is checking (T-395).

  ⚠ **Deviations, reported.** (1) **The label change is in `contracts`**, not on the surface: `CHECK_FAMILY_CATALOGUE` is where the launcher gets its words, and a surface-side rename would have left the contract disagreeing with the screen. It is a catalogue value, not a widening of the `CheckFamily` union, which is untouched. (2) **The checker now reads the project's style guides**, which it did not before — one extra request on mount, failing to `null` rather than to an empty list, for the reason above. (3) The walkthrough's beat `t2-03` was retitled and rewritten to describe the corrected screen, and says plainly that the previous photograph is what caught the defect. **The page is not recaptured here** — that is T-420's, sequenced last. **No migration, no personal data, no contract type change beyond the one catalogue label.**


**T-416 — The two scope searches.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-01.** *Plainly: under Accuracy, the first option is "check against the entire library you have access to", and beneath it a search over the library whose results show document titles; the attach-from-working-area picker gains the same search.* Assembled, not filtered, both ways (ADR-0053 §8): a search result the requester cannot reach is absent, never greyed — the search must run over the access-resolved set, not filter a wider one on the way out. **Done when:** both searches work and show titles; narrowing to searched documents lands on the plan's scope statement exactly as picker-narrowing does today; an unreachable document never appears in results (asserted). | *(Deps: T-415)*

  **As built. *Plainly: both places where you pick documents for a check now have a search box, results show titles rather than coded references alone, and the library scope has moved under the Accuracy check — which is the only check it governs.*** Under Accuracy the first option is now **What it checks against**: the sentence saying the default is the whole library you can reach, then the search, then the rows. The standalone *"Check against library documents"* card is gone; a card of its own beside the check list said the scope belonged to the run, which is the same mistake T-415 just corrected for depth.

  🔒 **A SEARCH BOX IS EXACTLY WHERE ASSEMBLED-NOT-FILTERED GETS BROKEN, so neither search here CAN break it.** The tempting shape is to ask the server *"find documents matching X"* and hide the unreachable ones on the way out — which discloses that they exist by the shape of what comes back. Neither search does that. Both are a filter over a list **already access-resolved on the server**: the grounding scope (computed from the same `liveLibraryFilter` both arms of the assembly gateway run) and the requester's own sandbox documents. **There is no wider set on this screen to narrow.** A document out of reach is not greyed and not ranked low; it never reached the browser, and no search can bring it back.

  **That claim is asserted rather than asserted-in-a-comment.** `LibraryScopePicker` and `AttachPicker` take their rows as a prop and reach nothing else, and the render suite reads their own source to prove it: neither function body contains `api.` or `fetch(`, and the page hands the first one `scope?.sources`, which is the server's access-resolved answer rather than the library list. That is a weaker-looking test than a wall test and a stronger one in practice, because the failure it guards is a future edit adding a fetch, not today's behaviour.

  **One search behaviour across both pickers** (`matchesQuery`), because they are one gesture done twice and two searches that matched differently would teach a person that one of them was broken. It folds case, matches reference, title and description, treats a null field as absent rather than crashing — most of a real corpus predates the description column — and **an empty query matches everything**: a search box is not a filter you must satisfy before the list appears. Each search states its own count beside it: *"3 of 24 match"* is how a person tells a search that found little from a library that holds little, and those are very different facts about a project.

  **The zero cases are statements, not empty lists.** Nothing in scope says so and shows no search box at all — an empty picker under a search box reads as a search that failed. A scope that could not be READ says the same thing rather than claiming zero, which is the Ask composer's own rule (T-292). A search that matches nothing says how many there are to clear back to.

  **Narrowing means what it meant.** The search only filters what is rendered; the chosen documents ride the same `scopeVersionIds` field to the same planner, and an HTTP-level test pins that the plan's coverage sentence still says *"the whole library"* unnarrowed and *"2 named library documents"* narrowed. Two paths into that field would be two chances for the plan to describe a scope the run did not use.

  ⚠ **Deviations, reported.** (1) **The attach picker's markup changed shape** — it is now a component with a class rather than inline `<label>`s; the walkthrough's capture step selects it by card and title and still matches, and was checked rather than assumed. (2) The walkthrough's beat `t2-04` prose was extended to describe both searches and the scope's move. **The page is not recaptured here** — that is T-420's. **No migration, no personal data, no contract change, no new endpoint** — both searches are filters over data the screen already had.


**T-417 — The plan reads as a step-by-step workflow.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-01.** *Plainly: the checker's plan page sets out the run as numbered steps in the order they will happen, so a person reads what will run as a sequence rather than a summary.* Rendering only: the step list underneath is unchanged and stays uneditable (ADR-0053 §4); coverage keeps its two-shape sentence; the weaker-cross-section caveat keeps its position above the run control. **Done when:** the plan renders as an ordered sequence; the existing plan tests (determinism, caveat position, coverage) still pass unchanged. | *(Deps: T-415)*

  **As built. *Plainly: the checker's plan now reads as a numbered workflow — step 1, then step 2, threaded down the page in the order they will happen — instead of a bulleted list of things that will occur.*** The card's lede says so in words (*"step by step, in the order it will happen"*), the steps are an ordered list with a numbered marker each, and a hairline runs from one marker to the next so the sequence is visible rather than inferred from the digits.

  🔒 **RENDERING ONLY, AND THE RESTRAINT IS THE TICKET.** The list underneath is the same list, computed in code from the same parameters, editable by nobody, human or model (ADR-0053 §4 and §12). **Nothing here sorts** — the planner already emits its steps in the order it will execute them, and a component that re-ordered them would be a second opinion about what the run does. A render test reads `CheckPlanCard`'s own source and fails if `.sort(`, a `TextInput` or a `TextArea` ever appears inside it, which is the future edit worth guarding rather than today's behaviour.

  **The existing plan tests pass untouched**, which is the ticket's own acceptance: determinism, the caveat sitting above the run control (it degrades loudly or not at all), the coverage sentence's shape, the refusal replacing the button rather than sitting beside it, and T-410's two inverted price assertions. Not one of them was edited.

  ⚠ **Deviations, reported.** (1) **The card's heading moved from a bare `<strong>` to the shared `.card-title` style, and its lede to `.card-lede`.** The checker's plan card had been the last surface still hand-styling those two roles that T-404 unified on the creator's; leaving it would have meant the two tools' plan pages disagreeing about what a card heading looks like on the very ticket that re-reads one of them. (2) The walkthrough's beat `t2-05` was retitled and its prose extended. **The page is not recaptured here** — that is T-420's. **No migration, no personal data, no contract change, and no planner code touched at all.**


**T-418 — A running check shows its steps completing.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-01.** *Plainly: once a check is running, a progress box shows the plan's steps ticking off as each completes, so a long run reads as working rather than hung.* The Run/Step rows already record state per step — this is a surface polling what exists, not engine work. Degrades honestly: a poll failure says the run continues and the page will catch up, never a false "stuck". **Done when:** the progress box tracks step completion against the same step list the plan showed; completion lands on the existing results view; a run finishing between polls is handled; no new engine state. | *(Deps: T-417)*

  **As built. *Plainly: when a check is running, the plan's own steps stay on screen and tick off one by one as each finishes — so a long run reads as working rather than as a page that has stopped.*** The plan card gives way to a **Running the check** box carrying the same numbered workflow T-417 built, with a tick against each finished step and the one in flight the only thing emphasised. A progress box where everything is emphasised says nothing about where the run is.

  🔒 **NO NEW ENGINE STATE, AND THE POLL READS WHAT WAS ALREADY THERE.** Every step of a run opens a Step row and closes it — ADR-0028's append-only tree, since the skeleton. The box counts **closed rows** against **the plan's own step count as the scale**. Counting the rows that came back instead would show *"2 of 2"* on a run that had opened two rows of six and call it finished. It computes no percentage, guesses at no elapsed time and estimates nothing remaining; a render test reads `RunProgress`'s own source and fails if `%` or `Date.now` ever appears in it, because each of those would be the surface asserting something the run has not.

  **The one honest problem this ticket had, and how it was solved.** The run endpoint is a single blocking request that returns when the whole check is done, so the browser could not learn the run's id from it until far too late to watch anything. Matching on the request text, or on *"the newest run"*, would be a guess that is wrong exactly when two checks are started at once. **So the browser opens the conversation first and passes its id in**, and polls `GET /conversations/:id` — a route that already existed, returning runs with their steps. `qaCheckBody` gained an optional `conversationId` (a contract change, noted in [contracts.md](contracts.md)). **This moves *when* the conversation row is created, not *what* is created**: a tool run has always opened one like every other run, and a caller passing none gets exactly the previous behaviour, asserted. **The id is checked against the requester's own project first**, so it is not a way to hang a run off somebody else's thread — a conversation elsewhere answers 404, principle 4, rather than a refusal that would confirm it exists.

  **It degrades honestly, and that is pinned in three assertions.** A poll that does not answer keeps the count it last had, says *"the check is still going — the result will appear here when it finishes"*, and says neither "stuck" nor "failed". The run is a fact on the server; a browser that has lost sight of it has learned something about the browser. **A run finishing between polls is handled by the request itself** — the blocking POST resolves, the box clears, and the result card takes its place. The poll is never the thing that decides a run is over. **A conversation that could not be opened is not a failure to run**: the check proceeds without one and what is lost is the progress box, which is not a reason to refuse somebody their check.

  ⚠ **Deviations, reported.** (1) **A defect found and fixed outside this ticket's letter, in a test.** `cycle.test.ts`'s scanned-PDF assertion counted the **whole** `sandbox_documents` table before and after an upload; the suite shares one database with concurrently running files, so it raced against whatever a neighbouring suite inserted in the window, and it began failing the moment this slice's new tests started creating documents. It is now scoped to its own project — the same fix, for the same reason, as the scoped count `qa-check.test.ts` already carries with its own note. The assertion is unchanged in what it claims. (2) **The plan card is hidden only WHILE the run is in flight and comes back beside the result**, which took a second pass to get right: the first version hid it once a result arrived, and that would have removed ADR-0053 §5's whole design — the before and after coverage sentences read against each other in one frame. A render test now pins the condition itself. (3) A new walkthrough beat `t2-06-progress` and its capture step. **The page is not recaptured here** — that is T-420's. **No migration, no personal data.**


**T-419 — The marked-up edit meets the design guide.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-01.** *Plainly: audit the checker's markup surface — the marks in the document, the findings panel, the tones and spacing — against the design rulebook, and fix what falls short.* T-404's pattern on the remaining tool surface: audit against [design-rules.md](../design/design-rules.md) and the tokens, findings listed in the closing commit so the fix is checkable against a list. **Done when:** the audit's findings are enumerated and each fixed or explicitly kept-with-reason; render tests pin what the audit tightens. | *(Deps: none)*

  **As built. *Plainly: the findings panel was written before the design system covered it, so it styled itself with numbers typed into the file — and two of its controls could not be reached by keyboard at all. It is now on the system, and both work.*** **Ten findings, each named, each fixed or kept with a reason.** Nine are in `findings-panel.tsx` and `packages/ui/src/styles.css`; the tenth is in the canvas marks and is kept. *(Review correction, 2026-09-01: the count is off by one — F1–F10 are all panel/CSS findings and the kept canvas-marks item is an eleventh.)*

  **F1 — Every size in the panel was a bare pixel value in an inline style, and three were off the scale entirely.** §A: *"All spacing is a multiple of 4px … use the semantic `space.*` tokens in component code — never a bare pixel value"*, plus the hard rule against hardcoding any raw px in app code. The file carried twenty-odd — `marginTop: 6`, `padding: 8`, `gap: 6`, `paddingLeft: 8`, `fontSize: 12.5`, `fontSize: 12` — of which **6px, 3px and 2px are not on the 4px scale at all**. ✅ **Fixed:** the whole panel moved to a class block in `styles.css`, on the scale. A render test asserts the file now contains no `style={{` whatsoever, which is the only form of this rule that cannot rot.

  **F2 — A finding card was the exact pattern §E deleted.** The migration map is explicit that `.proposed`'s *"rounded container with a left-border accent"* was **removed** in favour of the plain nested-card treatment — and this card had grown one back: `borderLeft: 3px solid …`, toned by severity. ✅ **Fixed:** plain nested card. **Severity is the badge's job**, and the badge pairs its colour with a word, which is what §D's colour-independence rule asks for and a coloured bar can never do. The card is now explicitly a **level-3 nested card inside a level-2 pane** (§A): `radius.md`, and no shadow of its own — a list of twelve shadowed slabs is precisely the *"if you can't say which of the four levels it is, make it flat"* case.

  **F3 — The accent used `var(--danger)`, the deprecated raw-hex pair, not `feedback.danger`.** The same defect T-411 found for the warning tone, in a different file. ✅ **Fixed by F2** — the raw danger reference is gone from the panel entirely rather than retargeted, because the thing that needed a colour no longer exists.

  **F4 — Two controls were anchors with an `onClick` and no `href`, so neither could be reached by keyboard.** *"Go to it"* on every finding, and the whole collapse control on every check group. §D requires a visible focus ring on every interactive element; an `<a>` with no `href` is not focusable, so there was nothing to ring. Both also failed the 32×32 minimum target. ✅ **Fixed:** real `<button>`s, both with `min-height: 32px` and the shared focus treatment. This is the finding with the largest practical consequence in the ticket — a keyboard user could not navigate to a finding at all.

  **F5 — The collapse control was not the system's collapse affordance, and had no chevron.** §B names `component.collapseToggle` for exactly this role. ✅ **Fixed:** a Lucide chevron at 2px in `currentColor` (§F.7), rotating with state, on the `collapse-toggle-*` component tokens, plus `aria-expanded` so the state is announced rather than inferred from what sits below it. ⚠ **One deliberate departure, named:** `--collapse-toggle-size` is 22px, below §D's own 32px target. It is the token for the **square icon control** in a pane header and does not describe a text-and-chevron row, so this control takes that component's colour and radius tokens and its own 32px height. **The 22px/32px tension in the system itself is reported here and not resolved** — it belongs to the nav rail's control, which this ticket does not touch.

  **F6 — The wording editor was a raw `<textarea>` with `style={{ width: '100%' }}`.** The one editing surface in the product growing its own font, border and focus behaviour. ✅ **Fixed:** the shared `TextArea` from `@infora/ui`.

  **F7 — The suggested-wording quote was a hand-built left-border blockquote with three inline pixel values** — sitting four lines from `.quoted-rule`, which is a real class doing the same job. ✅ **Fixed:** a `.suggested-wording` class beside it.

  **F8 — The focused finding was outlined in a background TINT.** `outline: 2px solid var(--feedback-info-tint)` uses a fill colour as a line: near-invisible against a pane, and not the pairing §D's contrast table measures — every `.tint` in that table is measured against its `.text` partner. ✅ **Fixed:** the tint is the fill and `feedback.info.text` is the line, with an offset. ⚠ **The same misuse survives at `.comment-thread.flash`** (a box-shadow ring in the tint), which is the comments surface and not this one — **reported, not fixed**, because widening the ticket to reach it would put an unreviewed change to a different feature inside a design audit.

  **F9 — The panel root hardcoded `fontSize: 12.5`**, which is the *value* of `ui.default` typed out rather than the token named. §A says `ui.default` is the base UI size and to reach for it first. ✅ **Fixed:** `var(--ui-default-size)`. ⚠ **Reported: `styles.css` carries roughly forty *(review count, 2026-09-01: twenty-six at base)* more bare `12.5px` literals** from before the token existed. They are correct values in the wrong form, they are spread across surfaces this ticket does not own, and a sweep of them is a candidate for **T-420** rather than something to smuggle into an audit of one panel.

  **F10 — The mechanical-fix summary rendered at `fontSize: 12`**, a size that is on no step of the type scale (the neighbours are 11.5 and 12.5). ✅ **Fixed:** `ui.default`, the nearest step, per §F.5's *"default to reusing the nearest existing step"*.

  **Kept with reason — the canvas marks themselves.** `mark--finding` uses `feedback.danger.tint` with a `feedback.danger.text` underline for required, and `surface.sunken` with a **dashed** `text.muted` underline for advisory. That is on-system, it is within §A's reserved status vocabulary, and §D's colour-independence is already satisfied by solid-versus-dashed rather than by hue. **No change**, and it is listed so the audit reads as complete rather than as silent where it looked.

  **Eight render tests pin what the audit tightened**, including the no-inline-styles rule, the absent left-border, both hit targets, the outline-versus-tint fix, and `aria-expanded`. ⚠ **One test had to be narrowed in the writing, and the reason is worth recording:** the panel's own comments deliberately name what was removed — `var(--danger)`, a bare `<textarea>` — because a removal nobody recorded is one that comes back wearing an innocent face. Asserting over the raw file would have made keeping that record impossible, so the assertions strip comments first and the claim is *"the code no longer does this"* rather than *"the file never mentions it"*. **No migration, no personal data, no contract change.**


**T-420 — The finesse pass: cluttered, compressed, and short of finished.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-01.** *Plainly: the owner's standing impression of both tools is that the screens feel cluttered and compressed and lack a level of aesthetic finesse. Audit the LIVE screens — not the photographs, which carry compression of their own — across both tools end to end: density, whitespace, hierarchy, alignment, type scale. Fix at the components and tokens wherever possible so every surface heals together.* Runs **last**, over everything this slice changes, so nothing is polished twice. Where a finding needs a token or rule the design system lacks, extend the system per its own extension section rather than deviating beside it — and where a change is a matter of taste rather than rule, it is listed for the owner rather than silently chosen. **Done when:** the pass's findings are enumerated in the closing commit; the walkthrough recaptures both tools' sections; the owner reviews the new photographs. | *(Deps: T-412, T-413, T-414, T-415, T-416, T-417, T-418, T-419)*

  **As built. *Plainly: the two tools were audited by running the app and looking at the real screens at the size they are actually used. The biggest cause of the "cluttered and compressed" impression turned out to be two things — every explanatory sentence ran the full width of the screen, and every small text box was being forced 40% taller than it asked to be. Both are fixed at the shared components, so every screen in the product healed at once.*** The app was started against the e2e substrate and driven to both tools at 1440×1000, full-resolution, and the screens were **read back as images** — not the walkthrough's downscaled shots, since the owner's complaint is partly about that compression.

  **F1 — `.field-textarea` had `min-height: 64px`, which silently overrode the `rows` prop.** ✅ **Fixed at the component.** `TextArea` takes `rows` and callers set it deliberately per context — 2 for a section's purpose, 3 for a brief — and a 64px floor discarded every value below three lines, making each `rows={2}` box roughly 40% taller than asked. In the creator's outline that turned every section into mostly empty box: **the owner's "compressed" impression arriving from the opposite direction — not too dense, too inflated.** The floor is now one line plus padding, so it still cannot collapse and no longer fights the prop. Every textarea in the product heals.

  **F2 — UI prose ran edge-to-edge, ~170 characters to the line.** ✅ **Fixed, and the design system extended to say so.** §C capped *document prose* at 560–600px with the reasoning *"never let editor text run edge-to-edge"* and had **no rule at all** for the prose that explains a control — so every page subtitle, card lede, field hint, check description and document description ran the full pane width. **This was the single largest contributor to the reported impression.** A `type.measure.ui` token (780px) joins `type.measure.prose` (600px) in [design-tokens.json](../design/design-tokens.json), regenerated through `build-tokens.ts`, and **§C gained a new rule** stating the principle, its two values and — explicitly — that form controls are *not* covered by it, because an input's width is a target size and not a reading measure.

  **F3 — the measure was already in the codebase twice, as a bare `780px`, without a name.** ⚠ **Found while writing F2's guard, and reported as a change outside both tools:** `.chat-inner` and `.chat-composer .inner` had capped the chat column at exactly 780px since it was built. That is independent corroboration of the value, and precisely the *"a decision made once and re-made by accident thereafter"* case a token exists to prevent. Both now name the token. **The chat surface is not one of the two tools**, and the change is a rename of an identical value, but it is a change and it is reported rather than absorbed.

  **F4 — `.field-input` used `padding: 7px 10px`**, on no step of the 4px scale (§A). ✅ **Fixed:** `8px 12px`. **F5 — its `font-size` fallback contradicted its own token**: `var(--body-dense-size, 12.5px)` while `body.dense` is 13px, so the rule disagreed with the token it was falling back from. ✅ **Fixed:** the token alone — a fallback that changes the design is worse than no fallback. **F6 — `.field-hint` was 11px and `.field-label` 11.5px as literals**; 11px is on no step of the type scale at all. ✅ **Fixed:** `ui.label`. **F7 — `.page-sub` was `13.5px` (no step) with a `6px` margin (no step)**. ✅ **Fixed:** `body.dense` and 8px. **F8 — `.check-family-desc` and `.source-row-desc` were 12px** (no step). ✅ **Fixed:** `ui.default`, the nearest step per §F.5.

  ⚠ **F7 TOUCHES SEVENTEEN SCREENS AND THAT IS THE POINT, but it is still the widest change in this slice.** `.page-sub` is the opening sentence of every page in the product. Capping its measure and snapping its two off-scale values heals the whole product's page introductions from one rule — which is what *"fix at components and tokens so surfaces heal together"* asks for — and it is a visible change to fifteen screens outside either tool. Reported loudly rather than mentioned.

  **F9 — the preset description sat hard against the preset buttons**, reading as their caption rather than as the answer to *"what does this one do"*. ✅ **Fixed:** 12px above. **F10 — the search count floated at the far end of a 1200px row** with nothing to anchor it. ✅ **Fixed** by the measure on `.list-search`: the search and its count are one control.

  **Guarded at the source, six assertions in `packages/ui/src/ui.test.tsx`** — the repo's own idiom for a rule that would break silently and still look plausible (T-401's `.banner` guard). A measure that quietly went away would not throw, would fail no render test, and would look exactly like the screens this ticket was raised about, which is how it got here. The guards pin the token's existence and both values, the measure on all six prose classes, that the token is referenced **by name** and never as a repeated `780px`, the textarea floor, and the field control's scale compliance.

  ── **TASTE, NOT RULE — LISTED FOR THE OWNER, DELIBERATELY NOT CHOSEN.** *(Ruled 2026-09-01: the owner delegated all five to the co-captain's judgement — "you should be able to make these choices and make sure you think it's both aesthetically and operationally useful." Decisions, recorded here as the single copy: **1 adopted** — form controls cap at the UI measure, an uncapped title input reads unfinished and costs eye travel; **2 declined** — outline sections stay cards, because a section groups its name, purpose and controls and now nests sub-sections, and a flat list confuses exactly when an outline grows complex; **3 declined** — one column stands, because the launch flow is a top-to-bottom sequence and a second column splits attention against it; **4 adopted** — the check rows flatten to a ruled list, five bordered boxes inside a card being much of the "cluttered" reading; **5 adopted** — the presets become one segmented pick-one control, since two buttons read as two actions where the semantics are mutually exclusive. The three adopted changes are **T-421**.)* Each of these would change how the tools look, none of them follows from a rule in the guide, and picking one silently is what the ticket forbids:

  1. **Form controls have no width cap.** A heading input is 1400px wide for a document title. Capping inputs at the UI measure would make both tools read as a column rather than a spread — but an input's width is a target size, and §C has no rule either way. *(The new §C rule says explicitly that this is open and unruled, so nobody later mistakes the omission for an oversight.)*
  2. **The outline's sections are cards.** They could be plain rows separated by a rule, which would roughly halve the outline's height at three sections. Cards were T-404's choice and this ticket did not revisit it.
  3. **The two tools are one long single column.** The launcher's answers and the outline could sit side by side at ≥1280px. There is no two-column pattern in §B and no breakpoint set in §C, so inventing one here would be guessing at a system the guide says to flag rather than assume.
  4. **The five check rows carry a border each.** A flat list with rules between them would be quieter; the border is what makes a ticked check read as the one carrying settings. Both are defensible.
  5. **The presets are two buttons.** A segmented control would say "pick one of these two" more plainly than a primary/quiet pair. §B has no segmented-control entry, so this would be a new component.

  ── **THE RECAPTURE, AND THE TWO DEFECTS IT FOUND BY BEING LOOKED AT.** The walkthrough was recaptured in full on a fresh seed — 66 shots, no duplicate-frame warnings — downscaled and rebuilt. **Both defects below were found by reading the photographs back as images and would have survived any amount of reasoning from the code:**

  ⚠ **(a) T-412's sub-sections were built, tested, and unphotographed.** The outline beat showed three sections and three *"Add a sub-section"* controls with nothing composed under any of them, so the slice's headline creator feature did not appear in the walkthrough at all. The capture now adds a sub-section under the baseline, and the beat's prose says what one is.

  ⚠ **(b) T-418's progress beat photographed the plan card.** The shot was indistinguishable from `t2-05-plan`. The progress box lives exactly as long as the run does, and against the stand-in router a whole check finishes in a couple of hundred milliseconds — the box appeared, the `waitFor` passed, and the run was over before the shutter. **The fix is in the capture recipe, not in the product and not in the substrate:** the run response is held for two seconds by a one-shot route handler in the browser, which no product code knows about and which cannot leak into the e2e suite or anyone's dev environment. Teaching the e2e server to be slow would have put a performance fiction into a shared fixture to make one screenshot work. *(The first attempt at that handler used route-then-unroute and raced — the second run hit a half-torn-down handler and killed the capture after `t2-06-run`; `times: 1` retires it instead.)*

  **The three claims the ticket names, each confirmed from the NEW photographs rather than asserted from the code:** the checker's launcher shows per-check options with **"How hard to look" under Accuracy** and the corpus family named **Accuracy** (`t2-02-draft`); the outline shows **`2.1 Survey dates and limitations` under `2 Baseline`** (`t1-05-outline-edited`); and the plan reads as **numbered steps 1 and 2 in order**, with the weaker-coverage caveat above the run control (`t2-05-plan`). Also read back: `t1-14-from-the-working-area`, showing T-413's pre-filled destination and its sentence, and `t2-06-progress`, showing *"0 of 2 steps finished"* with the step in flight emphasised. **No migration, no personal data, no contract change.**

  *(Review, 2026-09-01 — what this record and the slice's others left out, plus two fixes applied in review.)* (1) 🔴 **T-412 had re-introduced the §E-banned "rounded container with left-border accent" on the plan's sub-section rows** — the exact pattern T-419's F2 stripped from the findings panel three commits later — and this pass audited both tools without catching it. Fixed in review (the sub-row is now the plain nested-card treatment, indent and no accent bar) and pinned in `ui.test.tsx`. (2) **`design-tokens.json` was machine-rewritten wholesale** — 324 insertions for a two-token addition, hand alignment lost and em-dashes escaped; a semantic key-by-key diff confirmed nothing changed but the two additions, and the file's original hand formatting was restored in review with the tokens re-added in its own style, the generated outputs byte-identical either side. (3) **`measure.prose` (600px) is also new** — this record's "joins" implies it pre-existed; both measure tokens entered the system in this commit, and `measure.prose` is currently referenced by nothing. (4) **The cross-surface flagging is asymmetric**: F7's seventeen screens are flagged loudly while F1 (every textarea), F4/F5 (every input) and the `.card-lede` measure are equally product-wide and flagged as ordinary findings. (5) **T-419's nominated `12.5px` sweep was neither done nor declined** — this pass reduced the literals incidentally (to twenty-four) and left the sweep unowned; it stays a candidate. (6) **`.field-error` still sits at 11px**, the same off-scale size F6 fixed on `.field-hint`, in the same block — left for the owner's next design pass rather than changed in review, because F6's reasoning would change it and taste might not. (7) Elsewhere in the slice, corrected at source in review: T-412's wire comment and test title claimed a second nesting level is *refused* when the schema **strips** it — both now say strip, so nobody hardens against a refusal the door never performs.


**T-421 — The three adopted taste choices.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-01.** *(Minted 2026-09-01: the owner delegated T-420's five listed taste choices to the co-captain, who adopted three and declined two — the decisions and their reasons are recorded on T-420's moved record, the single copy.)* *Plainly: typing boxes get a maximum width instead of stretching the whole screen; the checker's five check rows lose their boxes and become a clean list with dividing lines; and the Quick/Full choice becomes one two-position switch instead of two buttons.* All three at the shared components on the tokens, T-420's own discipline — no screen touched individually, and the declined two (outline rows, two columns) are not built. **Done when:** the three render as decided, pinned the way T-420's fixes are pinned; the walkthrough recaptures whichever shots they change; nothing else about either tool moves. | *(Deps: none)*

  **As built. *Plainly: typing boxes stop stretching the whole screen, the five checks read as a clean list, and Quick/Full is one switch.*** All three were built at the shared components, so every screen in the product takes them at once, and all three were **read back as photographs** rather than asserted from the code — which is how three of the reported deviations below were found.

  **1 — A form control stops growing at the UI measure.** `.field-input` — the one class behind every text box, textarea, dropdown and picker in the product — now carries `max-width: var(--measure-ui)` (780px). It is a **maximum** and not a width, which is the whole safety of the change: a control that is deliberately the full width of a narrower parent is untouched, because a maximum never makes something smaller than its container already is. Confirmed on the photographs both ways: the creator's four dropdowns and its brief box now stop well short of their card's edge (`t1-02-launcher`), the outline's section headings sit as a column with their move and remove controls beside them (`t1-05-outline-edited`), and — the other half of the claim — the folder-structure dialog's inputs (`04-structure`) and the agent pane's ask box (`09-editor`) still fill their narrower containers exactly as before.

  ⚠ **Reported: the two positioning wrappers took the cap too.** `.field-select-wrap` and `.combobox` are capped as well as the control inside them. This is not scope creep, it is the change working at all: the dropdown's chevron is positioned against its wrapper's right edge and the picker's list stretches `left: 0; right: 0` across its own, so capping only the inner control would have left both floating in the space the cap had just freed.

  **2 — The checker's five check rows flatten.** `.check-family` loses its border, its radius, its padding box and its white fill; the rows now sit directly on the card with a hairline between siblings, which is §A's level-1 treatment for a dense list. The tick, the unfolding options and the copy are untouched. **No rounded-container-with-accent-bar anywhere in the result** (§E, and T-419's F2): the hairline is a **top** border on each row but the first — a divider between siblings, never a left edge — and the pin T-419's review added on `.proposal-section--sub` is unchanged and still passing.

  ⚠ **Reported: `.check-family--on` is gone, not restyled.** That modifier existed for exactly one job — darkening the row's border when its check was ticked — and a flat row has no container left to darken. What now says which check carries settings is the tick and the unfolded options, which is what a reader looks at anyway. The class is removed from the markup and the stylesheet, and pinned removed.

  **3 — Quick/Full is one segmented control.** A new `SegmentedControl` in `packages/ui`, since §B had no such component. **The rule is untouched**: a preset still sets the check families and the accuracy depth together as one honest choice (ADR-0053 §2), everything stays individually adjustable afterwards, and Full is still the default — all three pinned in `render.test.tsx` against the screen's own source and the contract's constant. It is a **radiogroup**, not a row of buttons (§D): a screen reader hears "one of two", the arrow keys move the selection, and the whole control is one tab stop rather than one per position. Verified live, not reasoned: focusing *Full check* and pressing → moved the selection to *Quick check*, `aria-checked` followed it, the focus ring showed, and the sentence underneath changed to the quick preset's own description. Built on the existing tokens with **no token of its own** (§F.3), so `design-tokens.json` is untouched and dark mode was mechanical — and photographed in dark mode as well as light, per §G.1.

  ⚠ **REPORTED, AND THIS IS THE ONE WORTH READING: TWO OF THE THREE FIRST SHIPPED INVISIBLE, AND ONLY THE PHOTOGRAPH SAID SO.** A `.card` is painted `surface.sunken`. `border.subtle` is a step **lighter** than that, so the dividers between the check rows — drawn with the token whose name says "hairline" — could not be seen on the one surface the list actually sits on. The segmented control had the same failure one step worse: its track was `surface.sunken` too, which is the role-correct name for a recess, and it vanished into the card completely, leaving one lone white button beside some plain text rather than a switch with two positions. Both are fixed by moving one step: the divider to `border.default`, the track to `surface.active`. **`surface.active` is a role stretch and is flagged as one** — its name is about a pressed state, not a track — but the alternative was a new token, and the token file already records this exact problem class against `surface.frameHover` ("surface.hover is tuned for white panes and disappears here"). The hover moved with it, to `surface.hover`, which now reads as **one step towards the selected position's appearance** — lighter in light mode, darker in dark — because the track had taken the step the hover used to occupy. Every one of these was caught by looking at a rendered screen; none would have failed a test or looked wrong in the diff.

  ⚠ **Reported: three files outside `packages/ui` and the checker screen changed, and each had to.** (1) **[design-rules.md](../design/design-rules.md) §C** carried the sentence *"Whether inputs should take a width cap of their own is open and unruled — do not guess one"* — written by T-420 so nobody mistook the omission for an oversight. It is now answered, so that sentence is replaced by the ruling, with its own reasoning (a target size, not a reading measure) and the note that this replaces it. (2) **§B gained a Segmented control entry**, because §F.4 requires one for any new component. (3) **`packages/contracts/src/checker.ts`** opened *"In plain terms: two buttons that set everything at once"* — a description of a screen that no longer exists. The comment now says one switch with two positions and dates the change. **No type, value, label or catalogue entry moved** — this is a comment, and not a contract change; `contracts.md` therefore gets no note.

  ⚠ **Reported: the capture recipe and the walkthrough's words changed.** The recipe selected the preset by `getByRole('button', { name: 'Quick check' })`; a position in a radiogroup is a `radio`, so that step now asks for a radio — still by role, so it still describes what the screen offers rather than how it is built. The beat prose says what the three changes are, and **it says them on `t2-02-draft`, not on `t2-03-adjusted`**: `t2-03` is scrolled past the preset control, and a sentence claiming something its own photograph does not show is exactly the defect T-420's recapture was raised on. `t2-02` shows all three at once — the capped draft picker, the switch, and the ruled list — and was read back as an image to confirm it before the sentence was written.

  ⚠⚠ **REPORTED LOUDEST: THE RECAPTURE RAN ON LINUX, AND ALL 66 SHOTS RE-RENDER SLIGHTLY.** This session had no macOS. The brand serif is a webfont and loads identically, but the sans stack resolves to the platform's own font — Liberation Sans here, the system font on a Mac — so every shot's text sets a fraction differently and a few rows shift by a pixel or two, on beats this ticket did not touch as well as on the ones it did. Measured on an untouched beat (`01-workspace`) the difference is about 7% RMSE, all of it type rendering: same layout, same colours, same content. **All 66 were committed rather than only the changed ones**, because a page carrying a mix of Mac-rendered and Linux-rendered beats would read worse than one rendered consistently. If the owner wants the asset set back on the original renderer, a recapture on a Mac restores it with no code change.

The gate ran instead on a **freshly created local Postgres 16 cluster with pgvector 0.6.0** — the cluster was dropped and recreated, so the "wiped volume" condition holds — and migrate, seed, the eval smoke tier and both e2e runs all ran against it. **This is Postgres 16 where CI runs 17**, and that difference is not something this session can close; CI remains the authority.
  *(Review, 2026-09-01 — one real defect, three record corrections, all fixed at source.)* (1) 🔴 **The divider fix did not fix the divider.** The record says the shade move was "checked on the photograph"; the photograph disproves it — `border.default` (#ececea) sits within 3/255 of the card's own fill (#efeeeb), the same imperceptible distance as the rejected `border.subtle`, just on the other side, so the five checks rendered with no visible separation at all. The system had no border step that reads on a sunken surface; **`border.strong` was added to the token file** (hand-edited in its own style, light and dark values, regenerated), the divider now uses it, and the pin asserts the strong token. (2) The record's claim that the new walkthrough sentences sit on `t2-02-draft` and **not** on `t2-03-adjusted` was false — the ruled-list sentence had been added to both captions; the duplicate is removed, which makes the claimed discipline true. (3) The arrow-key behaviour was described as "verified live" with nothing repeatable behind it; the step logic is now a pure exported function (`segmentStep`) with its own test, wrap-around included. (4) Two inline comments (the CSS and its copied test comment) called `surface.hover` invisible while annotating the very rule that uses it — corrected; the design-rules sentence was already right. Noted, not changed: the record's "photographed in dark mode as well" has no committed artefact behind it (the token arithmetic was verified in review instead); the segmented track itself is near-invisible on a card and the control reads through its white selected chip, which is acceptable and now said honestly; the outline heading's move/remove controls now sit against the capped input rather than the card edge — accepted as built. Three things were established before calling it environmental rather than mine: it **reproduces identically on `main` at `4831965` with every change here stashed**; it **passes on the first try at a longer budget, taking 39.5 seconds** against a 30-second default; and the whole suite takes **about ten minutes here** where the harness's own configuration comment says it "runs in well under a minute" — this container is roughly an order of magnitude slower than the machine the timeout was set for. So both e2e runs below were taken with the per-test timeout raised for the run only (`--timeout=180000`). **Nothing in the repository was changed to make them pass**: no test skipped, no timeout committed, no assertion weakened. Migrate clean and seed clean on the wiped cluster. `eval:smoke` green — **7 cases**, the smoke tier's true count (1 happy, 1 trap, 5 permission; 13 further cases belong to other tiers and did not run). The e2e suite run **twice on that one clean seed, both green — 64 tests each time**, at the raised budget explained above. All five counters clean, and no number of any kind was minted — the next free ticket, question, parking and ADR numbers all stand exactly where they stood before this commit. *(They are deliberately not typed out here: the ticket-number guard reads any such number in this file as a claim on it, which is how the first attempt at this sentence failed its own check.)* **No migration, no personal data, no contract change, no new ticket, question or ADR, and `design-tokens.json` and the generated token files are byte-identical to `main`.**


## Slice Knowledge — where the writing rules live

*(Minted 2026-09-01, Session K — [ADR-0054](../architecture/adr/0054-the-knowledge-section-and-style-guides-as-rules.md).)*

*(Review of the overnight build, 2026-09-02 — the eight records below verified claim by claim; what follows is what the review corrected or must say beside them.)* (1) **A false-provenance fallback fixed at source**: `evidenceFor`, the one function decision 3's honesty lives in, described an extracted rule whose clause wording failed to resolve as "a rule Infora proposed" — unreachable today because the store's CHECK forbids the state, and now honest anyway. (2) **The "structural" guarantee on the tidy-up pass is a strong convention, not a structural impossibility** — one call site plus a genuinely biting test; the over-claiming comment is corrected and the branded type that would make the word true rides T-435. (3) 🔴 **The build's largest unsaid thing: the test substrate was taught nothing** — no fake-router answer for extraction or judgement rules, no seeded rule set — so the whole workbench cannot be driven in a browser and the checker's photograph shows the pre-rules world; minted as **T-435**. (4) **The drafting brief is on the wire to every participant** where the ticket said the super user — kept, deliberately: the brief is compiled from rules every participant may already read, and hiding a derivative of readable material would be ceremony; recorded here because the build's own record did not say it. (5) The register's row edit was disclosed in the record but the report's "personal-data untouched" was false; three of four drawing additions (`ordinal`, `supersedes_rule_id`, the proposal decision columns) went unflagged where `statement` was flagged — all justified, named here for the standard the record set itself. (6) Two unscoped whole-table test reads — the exact shape of the flake this slice itself fixed — scoped in review. (7) The recapture commit's subject ("the checker names rules") overstates its own body and photograph; the launcher still counts clauses and points at the plan's coverage, which is what the record honestly says.

**T-430 — Spike: should the deterministic checks run on Vale?** ✅ **Findings 2026-09-01.** *Plainly: a free, proven tool already does the kind of checking four of our five rule kinds need. This asks whether we should use it instead of writing our own — properly, with evidence.* [ADR-0054](../architecture/adr/0054-the-knowledge-section-and-style-guides-as-rules.md) decision 9 records the session's position (borrow the vocabulary, do not take the dependency in V1, keep adoption an engine swap) **and is explicitly open to being overturned by this spike** — the owner asked for the evaluation in-session. Findings land in [spikes/](spikes/) with a recommendation of exactly one of: adopt now, adopt later behind our own rule shape with a named gate, or do not adopt. **Answer against the tree, not the documentation:** which of the four deterministic kinds its rule model expresses (and whether **scope** and **exceptions** survive); the integration shape and **how per-run configuration on disk is not a wall surface**; whether its line/column offsets map losslessly onto our locators (T-271); what pins its version, since a declared workflow promises the same inputs give the same result; **proof** its script-executing rule type can be disabled; whether it can report what it examined, for ADR-0053 §5's coverage; and honestly, how much of our own code it removes given the offset mapping, config generation and process management exist either way. 🔒 **The finding that matters most is the cheapest to act on:** whether T-423's rule shape maps one-for-one onto its rule types — if a field breaks that, say which, now. **Done when:** the spike document exists, the recommendation is one of the three, and either a ticket or a deferred-register entry with a gate follows it. | *(Deps: T-423)*
  **As built. *Plainly: the evaluation ran, and the answer is: not now, but keep the door open — and one change to the rule shape was made immediately so that door stays cheap.*** Run by the co-captain in the review that landed Session K's records, against the tree and the tool's own documentation; the full eight answers are [spikes/spike-vale.md](spikes/spike-vale.md). **The recommendation is the middle option — adopt later, behind our own rule shape** — with the gate named (a pilot firm imports a Vale-format package, or rule sets outgrow the in-house matcher) and recorded in the deferred register. **The finding that mattered arrived exactly where the ticket predicted (question 8):** ADR-0054's exceptions field was one mixed list of contexts, which would have made later adoption a migration of every accepted rule and made "proper names" depend on a detector nobody has built. Split in the same review into **excepted contexts** and **excepted terms**, and the scope vocabulary gained `paragraph` and `list` — decision 4's own example rule ("one idea per paragraph") could not previously express its own scope. **Also established:** Vale's script rule type has no off switch, so if it is ever adopted the guarantee that no script rule can run must be by construction (our generator never emits one, pinned by a test) rather than by configuration; and Vale reports findings but never what it examined, so ADR-0053 §5's coverage statement is our work under any engine.

**T-433 — The Knowledge screens are drawn before they are built.** ✅ **Closed by ruling 2026-09-02.** *Plainly: nobody has drawn this yet. Every screen in it is new, and the house rule is that a new screen is proposed as a drawing you rule on before anyone writes code for it.* [docs/design/README.md](../design/README.md) owns the lifecycle — *sketch → mockup → owner ruling → ticket → build* — and this session ruled the **design** without ever drawing it, which is the step the record says comes first for a surface the product does not have. Four screens carry real forks a drawing settles better than prose: the **two shelves** side by side and what a shelf row says about material shared between projects; the **create** flow (upload or start empty, pick registers, three parameters); the **review screen**, which is the hard one — a rule beside the client's own wording, grouped by register, showing three origins, with severity overridable and accept-all present; and the **proposal** view. ⚠ **The owner may waive this**, as they did for the creator's re-cut on 2026-08-31, in which case the ruled design stands as written and the drawing is skipped — but the waiver should be a decision rather than an omission. **The mockup dies at capture** — [docs/design/mockups/README.md](../design/mockups/README.md) is the register that says what is pending. **Done when:** the mockups exist under the folder's own convention and are indexed; the owner has ruled or waived; anything the drawing changes lands as a dated note on [ADR-0054](../architecture/adr/0054-the-knowledge-section-and-style-guides-as-rules.md), never as a rewrite. | *(Deps: none)*
  **As ruled. *Plainly: the owner chose to skip the drawing step — the build goes straight to screens, and the owner reviews them as photographs in the walkthrough afterwards.*** Waived 2026-09-02 in the same breath that started the overnight build ("I trust you and the agent's judgment"), the second waiver of this step after the creator's re-cut; recorded so the design lifecycle's own rule is seen to be set aside knowingly rather than forgotten. The co-captain's recommendation had been to draw first; the owner's call stands, and the capture is the check.

**T-422 — The Knowledge section, and its two shelves.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-02** (no migration). *Plainly: a Knowledge item appears in every project's left-hand menu. It holds two shelves — your firm's own material, and the project's.* [ADR-0054](../architecture/adr/0054-the-knowledge-section-and-style-guides-as-rules.md) decision 1. The **firm's shelf** lists its rulebooks and its saved starting outlines, is org-private, and is **the same shelf** the workspace rail's existing `knowledge` placeholder becomes — so it renders **marked as the firm's own and the same on every project**, in both places, or a consultant on three schemes will believe they are editing a per-project copy. The **project shelf** lists the style guides, readable by every participant and curated by the owner organisation's super user (T-397 as built — 404 for a member organisation, 403 `super_user_required` for the owner's own non-elevated person). 🔒 **Assembled, not filtered** (T-269): a shelf a viewer may not curate shows no disabled controls, and material they may not see is **absent**. **Standards and legislation are not a third shelf** — they are library reference material (T-304) and this screen links to the library rather than restating it. **Done when:** both shelves render from the existing routes with no new endpoint invented; the workspace door shows the firm shelf and **no project material at all**; `/settings` is untouched; another organisation's member never sees the firm shelf (asserted, not assumed). | *(Deps: none)*
  **As built. *Plainly: there is now a Knowledge page in every project, with your firm's own writing material on one shelf and the project's on the other.*** This is the ticket that put a SCREEN in front of three stores that had none. A **Knowledge** item now sits in every project's rail, holding two shelves — the firm's own (its drafting manuals, its saved starting outlines) and the project's (the style guides). The firm's shelf renders identically in the workspace door, where the rail's `knowledge` placeholder stopped being a note; both doors carry the same two sentences saying it is the firm's own and the same on every project, which is the mark decision 1 requires. **No endpoint was invented**: the screen composes `/organisation/rulebooks` (T-308), the creator's own starting-outlines route (T-414) and `/projects/:id/style-guides` (T-397). ⚠ **One thing did not survive contact.** T-414 built the saved outlines on the document creator's project-scoped route, so listing them runs that tool's entitlement check — which has no answer outside a project. The workspace door therefore does not fetch them and **says so in one sentence** rather than showing a shorter version of the same shelf; that sentence is the only difference between the two doors, and adding an organisation-scoped outlines route was refused because the ticket's own done-when forbids a new endpoint. **Assembled, not filtered, is pinned twice**: a member's read of the firm's rulebooks answers 404 (T-308's tier, unchanged) and the shelf renders that as an ABSENT list rather than an empty state claiming the firm has no manual; and a viewer who may not curate the project's shelf is shown no **New style guide** control at all, never a disabled one. The wall is asserted rather than assumed in `apps/api/src/knowledge.test.ts`: two firms on one project each list their own manual and neither can see the other's, while both read the project's guide because it binds both.

**T-423 — The rule set: the store, and its versions.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-02** (migration **0064**). *Plainly: a style guide stops being only a document and gains a list of rules, which is what the tools will actually read.* Migration **0064**, drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) drawer 7 **before** it is written. [ADR-0054](../architecture/adr/0054-the-knowledge-section-and-style-guides-as-rules.md) decisions 2–5. A rule carries its **kind** (term / pattern / structure / measured / judgement), its **scope** (document, section, paragraph, sentence, heading, list, caption, table — amended in review 2026-09-01, T-430), its **exceptions** in two typed halves — **excepted contexts** (quotations, references, code, headings) and **excepted terms** (an authored list of exact words, the honest mechanism for proper names) — *(split in review 2026-09-01, T-430’s finding)*, its **register** (`DOCUMENT_LANGUAGES` + *all* — **not** a new vocabulary, decision 5), whether it **raises findings or only steers drafting**, its **severity**, and its **origin** (extracted / typed / Infora-proposed). 🔒 **An extracted rule points at the clause it came from** — `project_style_guide_clauses` is **not replaced**, because ADR-0048 §5's verbatim quotation resolves through it. **The set is versioned** and an amendment is a new version, on T-397's retire-never-edit precedent: the stored rule text is what past findings quoted. **A named person rides this ticket** — who created a set — already registered in [personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md) at ruling — the build keeps the row true, never re-adds it. **Done when:** the shape holds all three origins and the pointer is non-null exactly when the origin is *extracted*; a version is immutable once saved. | *(Deps: T-422)*
  **As built. *Plainly: a style guide now has a list of rules behind it — each one small enough to answer yes or no, and each saying where it came from.*** Migration **0064**, built from drawer 7's drawing and reduced to narrative in the same commit. ⚠ **The two tables are named `project_style_guide_rule_sets` and `project_style_guide_rules`, not the drawing's `rule_set_versions` and `rules`** — [personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md) had already registered the second under that name when ADR-0054 was ruled, and a bare `rules` names nothing in a schema this size; both now sit beside the two style-guide tables a reader would look for them next to. 🔒 **The clause store is not replaced and the pointer is a CHECK**: `(origin = 'extracted') = (clause_id IS NOT NULL)`, so an extracted rule cannot lose its pointer and a typed one cannot acquire a quotation it never earned. A second guard lives in the save path, because only a read can enforce *what* a pointer points at: a clause belonging to another guide is refused rather than repaired. 🔒 **Immutability is two triggers**, not a habit — a saved version rejects UPDATE and DELETE outright, and a saved rule rejects any change at all; the one mutation the store permits is a *pending* proposal being decided, and only its two decision columns move. Without that, decision 7's stored version stamp would point at something that could change underneath it. **The ruled vocabularies are CHECKs too** — the five kinds, the three origins, the eight scopes, the four excepted contexts, the register list (`DOCUMENT_LANGUAGES` + `all`, deliberately not a new vocabulary) and the two enforcement values — because a value the schema accepts and no code can set is a claim one of the two makes falsely. **One addition to the drawing, stated rather than smuggled:** every rule carries a `statement` — the rule in one sentence. The drawing put a judgement rule's sentence in the payload; the review screen, the compiled brief and a finding from a typed rule all need one for every kind, and deriving it at three call sites would have been three answers. It is **never** what a finding quotes: that is always the clause's own wording, and a test asserts the two differ. **Three named people ride the tables** — who accepted a set, who proposed a rule, who decided it — all three already registered at ADR-0054's ruling; the register's row was corrected to name both built tables rather than a new row being added.

**T-424 — Extraction: an uploaded standard becomes proposed rules.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-02** (no migration). *Plainly: you upload your writing standard and Infora reads it, pulls out the rules, and sorts them into kinds — including the ones your standard never wrote down for the kind of writing you picked.* [ADR-0054](../architecture/adr/0054-the-knowledge-section-and-style-guides-as-rules.md) decisions 2, 4 and 5. 🔒 **Splitting is the work, not a detail:** a clause saying three things becomes **three rules**, each one atomic and answerable yes or no, because a bundled rule is conflated by the model that later checks against it (decision 6). **Gap-filling** proposes rules per selected register from Infora's own baseline, **marked as Infora's own** and never claiming the client's guide said them. **The upload is optional** — the same path from an empty start is the baseline alone. Three creation parameters and no more: a name, whether Infora fills gaps, and the default severity. **Done when:** extraction reports how many rules carry a client-wording pointer, the way the rulebook loader reports how many clauses can be quoted; a document that yields nothing says so at upload rather than producing an empty set that looks configured. | *(Deps: T-423)*
  **As built. *Plainly: uploading your writing standard now turns it into a list of rules you can correct before anyone is bound by them.*** `POST …/style-guides/:id/rule-sets/extraction` reads the guide's stored clauses, shows them to a model under markers `[C1]`, `[C2]`…, and hands back proposed rules. 🔒 **It stores nothing** — a test asserts no version and no rule row exists after an extraction — because decision 2 puts the review step between extraction and saving *always*, and a stored draft set is what somebody eventually starts checking against by accident. 🔒 **The pointer is ours, never the model's**: the model names a marker and the `clauseId` and the wording are then taken from the clause we loaded, so a rule that claims to come from the client's document carries that document's words **byte for byte** (asserted against the stored row, not against a literal). A rule naming a clause the run never showed is discarded and counted. **Splitting is instructed three times** in the prompt and the admission rules cannot undo a bundling, which is the honest limit of what code can enforce here. **Gap-filling is a shipped baseline, not a generation** — eleven rules of ordinary good technical writing, each declaring the registers it belongs to — because a "baseline" a model invented per run would differ between two clients on the same day and could not honestly be called Infora's own. A baseline rule is proposed only where nothing extracted covers its topic for that register; the topic tag is model-supplied and the cost of it being wrong is a duplicate or a missing proposal that a person sees before anything binds. **The upload is optional and now has a door**: `POST …/style-guides` accepts a name with no file, storing a guide with no clauses and `source_format = 'none'` — honest in both directions, since nothing can be quoted from it and the shelf says 0 clauses rather than implying a document nobody uploaded. ⚠ **One guard the ticket did not ask for and the design needs:** a pattern rule's expression is written by a model and will run over every section of every draft, so `usablePattern` refuses one that is over-long, will not compile, or carries a nested quantifier (the catastrophic-backtracking shape). A refused pattern is **demoted to a judgement rule**, never dropped — the obligation the clause imposed is real — and a test asserts no shipped baseline pattern would be refused.

**T-425 — The review screen: correct it, then save it.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-02** (no migration). *Plainly: you see every rule Infora found, next to the exact words in your document it came from, and you fix, delete and add before anything binds anybody.* [ADR-0054](../architecture/adr/0054-the-knowledge-section-and-style-guides-as-rules.md) decisions 2 and 3. Rules common to every register first, then the register-specific ones. Each row shows its **origin** plainly — your document's own wording, typed by a person, or proposed by Infora — and severity is overridable per rule. **The owner organisation's super user saves, and that is what makes it bind.** ⚖ **Accept-all is permitted** *(owner-ruled 2026-09-01: "it is down to the client or the user to behave properly. We don't need to plan for that")* — this does **not** reopen ADR-0048 §3 or ADR-0053 §6, which govern accepting changes into a **work product**; here the client is accepting their own configuration of their own standard. **Done when:** an extracted rule renders beside its source wording; a typed rule renders with none and does not fake one; saving produces a new version; nothing binds before the save. | *(Deps: T-424)*
  **As built. *Plainly: you see every rule Infora found, next to the exact words in your document it came from, and you fix, delete and add before anyone is bound by them.*** The create step asks four things — a name, an optional file, the registers, and the two parameters — and then hands back the proposed list on the same screen; the review step is not a place you can navigate to, because it is what the extraction returns and it is stored nowhere. 🔒 **The absence of a quotation is rendered, in words.** An extracted rule shows the client's own wording under an address (*Your guide, 4.2*, or *unnumbered clause* where the guide numbered nothing); a typed or Infora-proposed rule shows a sentence saying a finding from it will name where it came from instead of quoting one. There is no fallback branch — a plausible blank is exactly what makes an invented quotation possible — and a render test asserts a typed rule produces no `rule-wording` element at all. **Rules common to every register come first**, keeping their extracted order within each group, because a reader checking whether a set is right must get the everything-rules right first. **Severity is a per-rule control** on every row, which is what makes the set-wide answer only a default. ⚖ **Accept-all is what the screen does**: Save takes the list as it stands, and there is no per-rule tick on the wire, because a flag would describe a gate the owner ruled out of existence. **The save sends the whole list, never a diff** — a version is the set as it stands, and a diff would need a base version that goes stale the moment two people are reviewing. **The tier is T-397's:** a consultant reads the set that binds them and gets a 404 on the save; the owner's own non-elevated person is told `super_user_required`. ⚠ **The drafting brief is stored empty by this ticket** and filled by T-429, which owns the compiler — a brief nothing produced is not the same as a brief with no rules in it, so it is not faked here.

**T-426 — Anyone proposes; the super user decides.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-02** (no migration). *Plainly: if a rule is wrong, the person who found it can say so, and the client's senior person accepts or declines.* [ADR-0054](../architecture/adr/0054-the-knowledge-section-and-style-guides-as-rules.md) decision 2. 🔒 **A proposal is visible to its author, that person's own organisation, and the owner organisation — never to another firm on the project** (ADR-0048 §6's precedent: a rival learning which rules a competitor is arguing about is the wall breach nobody thinks of as crossing the wall). **The proposer is told when it is accepted or declined** — the one notification this whole design adds, and it is a reply to the person's own act rather than a broadcast (ADR-0054 decision 8; ADR-0049's set is otherwise untouched). **A named person rides this ticket** — who proposed, who decided — already registered in [personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md) at ruling — the build keeps the row true, never re-adds it. **Done when:** a rival organisation's member cannot read a proposal (asserted); accepting one produces a new version; declining records no reason, on the finding-dismissal precedent. | *(Deps: T-425)*
  **As built. *Plainly: if a rule is wrong, the person who found it can say so, and the client's senior person accepts or declines — and no rival firm ever learns the argument happened.*** A proposal rides the same table as a rule, carrying a state, its proposer and its decider, exactly as drawer 7 drew it. 🔒 **The wall is one predicate with two readings, applied in the read's own WHERE**: the owner organisation sees every proposal on its own project, because it is the party that decides them and cannot decide what it cannot read; everyone else sees their own organisation's and nothing else, which covers the author since authorship implies membership. **Asserted in both directions** — a second consultancy on the same project does not see the first's proposal and its decision route answers 404, while the author, the author's colleague and the owner's super user all see it. **Accepting produces a new version** with the proposal folded in — replacing the rule it supersedes, or appended — and nothing is edited in place; **declining records no reason**, and a `reason` sent in the body is simply not a field, which a test checks by sending one. A decided proposal cannot be decided again. **A proposal is always `typed`**, whatever the body claims: nobody extracted it from the guide, so it has no wording behind it and the store's CHECK would refuse a pointer anyway. A proposal against a guide with no accepted set is refused — there is nothing to amend, and inventing a version to hang it off would make a proposal into a rule set nobody accepted. 🛑 **THE NOTIFICATION IS NOT BUILT, AND THIS IS THE TICKET'S ONE STOP.** ADR-0054 decision 8's single exception — the proposer is told when their proposal is decided — would need a fourth `NotificationEventType` and a fifth `NotificationSubjectKind`, both of which are fixed unions, and the notification set **has no emitter at all**: T-330 is open and waits on T-323, which waits on the parked T-316. Widening a fixed union is a stop-and-report trigger for this session, so the build stopped there and did not improvise. **What ships instead:** the proposer sees the outcome on the style guide's own page, where they made the proposal, with the decider named. The ticket's stated done-when is unaffected — it names the wall, the new version and the reasonless decline, and all three are built and asserted.

**T-427 — Every run records the rule-set version it used.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-02** (no migration). *Plainly: a check and a draft each store which version of the writing rules they ran against — stored, not shown.* [ADR-0054](../architecture/adr/0054-the-knowledge-section-and-style-guides-as-rules.md) decision 7, and the owner's correction that produced it. 🔒 **Stamped once on the RUN, never on each finding**, and **not displayed** — the owner ruled explicitly against a screen repeating *"checked against style guide v3"* down a list. ADR-0053 §2's per-finding `checkFamily` is a different field and is untouched. **Done when:** both tools' runs carry it; no finding carries it; no surface renders it. | *(Deps: T-423)*
  **As built. *Plainly: a check and a draft each now store which version of the writing rules they ran against — stored, and shown to nobody.*** ⚠ **It is stored as a bound workflow parameter rather than as a column, and that is a deviation with a reason.** A column on `runs` or `plans` would have needed a second migration, and 0065 belongs to the parallel session — so the choice was between a parameter and nothing. The parameter is defensible on its own merits: a run already stores what it ran against exactly this way (`families`, `depth`, `template_id`, `scope_version_ids`, the upload fingerprints), and the rule-set version is a fact of the same class. **The co-captain should rule on whether it stays there.** **Both workflows bumped a version** — `qa-check` to 2, `document-creation` to 3 — rather than being edited in place, because a plan records the version of the workflow it ran. 🔒 **Stamped once**: on the checker it rides the `measure` step, which expands exactly once and is the step that totals up what the run read, while the section check fans out — a test runs a 30-section draft, asserts the section check expanded many times, and asserts exactly one step in the whole plan carries the stamp. 🔒 **No finding carries it** — every returned finding and every stored row is asserted not to contain the version id, and `checkFamily` is untouched. 🔒 **No surface renders it, by construction rather than by care**: `ToolPlan` carries no step inputs at all, so the value cannot reach a screen, and a test asserts the whole run response contains neither the id nor the parameter name. Nothing reads it either — both adapters map only the inputs they declare. **Resolved in the same planner the run binds from**, so the plan the user saw and the record of what ran cannot name different rules (T-309's one-planner rule, applied to one more fact). The drafting run narrows to the guides the author selected, matching the drafting read itself; the check uses every live guide, because a rule that binds you binds you whether you remembered it or not.

**T-428 — The checker reads accepted rules, and four kinds of five stop costing a model call.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-02** (no migration). *Plainly: the writing check gets cheaper and more certain, because most rules can now be settled by ordinary code.* [ADR-0054](../architecture/adr/0054-the-knowledge-section-and-style-guides-as-rules.md) decisions 4 and 6. Term, pattern, structure and measured rules run as **code**; only judgement rules reach a model, one atomic yes/no statement each, returning findings keyed to the rule. 🔒 **ADR-0053 §2's check families do not change** — the kinds route into them: term/pattern/judgement report through the style-guide check, structure through completeness, measured through readability (scored, outliers flagged, never pass/fail). 🔒 **Scope and exceptions are honoured** or the terminology check fires on *the Project Board* and gets switched off. **Coverage (ADR-0053 §5) states rules, not only clauses** — how many rules were applied, of how many, per register. **Done when:** a term finding is classified **mechanical** by T-398's existing code test and reaches the bulk lane; a judgement finding quotes its rule; a finding from an Infora-proposed or hand-typed rule **does not quote the client's guide**. | *(Deps: T-425, T-427)*
