  **As built. *Plainly: the writing check got cheaper and more certain, because most rules can now be settled by ordinary code instead of by asking the AI.*** A new in-house matcher (`packages/capabilities/src/rule-matcher.ts`) settles **term** and **pattern** rules per section in code, **structure** rules against the draft's headings, and **measured** rules by arithmetic; only **judgement** rules reach a model, one atomic statement each under a `[J#]` marker, and the same admission rule governs them as governs a clause — an unresolvable marker is dropped and counted. 🔒 **ADR-0053 §2's families do not change**: term/pattern/judgement report through style, structure through completeness, measured through readability — and a measured finding is **always advisory**, whatever severity the rule carries, because readability is scored and never pass/fail. 🔒 **Scope and exceptions are honoured by a masking pass that preserves offsets** — every excepted span becomes the same number of spaces, so a match's index into the mask is its index into the real text and an anchor needs no second search. A test asserts *the Project Board* is spared while *the project* is not, and that a rule excepting quotations fires once where it would otherwise fire twice. 🔒 **A guide that has been restructured into rules is not ALSO read as prose** — otherwise the model would be asked, at a cost, to judge a clause a code pass has already settled, possibly to a different answer. A guide with no accepted set behaves exactly as it did before this ticket, which is why the exclusion is a parameter and not a rewrite. **The firm's rulebook is untouched and stays prose**, because ADR-0054 leaves that question explicitly open. **The four done-when assertions all hold at the route**: a term finding carries a replacement and `classifyFix` — T-398's existing structural test, unchanged — classifies it `mechanical`; an extracted rule's finding quotes the stored clause **byte for byte** against the row itself and never the rule's own statement; and a finding from an Infora-proposed rule carries `draft` evidence naming whose rule it is, with no `quote`, no `clause` and no trace of the client's guide anywhere in it. ⚠ **`DraftEvidence` is used for a third case and this is stated, not smuggled.** A typed or Infora-proposed rule has no client wording, so `RulebookEvidence` would have to invent a clause, a quote and a reference — and on screen an invented quotation is indistinguishable from a real one. `FindingInput` is a fixed union and widening it is a stop-and-report trigger, so the honest existing shape was used and `contracts/finding.ts` now records the third use in its own comment. **The co-captain should rule on whether that is right.** **Coverage states rules, twice.** The plan's sentence and the run's carry *N of M accepted rules applied*, with a per-register breakdown before the run; `steers_only` rules are excluded from `applied` and the difference is stated, because counting rules that cannot raise a finding would inflate the sentence — the same class of error as understating it. ⚠ **Register is not narrowed at the run, and that is a deliberate deviation.** The checker's launcher asks for no register, so a rule tagged `technical` cannot be matched against a document nobody has declared a register for. Rather than silently skipping every register-specific rule — a failure that would be invisible in a clean result — every accepted rule is applied and the coverage names the breakdown, which is the ADR's own quick/full argument applied here: prefer the failure the user can see. ⚠ **The launcher's static style note was not extended** to count rules per guide, because `StyleGuideRecord` is a type alias of `RulebookRecord` and breaking that alias is the drift its own contracts note warns about; the note now points at the plan's coverage, which is where ADR-0053 §5 puts this sentence anyway.

**T-429 — Drafting: the compiled brief, and the tidy-up pass.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-02** (no migration). *Plainly: the AI is told your judgement rules as a short brief you can read, and the mechanical ones are applied to its own output afterwards instead of being asked for.* [ADR-0054](../architecture/adr/0054-the-knowledge-section-and-style-guides-as-rules.md) decision 6. The brief is **compiled once when the set is saved**, stored, reused, and **readable by the super user** — same rules in, same brief out. Term and pattern rules are applied **after generation**, to the model's **own fresh output only**, inside the invoker's own sandbox, before any human has seen it. 🔒 **This is not a write path over a human's text** and ADR-0048 §3 is untouched — a test pins that the pass never touches text a person wrote. Term rules also go in as a short preferred-wordings list. ADR-0053 addendum A1's precedence is unchanged and now fires less often. **Done when:** the brief renders; the same set produces the same brief; the normalisation pass is asserted not to touch human text. | *(Deps: T-425)*
  **As built. *Plainly: the AI is told your judgement rules as a short brief you can read, and the mechanical ones are applied to its own output afterwards instead of being asked for.*** 🔒 **The brief is compiled once, at save**, from the judgement and steering rules — sorted and formatted and nothing else, so the same rules produce the same bytes whatever order they arrive in, which a test asserts by saving the same set reversed. Rules the tidy-up pass applies afterwards are deliberately **not** in it: asking for them in the prompt as well would spend context on them twice. It is **readable by the owner's super user** on the guide's own page, verbatim and in the mono face, because paraphrasing what the model is told would defeat the point of showing it. **Term rules also go in as a short preferred-wordings list**, because a draft written correctly the first time needs no normalising — a better outcome than one normalised afterwards. 🔒 **THE ASSERTION THIS TICKET EXISTS FOR IS THE NEGATIVE ONE, and it is structural rather than careful.** `normaliseFreshOutput` takes **only the sentences the drafting call produced**, and the builder assembles the author's own section headings without ever passing them through it. The test builds a document whose **author-written heading breaches an accepted term rule** and whose model-written sentence beside it breaches the same one: the heading comes out unchanged and the sentence is corrected. ADR-0048 §3 is untouched — the pass has no access to text a person wrote. Exceptions are honoured here too, so a rule that spares *the Project Board* in a check spares it in a draft. ⚠ **Only TERM rules are applied; pattern rules are counted and reported, not fixed** — and that is a deviation from decision 6's *"term and pattern rules are applied after generation"*. A pattern rule's stored shape carries an expression and **no replacement**: there is literally nothing to write in place of the breach. The run therefore reports `unfixed`, in the same spirit as `withheld` and `unreachableSources`, rather than leaving it silent. **The co-captain should rule on whether decision 6 needs a dated note.**

**T-435 — The test substrate learns the rules workbench.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-02** (no migration). *(Minted 2026-09-02 in review — the largest thing Slice Knowledge's build did not say: the browser-test stand-in was taught nothing about extraction or judgement rules, and the seed accepts no rule set, so the entire upload-extract-review-accept surface cannot be driven end to end in a browser and the checker's photograph necessarily shows the pre-rules world.)* *Plainly: the pretend AI that the browser tests and the walkthrough photographs run against does not know how to answer the two new kinds of question the rules work asks it, and the demonstration project has no accepted rules — so nobody can photograph or browser-test the new screens doing their real job.* The fake router needs an answer shape for the extraction prompt (clause-marked rules) and for judgement rules; the seed needs one accepted rule set on the Wrenfield guide, built through the real acceptance path. While here: give the tidy-up pass's input a branded type so its person-text guarantee becomes structural rather than one call site plus a test (the review corrected the comment that over-claimed this). **Done when:** the workbench can be driven end to end against the substrate; the walkthrough's checker beat photographs a rules-backed check; the branded type exists and the comment un-hedges. | *(Deps: none)*

  **As built. *Plainly: the pretend AI the browser tests and the walkthrough photographs run against now knows how to answer the two new kinds of question the rules work asks it, and the demonstration project ships with one accepted set of writing rules — so the new screens can be driven, and photographed, doing their real job.*** Three pieces, and each closes one of the done-whens.

  **The substrate learned both prompts.** The fake router in `apps/api/src/e2e-server.ts` gains an **extraction** branch — it reads the clause markers `[C1]`, `[C2]`… back off the prompt the route really built and answers with four clause-marked rules plus **one rule naming a clause that was never shown**, so the admission rules are exercised through a browser rather than only in a unit suite — and its section-check branch now answers **judgement rules**. 🔒 **Everything is read back off the prompt: the markers AND the section text.** A rule set that grows a judgement rule renumbers `[J#]`, and a check that runs section by section shows the branch a different section each time; a finding is therefore returned only where its rule is really on offer and its quote is really in the section under check. Answering blind would have put a permanent false discard count on the coverage sentence every screenshot carries.

  **The seed carries one accepted rule set** on the Wrenfield project style guide, accepted by the owner's super user (Rachel Bowen) — five rules spanning the kinds that make ADR-0054 decision 4 visible: a **term** rule and a **pattern** rule the code pass settles for nothing, two **judgement** rules extracted from the guide's own §2.4 and §3.2, and one **Infora-proposed** baseline rule filling a gap the guide is silent on. Four point at the clause they came from; the fifth points at none, which is migration 0064's CHECK stated as the property it exists for.

  ⚠ **DEVIATION — the seed does not literally call the acceptance path, and here is why.** `saveRuleSet` lives in `@infora/data`, and `@infora/data` depends on `@infora/db`, the package the seed is in. Importing it would be a dependency cycle **and** a widening of the one line in `scripts/dep-rules.mjs` that says db is depended on and never depends back — a stop-and-report trigger. So the rows are written in `packages/db/src/rule-set-seed.ts` with the same columns, and a new test, `apps/api/src/seed-rule-set.test.ts`, puts **the same rules** through the real `saveRuleSet` and the real `compileDraftingBrief` and compares the two stored results column for column, plus the drafting brief byte for byte. `apps/api` is the only package that can see both halves at once. The seed drifting into a shape no real save could produce now fails a test rather than passing unnoticed. **The co-captain should rule on whether that is the right resolution or whether the save belongs somewhere both can reach.**

  ⚠ **The section check's old MECHANICAL finding was removed from the substrate, deliberately.** It used to be invented by the fake router; it is now raised for real by the code pass over the seeded **term** rule, before any model call happens. So the accept-all-above-the-rewrites layout (ADR-0053 §6) is still photographable, and the half of it that is supposed to cost nothing genuinely costs nothing.

  **The branded type, and the comment that can now be honest.** `normaliseFreshOutput` no longer takes `readonly string[]`. It takes **`FreshModelOutput`**, whose brand key is a `unique symbol` `rule-matcher.ts` never exports — so the only expression in the codebase that produces one is `freshModelOutput(claims)` in the same file, and that takes **the claims a drafting call returned**, not strings. A bare string array cannot be passed in at all: it does not type-check. *(Review correction, 2026-09-02: the stronger form this sentence first took — that person-written text cannot be passed — is false; `freshModelOutput` is exported and takes any claims-shaped list, so passing person text is possible but now requires a deliberate wrap through the named door, which is the honest size of the guarantee.)* The review of 2026-09-02 had corrected this comment from *structural* to *a strong convention*; the word is now true, and the comment says which change made it true. The biting test in `document-builder.test.ts` — an author heading and a model sentence breaching the same rule, opposite fates — is unchanged and still passing.

  **Verified end to end against the running substrate**, not only in tests: signed in as the owner's super user over HTTP, the extraction route returned 11 proposed rules (4 extracted with the client's wording, 7 Infora-proposed gap fills, and the invented clause pointer refused), and posting them back saved rule-set **version 2** — upload → extract → review → accept, driven the whole way. The seeded world was reseeded afterwards.

**T-434 — The record catches up with what got built.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-02** (no migration). *Plainly: once these two slices land, the written record has to say the product now does this — otherwise the next person reads a design that no longer matches the screens.* The standing rule is that **a surface is not finished when it merges** (CLAUDE.md). Two different destinations, and the split is the ticket rather than a formality. **The Knowledge section goes to its component doc** — [component-4-context.md](../architecture/components/component-4-context.md), because it is **configuration, not a tool**: the walkthrough carries a section per standalone *tool* and forcing a settings surface into it would break that charter. The component doc gains the section, the two shelves, and the rule set as the guiding channel's first structured material — retiring its standing note that the style guide is prose. **External issue goes to the journey** — [user-stories.md](../architecture/user-stories.md) and the walkthrough — because it happens **to the deliverable the journey follows**: the story gains a final beat where the accepted chapter leaves the platform to someone with no account. **Done when:** component 4 describes what was built rather than what was designed; the journey carries the external-issue beat and the walkthrough photographs it; no design block from these slices is left sitting on the board. | *(Deps: T-429, T-432)*

  **As built. *Plainly: the written record now says what the product actually does, and the walkthrough has photographs of the two new things it does.*** The split was executed as ruled and not inverted.

  **Knowledge went to the component record.** [component-4-context.md](../architecture/components/component-4-context.md) gains **§9 — The Knowledge section, and the rule set**: the two shelves and the one-shelf-two-doors rule, what a rule set stores and why a rule is typed by how it can be enforced, the five screens, the curation tier, what the two consumers do with an accepted set, and what was deliberately not built. It is **configuration, not a tool**, so it gets no walkthrough section — forcing a settings surface into a page whose charter is the journey and the standalone tools would break that charter, which is the ruling this ticket carries.

  ⚠ **Two standing claims in that doc were STALE and were corrected in the same pass**, because "describes what was built" is the done-when: §1 still said ADR-0048 §4 rules the firm's rulebook **guiding** material — its own dated addendum of 2026-08-30 moved it to **informing** — and it still ended *"Programme and project context still have no store here"*, which stopped being true when T-397 gave the project style guide one and T-414 added the saved outlines. Both now read as built, and the guiding channel's entry records that it carries **structured** material as well as prose.

  **External issue went to the journey**, because it happens **to the deliverable the journey follows**. [user-stories.md](../architecture/user-stories.md) gains a final beat on the lead reviewer's story: the accepted chapter is issued from the library to a consultation respondent with no account, the screen says the honest thing rather than the flattering one, everybody below the project's chosen line asks instead, and the log later says she opened it. The walkthrough gains **four photographs** of it, and a fifth cast member with no Infora account.

  **One capture at the end covered everything this branch changed** — 70 shots, seed first then servers, downscaled to 1440 and rebuilt. The four new frames are `26a-external-issue`, `26b-external-link`, `26c-external-document` and `26d-transmittal-receipt`. 🔒 **The recipient's page is photographed from a browser context carrying no cookies at all**, because photographing it from Rachel's own browser would prove nothing — she can already read the document. That visit is also what **records the first open**, so the receipt in the transmittal-log shot was written by the previous beat actually happening rather than staged. **Every changed frame was read back as an image**, and the three the ticket names show what is claimed: the recipient's page carries one revision with no rail and no way further in; the log's external row reads *"Opened Sep 02, 2026 · Link expires Oct 02, 2026"* beside Mrs Patel's name; and both checker beats now photograph a **rules-backed** check — a mechanical fix quoting the project style guide's §2.1 verbatim, a `Required` finding quoting its §2.4, a rewrite measured against the Infora-proposed rule the project accepted, and one finding quoting the firm's own §4.7 as *"your firm's rulebook"*. The coverage sentence reads *"5 of 5 accepted rules applied"* where it used to name only clauses. *(Review precision, 2026-09-02: all five photographed facts are true of the capture as a whole; attribution by frame — the §2.4 and firm-rulebook findings are visible in `t2-12-dismiss`, and the coverage sentence in `t2-06-run`, not in the two beats this sentence gestures at.)*

  ⚠ **THREE THINGS DID NOT SURVIVE CONTACT, all in the capture and all recorded here rather than only in the report.** (1) The checker's mechanical finding **moved section**: it used to be invented by the stand-in router in §3, and is now raised for real by the code pass in §1, so the drift beat had to be staged on the phrase the rule actually names. (2) That move exposed a **real product property** the old fixture had been hiding: an anchor is an absolute span, and a bulk apply runs descending so one span never moves the next **within that call** — but two SEPARATE accepts have no such protection, so taking the mechanical fix above the rewrite drifts the rewrite and its accept is refused. The capture now takes the rewrite first; the shots keep their order and their claim, because `t2-10` photographs the **layout** (accept-all above the rewrites), which is what ADR-0053 §6 is about, and not which is clicked first. **The co-captain should rule on whether the product ought to re-anchor surviving findings after an apply** — today the honest banner is the whole answer. (3) The walkthrough prose for the recipient's page was **written before the shot and corrected after reading it**: it claimed the project's standing note and the stated reason appear there, and neither does — the seeded project sets no standard message, and the page does not render the reason.

  **Nothing from these two slices is left sitting on the board.** The [fold-in register](plan.md#the-fold-in-register) gains a row for each, saying where it went and when.

## Slice External Issue — a deliverable reaches someone with no account

*(Minted 2026-09-01, Session K — [ADR-0055](../architecture/adr/0055-external-issue-to-a-party-with-no-account.md); built from 2026-09-02. Records move here ticket by ticket as they close.)*

*(Review of the overnight build, 2026-09-02 — one serious hole, three real defects, all fixed in the review that merged this.)* (1) 🔴 **The project request queue broke the wall at the two permissive permission levels**: the approver widening short-circuited both cuts for every row, so a rival firm's people would have received each issue's recipient, message and live link token — and the token is the access, so that was document content across the wall. The widening now covers rows still awaiting a decision and nothing else (a pending request has no token to leak); a test drives it as the rival at the permissive level, against a project that genuinely holds decided rows. The builder's own rival test ran only at the strictest level, which is why it could not catch this. (2) **The reason a request was declined was stored and shown to nobody who asked** — the queue dropped answered rows on the spot, so the record's "the person who asked reads it" was true of no screen; declined rows now stay listed for the parties who may read the reason, the answer shown where the ask was made. (3) **The rewritten transmittal shape rule re-armed the exact trap it was rewritten to close** — still no fallback branch, so a fourth kind added later would again slip through unchecked; `ELSE false` added. (4) **A requester's chosen link duration was collected, unstorable, and silently replaced by the default on approval**, under an on-screen promise that nobody retypes what was asked — stored and honoured now, the approver's explicit choice still winning. Also in review: the schema snapshot the parallel build rightly left was regenerated on the merged tree (the generator is silent again); the page a recipient reads — the one screen rendering outside the session gate — gained its first tests, including that every link on it stays inside the token's own file routes; a dead client binding was removed; and three deviations the build's own records omitted are said here — no browser-suite run (instructed, run in this review), no seed or walkthrough material (the beat is T-434's), and small substrate touches (the sessionless route exemption, the file-type export, the dev-proxy prefix). One judgement left as built and noted: `mayIssue` and `mayApprove` are today one fact under two names — if they ever diverge, the shape wants revisiting.

**T-431 — External issue, from the library.** *Plainly: send a finished document to a landowner or a consultee who will never have a login — they get a link to that one document and nothing else.* [ADR-0055](../architecture/adr/0055-external-issue-to-a-party-with-no-account.md) decisions 1–6. Migration **0065**: a third `kind` on the existing transmittal table (`external`), extending ADR-0035 §1's discriminator and its CHECK so no round, edit lock or snapshot can attach; plus a **recipient record** — name and email, **never an Organisation, never a Participant, never a Membership**. 🔒 **No clause of the wall changes and none may:** there is no grant to resolve, because the link is the access. The link serves **one named version** and **expires**; a later version does not retract it (ADR-0013, and the ISO 19650 position that an issued document is a snapshot). **No acknowledgement gate** — the download is the receipt, recorded. The sender supplies the **email, the reason, and the message**; the owner organisation's super user may set a **standard message** carried on every external email. **The door is in the library**, on the deliverable — not a tool, not a rail item. ⚠ **Stated on screen, not only here:** anyone holding the link is the recipient, so the record is exactly as strong as the email it replaces and must not read as stronger. **A named person with no account rides this ticket** — recipient name, email, reason and message — already registered in [personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md) at ruling — the build keeps the row true, never re-adds it. **Done when:** a link serves one version and nothing else of the project; it expires; the transmittal log answers "who was this issued to" in the one place it already answers it for the other two kinds. | *(Deps: none)*
  **As built. *Plainly: a finished document can now be sent to someone outside Infora as an expiring link, and the record keeps who sent what to whom and why.*** The door is on the deliverable in the **project library**, beside the transmittal that stays inside the project: a modal takes the recipient's name, their email address, why the document is being sent and the message that goes with it, and hands the sender back the link. **There is no mail transport yet** — T-323 (the SES seam) and T-330 (the sending) wait on external lead time, so the link is handed to the sender to convey, and nothing in what leaves the platform carries document content beyond the link itself, which is T-330's rule applied before its own ticket lands. **Migration 0065**, hand-written from drawer 5's drawing because migration 0064 belongs to a session running in parallel and `drizzle-kit generate` would have emitted a snapshot missing its tables; the snapshot is resynced at merge. ⚠ **The CHECK had to be rewritten, not extended:** it was a `CASE` over the two known kinds with no `ELSE`, and a CHECK that evaluates to NULL *passes* — so adding `external` to the enum alone would have silently unbound `round_id` and `direction` for exactly the kind the ADR promises can never touch a review cycle. A test now inserts a would-be external transmittal carrying a direction and asserts the database refuses it. **The recipient's page has no session behind it and no shell around it** — it is the one route rendered outside the session gate, and it resolves an opaque token to one version: not the library, not the project, and not a later revision, each asserted. An expired link and an invented one return the identical 404, so a guesser learns nothing from the difference. **Who may issue is the project setting from the start**, defaulting to the strictest of ADR-0055 §7's three levels, so no project discovers the choice by finding a document already gone; T-432 makes it configurable and gives everyone below the line the request. **The transmittal log answers "who was this issued to" in the one place it already answered it** for the other two kinds, cut per viewer exactly as ADR-0035's addendum cuts the distribution list: the owner and the sending organisation read the person, the producing organisation reads that its document left, and a rival firm on the project — given a live share and an acknowledgement, so the test proves the cut and not merely the wall — reads nothing. 🔒 **Two things deliberately NOT built, and both are reported rather than quietly skipped.** *No record of the link being opened*: ADR-0055 §5 calls the download the receipt, but an open timestamp is behavioural data about a named person, outside the four fields the register carries and the same shape as the notifications table's `read_at` — it is one column and one write whenever the owner rules it. *No self-service erasure surface* for the recipient's four fields: the row carries no append-only trigger, so the deletion the register promises is possible, but nothing on a screen does it.

**T-432 — Who may issue, and the request that goes to whoever may.** *Plainly: the client decides who is allowed to send documents outside the project — and anyone else can still ask, with someone who is allowed approving it.* [ADR-0055](../architecture/adr/0055-external-issue-to-a-party-with-no-account.md) decision 7. A whole-project setting on the owner-super-user tier (`conflict_attestation_required` and `review_period_default_days`'s precedent), three levels: **any member of any organisation** / **any super user of any organisation** / **only super users of the project-owning organisation**. Everyone below the chosen line **requests**, carrying every fact the issue needs, and someone above it approves or declines — so on the strictest level a consultant's request is approved by the client, which is the point of that level. 🔒 **Assembled, not filtered** (T-269): a person who may not issue sees the **request** action, not a disabled issue button. ADR-0049's notification set gains nothing — a pending request is a queue on the surface, not a tray event. **Done when:** each of the three levels is asserted from both sides; a declined request records the decision; the setting is refused to a member organisation the way every other whole-project setting is. | *(Deps: T-431)*
  **As built. *Plainly: the client now chooses who is allowed to send documents out of the project, and everybody else can still ask, with somebody who is allowed approving or declining it.*** The three levels are one stored setting on the owner super user's tier, and **one endpoint carries both acts**: whoever posts an external issue either sends it or, if the setting puts them below the line, asks for it — T-389's withdraw-or-propose shape, and for the same reason, because two endpoints would be two answers to what an external issue is and a caller could then pick. **Assembled, never filtered** (T-269): the library's button reads *Issue externally…* or *Request external issue…* off a `mayIssue` the server computes, so nobody is shown a disabled control, and the queue of pending requests appears only for people who can answer it. **The request carries every fact the issue needs** — deliverable, revision, recipient, reason, message — and the database freezes all of them, so approving sends exactly what was asked for and an approver cannot quietly redirect somebody else's request to another address or another document. It also issues **the revision that was asked for** rather than whatever has since become current. ⚠ **On the middle level, the approver may be a different firm's super user** — that is ADR-0055 §7 as written, which explicitly supersedes the session's own recommendation that the sending firm approve its own; the test asserts it happening across firms rather than assuming it. **A decline is answered, not merely refused:** the reason is required by the endpoint and by the CHECK, and the person who asked reads it — the withdrawal reason's precedent (T-389). A request is **answered once**; a second answer is a 409 in front of the trigger that would refuse it anyway. **No notification was added**, per ADR-0055's own Consequences: a pending request is a queue on the library screen, where the door is, and not something that chases anybody into a tray. All three levels are asserted from both sides, and the setting is refused to a member organisation exactly as every other whole-project setting is.

**T-436 — The opening of an external link becomes part of the issue record.** ✅ **Built 2026-09-02** (migration **0066**). *(Minted 2026-09-02 on the owner ruling completing ADR-0055 decision 5 — the build had stopped exactly here, correctly, because it was a fifth stored fact about a person with no account.)* *Plainly: when someone outside Infora opens the link they were sent, the deliverable's record now says so — "opened on the 4th" — beside the send itself, in the same library log that lists every other transmittal. Nothing about the person is inferred: whoever holds the link is the recipient, and the fact belongs to the document's issue history, not to a file about them.* First-open timestamp on the recipient row (a later open changes nothing — the receipt is that it was read, not how often); shown wherever the row's state already shows, in the library's transmittal log external rows included; the register carries the fifth fact from this ruling. **Done when:** the first open is recorded once and rendered beside the send; the identical-response rule for expired and invented links is untouched (recording must not create a distinguishable path); the rival-firm cut and the producing-organisation posture are unchanged and re-asserted; no other fact about the recipient is stored. | *(Deps: none)*

  **As built. *Plainly: the deliverable's record now says when the person it was sent to first opened it.*** One column, `external_recipients.opened_at`, written once on the first successful open of the link and never moved afterwards — the receipt is that the document **was read**, not how often it was looked at. It is rendered beside the send in the **library's transmittal log**, the one place that already answers *"who has this been issued to?"* for all three kinds: an external row now reads **“Opened Sep 02, 2026”** *(review correction: the record first quoted the ticket's illustrative wording as if it were the render)* or **“Not yet opened”** next to the link's expiry. Migration **0066**, built from drawer 5's drawing, with the drawing reduced to narrative in the same commit.

  🔒 **THE CAREFUL EDGE HELD, AND IT IS TESTED WHERE IT MATTERS.** Recording an open must not make an expired link distinguishable from an invented one — telling a guesser that a token once existed is telling them the guess was close. The write sits **only on the success path**, after `liveRecipient` has already resolved a live token, so every refusal takes exactly the code it took before this ticket. The existing identical-response test was extended to prove it **after a real open has been written**: the expired and the invented token still return the same status, the same body and the same headers (bar the per-request id, which is unique by design), and neither refusal writes anything.

  🔒 **THE STORE ENFORCES "ONCE", NOT THE ROUTE.** 0065's immutability trigger refused every update to a row that was no longer `requested`, which would have made this column unwritable. It was **rewritten rather than replaced**: the frozen identity — the deliverable, the version, and the four personal fields — is untouched, so an approver still cannot redirect somebody else's request. One narrow door admits `opened_at` on an **issued** row that has none, with nothing else moving in the same statement. Three refusals fall out and all three are asserted against the database directly: a second receipt, a cleared one, and one recorded against a request nobody approved.

  **The two cuts were re-asserted rather than assumed.** The **producing organisation's posture is unchanged** — it still reads that its document left the project and still does not read to whom — and it now reads the receipt as well, because *the document was read* names nobody. The **rival firm still reads no external row at all**, so there is no receipt for it to read either; the test that already gave the rival a live share and an acknowledgement was left to prove the cut, and the new field widened nothing. `openedAt` therefore sits **outside** the recipient-withheld cut, and the reasoning is recorded in [contracts.md](contracts.md) rather than only here.

  **No other fact about the recipient is stored**, and that is now asserted against the table itself rather than against a reading of the code: a test reads `information_schema.columns` for `external_recipients` and pins the exact column list. The register's row was already written at the ruling; it gains only the built marker and the migration number.

  ⚠ **A REAL TRAP FOUND, AND IT WAS NOT THIS TICKET'S DOING.** Migration 0065 carries a **hand-set journal timestamp** — `1788460000000` in `migrations/meta/_journal.json`, about 35 hours ahead of the clock the session that wrote it ran on. Drizzle's migrator applies only entries whose `when` is later than the newest one already recorded in the database, so this migration's honestly-generated timestamp sat **before** 0065's, the file was **skipped in silence**, and `pnpm --filter @infora/db run migrate` still printed *"migrations applied clean"*. It was found by a test failing on a column that should have existed, not by reading the log. 0066's `when` is set to one tick after 0065's, the migration header records the trap, and **the next migration after this one must be later again**. **The co-captain should rule on whether `migrate` ought to fail loudly when a journal entry is older than the last applied one** — the silence is the dangerous half, not the timestamp. *(Ruled in review, 2026-09-02: the one-tick fix preserved the landmine — both entries still sat ~31 hours in the future, so anything generated before that instant would be skipped on any database already carrying them. Both timestamps are pulled back to honest past values — safe because no long-lived database has applied either — and the repository now refuses the whole class: `check:migrations` asserts the journal ascending, nothing future-dated, and every entry's file present, wired into `pnpm run check` and therefore CI. It would have caught the original trap and the deferral both.)*

## The app builder — ticketed 2026-09-06, post-V1, built locally ahead of deployment

*(Minted 2026-09-06, Session AB — [ADR-0056](../architecture/adr/0056-the-app-model.md) and [ADR-0057](../architecture/adr/0057-connections-and-stored-credentials.md); research first, then two drawings, then the build. Records move here ticket by ticket as they close.)*

- **T-437 — The UI research pass: what a builder and a viewer see in Retool and Lovable.** *Plainly:* before Infora's app-builder screens are drawn, look at how two products that already do this arrange the job on screen, and write down what to copy and what cannot be copied. The owner's instruction (2026-09-06): *"we should look at what their interfaces and workflows look like first before trying to define the interface for infora."* Three jobs, in a reference document (`docs/reference/app-builder-ui-review.md`, indexed in the folder's README, **context never authority**, the `legora-ui-review.md` precedent): (1) **the builder's flow** — how each orders connect-data, define-tables, draw-the-interface, set-the-schedule, write-the-agent's-instructions; where the AI assistant sits and what it prompts the user to think about (ADR-0056 §2b's guiding duty); (2) **the two seats** — building versus using a deployed app, which Retool separates sharply and Lovable barely does; (3) **where their model is not ours** — single-firm, no wall inside a project, no organisation stamp on a row, no template stripped of client data — stated plainly so the drawings do not import a shared-workspace assumption; and (4) **a third product with a different job — Nomic's platform** (added by the owner 2026-09-06: *"it's not an app builder but it is a company building specific app solutions which i believe could be built in infora by users to their own specifications"*). Nomic reportedly offers pre-built agents for engineering firms — drawing review, submittal review, code compliance, RFI research among the claims — over the firm's documents where they already sit; **this ticket's research verifies that catalogue rather than inheriting it** *(reworded in review 2026-09-06 — the board had stated the unverified catalogue as fact)*. That is Session X's first layer as a product. The research takes its catalogue apart: for each agent, what it takes in, what it puts out, how it is shown to a non-engineer, and **which of them a firm could build on Infora as a playbook through the stepped builder, and what the builder would have to offer for that to be possible** — a PDF markup step, a connection to the authority corpus, an app table the output lands in. This is the *catalogue* view the two builders lack, and it says what Infora's own supplied playbooks (ADR-0056 §11) should be. Screenshots or described screens, sourced. **Done when:** the document exists with all four sections, is indexed, names for each of ADR-0056's steps which product's pattern (if any) the drawing should start from, and lists which of Nomic's agents are buildable as playbooks and what each needs from the builder. **Deps:** none.
  **As built. *Plainly: before drawing Infora's own app-builder screens, we wrote down how two real products arrange the same job, and what Nomic actually sells.*** The document is [app-builder-ui-review.md](../reference/app-builder-ui-review.md), indexed in the reference folder, with the four sections the ticket named, a per-step pattern table for the drawings (§5), the Nomic catalogue taken apart and mapped to playbooks (§4c), and a findings-versus-proposals section (§6) so nothing reopens a ruling silently. **What the research found that the ticket did not expect.** *Retool has two builders now*: its drag-and-drop editor became a "classic app" on 28 May 2026 and a chat-first builder (Chat · Data · Code beside a live preview) took its name; the classic editor's AI assistant is withdrawn on 30 September 2026. *Both builders are chat-first with no wizard*, so ADR-0056 §2b's stepped, walked-through flow has no direct precedent — the nearest things are Lovable's Plan mode (questions before building) and Nomic's three-question workflow builder. *Neither product has a row that belongs to the organisation that entered it, a submission state, or a per-screen "who may open it" asked while building* — the acceptance question and the who-may-open question are drawn fresh. *The playbook rule is the market's own*: Lovable's Remix copies schema and never records or secrets. **The Nomic verdict:** the company is Nomic AI, which announced its pivot to architecture, engineering and construction on 3 November 2025; the catalogue the board attributed to it — drawing review, submittal review, code compliance, project research including RFI responses — is real and sourced; and *"not an app builder" was half wrong*, because Nomic also ships a plain-language workflow builder (describe what it does, what files it needs, what it produces; share as Can run / Can edit) and a developer API. Most of its catalogue maps to Infora's **existing tools** (the checker, Ask, the creator, the extractor) rather than to an app with tables; two agents — a submittal register and a compliance register — are buildable as playbooks if the builder gains a document-input step, a file column on an app table and a marked-up file as a run output, none of which the returns app needs and none of which is proposed here. **One PROPOSED amendment** (draft-versus-published definitions, from Retool's release model) is recorded on T-439's entry and in the review's §6, untouched in the ADRs. **Method and honesty:** three machine-read passes over the vendors' own documentation on 2026-09-06, every load-bearing page re-fetched by the session itself; no hands-on use, no screenshots downloaded (each described screen names the page that carries it), no working files claimed. **Deviations:** the reference folder's index carried the landscape document's row twice, and the duplicate was removed in the same commit as the new row; the walkthrough, e2e and docker were not run, because a document needs none of them — the gate was `pnpm run check` with its exit code read directly.

- **T-438 — Two drawings: the builder's stepped flow, and the returns app seen twice.** *Plainly:* draw the two screens the owner asked for before anything is built, and only those two. **The builder's stepped flow** — the steps in the owner's words (data connections, the interface, how often it runs, the analysis or prompts given to the agent) plus the table step with its **"does this hold contractual data?"** acceptance question, showing where the agent prompts the builder (ADR-0056 §2b). **The returns app as a contractor and as the client** — the same app, two viewers: the contractor's form and own-rows-only view; the client's dashboard over every contractor's rows, and the accept/reject act. Per [docs/design/README.md](../design/README.md): drawn in `docs/design/mockups/`, ruled on by the owner, deleted at capture. Lists, the playbook shelf and the share/approval dialogs follow the kit and are **not** drawn. **Done when:** both mockups are approved by the owner, with the step order confirmed. **Deps:** T-437. **🟡 Drawn; first look taken 2026-09-06 — owner: *"these are perfect"* — second look pending.** Both mockups are in [docs/design/mockups/](../design/mockups/README.md) — `app-builder-stepped-flow.html` (the table step with the contractual-data question, and the interface step) and `returns-app-two-seats.html` — each naming the T-437 pattern it starts from. Not closed: this ticket's own text needs two looks, and the forks in each mockup's notes and the two PROPOSED items still need a ruling each before anything reaches an ADR addendum; the step order drawn (what the app is → tables → connections → interface → schedule → analysis → check and open) is the first thing to confirm or re-cut; the open forks ride each mockup's notes. *(**PROPOSED, 2026-09-06, from drawing 2 — not applied, for the owner:** a contractor's row in `draft` state read by its entering organisation only, the owner reading it from `submitted` onward — today ADR-0056 §2 reads every row by its organisation and the owner, so the client sees a return the contractor has not finished; the drawing shows the ruled behaviour quietly and recommends the change. Also on the drawing: whether a rejection carries a reason, which drawer 9 as drawn says it does not.)*
  **As built. *Plainly: the two screens the owner asked to see before anything is built were drawn, shown, approved on the first look, and every open question on them was ruled the same day.*** Two mockups in [docs/design/mockups/](../design/mockups/README.md), on the design tokens and the seeded Wrenfield–Ashcombe project, each naming the T-437 pattern it starts from: **`app-builder-stepped-flow.html`** — seven steps in the owner's words (what the app is and who it is open to → the tables → data connections → the interface → how often it runs → analysis and prompts → check and open), the table step with its *"does this hold contractual data?"* question recorded in the form and asked by the agent in its own pane, and the interface step where the agent asks who may open each screen; **`returns-app-two-seats.html`** — the same app as Nadia Okonjo at Redgate Ecology (a form and her own organisation's returns) and as Rachel Bowen at Trentmoor Energy (every organisation's rows, the totals, the latest insight, the accept-or-reject act). The owner's first look, 2026-09-06: *"these are perfect."* The owner then asked for Claude's recommendation on each fork riding the notes and confirmed all six in one line (*"okay let's write the addendum and do the other things and give me a report for my co-captain"*) — recorded as a wholesale confirmation, not a per-item readback, in [grill-history.md](../grill-sessions/grill-history.md) and as ADR-0056's 2026-09-06 addendum: step order as drawn; a working and a published copy of the definition; a draft row read by its entering organisation only; a required reason on a rejection; the agent as a pane; a chat that fills the steps in declined. **What changed on the record because of the rulings:** drawer 9 re-drawn (four `published_*` columns on `apps`, `rejection_reason` on `app_rows`, the draft narrowing on the read predicate); the personal-data register's decider row (a reason is now recorded) and app-instance row (who published); `CONTEXT.md`'s App and App table terms; T-439–T-442 re-cut to match. **The drawings were updated to the rulings** — the client's screen no longer shows a contractor's draft, the contractor's rejected row shows its reason, and each fork note now says how it was ruled — and stay in the mockups folder until T-447 photographs the built screens and deletes them. **Deviations:** the session brief read this ticket as needing the owner to see the drawings twice; the ticket's own done-when is *approved, with the step order confirmed*, and both are met on the first look plus the rulings — the co-captain should say if a second sitting is still wanted. Rendered with headless Chrome and read by eye before committing; no e2e, docker or walkthrough capture, since nothing runs.

- **T-439 — Drawer 9's first migration: the app substrate.** *Plainly:* the tables that hold apps and the rows people type into them, built exactly as drawn. `apps`, `app_scope_grants`, `app_tables`, `app_rows`, `app_table_shares`, `app_runs`, `app_exports`, `playbooks` from [data-model.md](data-model.md) drawer 9 — **not** the three connection tables, which wait for deployment. The hand-written half the drawing names: the `CHECK`s (closed pair; decided pair; `state` null iff the table has no acceptance step), the never-update-an-accepted-row trigger, the playbook rows-only-for-reference-tables trigger, append-only on shares, runs and exports. Contracts: the `definition` and `columns` shapes in `packages/contracts`, so the read path never parses JSON to decide access. **Personal data:** the six drawer-9 rows in [personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md) are already registered at ruling; this ticket makes them true and updates their "drawn" marks to built. **Done when:** the migration applies on a wiped database, `check:migrations` and `check:personal-data` pass, drawer 9 reduces to narrative and a pointer in the same commit, and a schema test proves an `UPDATE` on an accepted row is rejected. **Deps:** T-438 (nothing is built before both drawings, by the owner's ruling). *(**Re-drawn 2026-09-06 on ADR-0056's addendum, before this migration is written:** `apps` gains the published copy — `published_definition`, `published_version`, `published_by_participant_id`, `published_at`, null together until first published (ruling 2); `app_rows` gains `rejection_reason`, required exactly when the state is `rejected` (ruling 4); and the read predicate reads a `draft` row by its entering organisation only (ruling 3). The register's rows are updated at ruling; the hand-written `CHECK`s grow by two.)*
  **As built. *Plainly: the tables that hold apps and their rows now exist, and a row is readable by exactly the people the rules say.*** Migration **0067** created drawer 9's eight tables — `apps`, `app_scope_grants`, `app_tables`, `app_rows`, `app_table_shares`, `app_runs`, `app_exports`, `playbooks` — from the drawing as reviewed, and **not** the three connection tables, which wait for the deployment's secrets store. Schema in [drawer9-apps.ts](../../packages/db/src/schema/drawer9-apps.ts); drawer 9 in [data-model.md](data-model.md) reduced to narrative and a pointer in this same commit, which is the state rule running end to end for the third time. **The hand-written half is eight `CHECK`s and eight triggers**, each argued in the migration: the published quartet and the closed pair move together; a scope grant names exactly one grantee; a decided row names its decider and its time; **a rejection carries a required reason and only a rejection may carry one**; `state` is null exactly when the table has no acceptance step (cross-table, so a trigger); **an accepted row is never edited, retired or deleted in place**; the two grant tables are append-only intervals whose revocation is never reopened; `app_exports` is insert-only; an app run's two actor stamps cannot disagree with Drawer 3's; and **a playbook is refused if a `rows` key appears anywhere in either JSON column**. **Twenty-six database tests** ([app-substrate.test.ts](../../packages/db/src/app-substrate.test.ts)) drive each of those at the database rather than at a route, including the two the ticket named by name (an `UPDATE` on an accepted row is rejected; a rejection with no reason is rejected). Contracts: [app-builder.ts](../../packages/contracts/src/app-builder.ts) types the definition, the columns and the row, with the request bodies in `endpoints.ts` so the principle-3 guard sees them; a dated why-note is in [contracts.md](contracts.md). The six drawer-9 rows in [personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md) moved from *drawn* to *built*; none was re-added.

  **Three deviations, all deliberate and all argued in the files that carry them.** **(1) `users.may_build_apps` is a column outside drawer 9**, added by this migration because the slice has exactly one and the toggle is T-440's surface. ADR-0056 §12 fixed the policy and left the control to the build; it sits at user grain because the decision is the organisation's about its own person, and `org_role = 'admin'` does not confer it implicitly. **(2) The `decided_pair` CHECK carves out one state.** The drawing said the decider and its time are *"set together with accepted/rejected, null otherwise"*; a superseded row that was **accepted** still has to name the person who accepted it, because the correction does not unhappen the decision, so `superseded` may carry the pair or not and every other state may not. Requiring null there would erase the attribution the constraint exists to keep. **(3) A rejected row is not flipped to `superseded`.** The drawing says a correction flips the old row; the `rejection_reason` CHECK the same drawing requires (non-null **iff** rejected) means flipping a rejected row would force its reason to be erased — which is ruling 4 undone. So a rejected row keeps its state and its reason, and supersession is read off the correcting row's `supersedes_row_id`, which is exactly how the approved mockup draws it (*"Rejected · superseded"*). The **accepted** case flips as drawn, and it is the one transition the frozen-row trigger permits.

  **The one drawn widening was built and nothing else was:** `step_type` gained `app_step` and no other vocabulary moved. **Gates:** `pnpm run check` with its exit code read directly; the migration applied on a wiped volume with the column queried rather than the "clean" line trusted; `check:migrations` and `check:personal-data` green.

- **T-440 — The app instance: create, scope, own, share, close.** *Plainly:* an app appears in a project's Tools section, someone owns it, the right people can open it, and the project owner can share one of its tables with another firm or hand the app to one of their own people. Routes and screens for: creating an app in a project (only by a person their organisation lets build — an org-admin toggle per user — **Claude's mechanism** for §12's ruled policy, which fixed who decides and not the control *(label added in review 2026-09-06)*); its participant scope on the ADR-0036 ladder, live-mutable; **the access predicate in the one gateway** — a row is readable when *entering organisation = reader's organisation, or reader's organisation is the project owner, or an open share exists for the reader's organisation*, all within scope, and **nothing else** — with a `draft` row read by its entering organisation alone (ADR-0056 addendum 2026-09-06, ruling 3); the owner's table share, audited and revocable; reassign-or-close when the owner or builder loses the right or leaves the project, with **no notification — the owner declined the proposed *app-needs-an-owner* event (2026-09-06)**: instead the ownerless app is **marked defunct in the project**, visibly not working on its card and its interfaces, until reassigned or closed (ADR-0056 §5's dated note; ADR-0049 untouched). **Done when:** a three-organisation e2e on the seeded firms proves Org B's rows are invisible to Org C, visible to the owner, and visible to C only while a share is open; revoking B's membership leaves B's accepted rows readable to the owner and its unaccepted rows dark; and an app whose owner is removed cannot run until reassigned. **Deps:** T-439.
  **As built. *Plainly: an app now appears in a project, someone owns it, the right people can open it, and a row is readable by exactly the people the rules say.*** The predicate is one pure function in [`packages/governance/src/app.ts`](../../packages/governance/src/app.ts) — *entering organisation, or the project owner, or an open share, all within the app's scope, and nothing else*, with a `draft` row read by its entering organisation alone — and it is **called** from the routes rather than restated in them. ADR-0056's research found that every app-builder incident it read came from access rules written into the app rather than enforced by the platform, so the file says in its own header that a second copy is the failure mode. Routes in [`apps/api/src/apps.ts`](../../apps/api/src/apps.ts); screens in [`apps/web/src/screens/apps.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/apps.tsx), which compute **no** permission of their own — `mayCreate`, `mayBuild` and `isProjectOwner` are the server's answers.

  **The org-admin toggle is Claude's mechanism, and it is labelled as such** (§12 fixed who decides, not the control): `users.may_build_apps`, at user grain because the decision is the organisation's about its own person, set through `PATCH /organisation/users/:userId/app-building` by that organisation's own admin and nobody else. `org_role = 'admin'` does **not** confer it — an implicit grant would be a policy nobody chose. The seed turns it on for the three Wrenfield super-users and deliberately leaves Owen Vance without it, so there is a seeded person inside a building firm who may enter rows and may not build.

  **DEFUNCT is derived and rendered, never stored and never notified.** An app whose owner's Participant interval has closed reads `state: 'defunct'`, names nobody as its owner, says on its own page what is wrong and what fixes it, and refuses to run with `409` and the sentence *"the app has no owner and is defunct until it is reassigned"*. ADR-0049 is untouched: nothing emits an event. Reassign-or-close is the project owner's act and the app's own firm's, both at the super-user tier.

  **What was verified, driven as the other party rather than inferred.** Fourteen API tests on a three-organisation fixture ([apps.test.ts](../../apps/api/src/apps.test.ts)) and one end-to-end spec on the seeded world ([app-substrate.spec.ts](../../e2e/tests/app-substrate.spec.ts)) covering: a colleague inside the building firm refused creation; an unpublished app invisible to the client and to the peer firm, and its working copy withheld from both after publication; publishing stamping who and when; a share refused to the builder and to the peer and taken from the project owner; a share to an organisation with no seat refused; scope revocation closing the door on the next read and a re-grant reopening it; **Marcus Webb enrolled, given the app, then removed — the real event, not a fixture — leaving the app defunct and unrunnable until it is handed back**; a reassignment to somebody who may not build refused; and a scheduled-shape run recording the **published** version with its two actor stamps agreeing. Twenty-one unit tests pin the predicate itself in `packages/governance`.

  **Deviations, stated loudly.** **(1) A builder cannot run an unpublished app either.** The ticket's assertion reads *"nothing can run an unpublished app except its builders"*; a run must record the **published** version (drawer 9's own correction), and an unpublished app has none — so the rule is enforced by REACH (only builders can see an unpublished app at all, and everyone else gets a 404 on the run route) and a builder is then told, in words, to open it first. **(2) Reassignment admits the app's own organisation as well as the project owner.** §7 puts reassign-or-close on the project owner; a consultancy whose builder leaves must be able to hand its own app to a colleague without asking the client, which is what §12's *"reassigned or dies"* is addressed to. Both are super-user acts. **(3) The row halves of this ticket's *done when* are proved by the same e2e spec, extended by T-441 in the very next commit** — Org B's rows invisible to Org C, visible to the owner, and visible to C only while a share is open — because the row routes are T-441's. **(4) One line of T-440's surface rode T-439's commit**: `OrgUser.mayBuildApps` had to be selected in the existing org-users route for the tree to typecheck at T-439.

  **Gates:** `pnpm run check` with its exit code read directly; the e2e suite on the seeded world.

- **T-441 — App tables on screen, and the acceptance flow.** *Plainly:* people type rows into an app's tables; every row remembers who typed it; where the builder chose an acceptance step, a row goes draft → submitted → accepted or rejected, and a correction is a new row. The generic table screens (list, enter, edit-before-acceptance with the prior version kept, retire) and the submission flow for tables with `has_acceptance`: submit, the owner's accept/reject with the decider stamped and **a required reason on a rejection, read by the submitting organisation on the row** *(reversed 2026-09-06, ADR-0056's addendum ruling 4)*, supersede-by-correction, the superseded row still visible as such. The owner sees every organisation's rows; a member sees its own. **Done when:** the e2e walks a contractor submitting, the client accepting, the contractor correcting, and asserts the accepted row cannot be edited or retired by the contractor and the superseded one still shows. **Deps:** T-440.
  **As built. *Plainly: people can now type rows into an app's tables, submit them, and have the client accept or reject them — and a half-finished return is nobody's business but the firm writing it.*** Routes in [`apps/api/src/app-rows.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-rows.ts), screens in [`apps/web/src/screens/app-rows.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/app-rows.tsx). **One component renders both seats** — the contractor's form and the client's list — with no `viewer` prop, no `isOwner` branch and no `role`: what makes one app behave as two is the read predicate, not a screen deciding what to draw (ADR-0056 §4). Every act a row offers (`mayEdit`, `maySubmit`, `mayDecide`, `mayCorrect`, `mayRetire`) is the **server's** answer, computed beside the predicate that decided the row was visible at all.

  **The draft cut is proved BOTH ways, driven as the other parties.** Calder & Hale reads its own draft; Trentmoor Energy — the project owner — reads nothing, and neither does Redgate Ecology; naming the row directly answers the same 404 the silence gives. From `submitted` onward the owner reads it, and Redgate reads it **only while Trentmoor's share of that table is open** and never sees a draft even then. **A rejection carries a required reason**, refused by the route and refused again by the database with the route out of the picture, and the reason reaches the submitting organisation on the row with the decider's name beside it. **An accepted row is the owner's record**: the submitting organisation's edit and retire both answer 404, and a direct `UPDATE` at the store is refused by the trigger.

  **An edit before a decision keeps the prior version** as a row of its own, which is left out of the list rather than shown as a second entry — a prior version is history of the row above it. **A correction is a new row**: an accepted row flips to `superseded` and still shows; a **rejected** one keeps its state and its reason and reads as superseded through the correcting row's pointer.

  **Verified:** 14 API tests ([app-rows.test.ts](../../apps/api/src/app-rows.test.ts)) on a three-organisation fixture, plus a second end-to-end test in [app-substrate.spec.ts](../../e2e/tests/app-substrate.spec.ts) on the seeded world — which also closes the row half of T-440's *done when*.

  **Deviations, stated loudly.** **(1) A rejected row is not flipped to `superseded`.** Drawer 9 says a correction flips the row it corrects; the `rejection_reason` CHECK the same drawing requires (non-null **iff** rejected) means flipping a rejected row would force its reason to be erased — ruling 4 undone. So the flip applies to an **accepted** row only, and supersession of a rejected one is read off the correcting row's `supersedes_row_id` — which is exactly how the approved mockup draws it (*"Rejected · superseded"*). **(2) A `submitted` row may still be edited by the organisation that entered it.** The drawing's words are *"an edit before acceptance"*, and `submitted` is before acceptance; the prior version is kept either way. If the owner would rather a submitted return froze until it is decided, that is a one-line narrowing. *(Ruled the other way 2026-09-07 — ADR-0056's second addendum, ruling 1: a submitted row freezes, no edit and no retire, until accepted or rejected; narrowed in that day's ruling commit with a test.)* **(3) The screens follow the approved mockup's behaviour, not its layout.** `returns-app-two-seats.html` draws a form beside a list, tiles of project totals, an insight panel and an inline accept-or-reject strip; what is built is the same acts and the same states in the plain kit — the totals and the insight are T-443's, and the drawing's own note says the screens themselves are what the builder's agent writes at T-442. The mockup stays in `docs/design/mockups/` until T-447.

- **T-442 — The stepped builder with its agent, writing browser-only screens.** *Plainly:* the screen where a person defines an app step by step, with an agent that asks the right questions and writes the app's screens. The steps in the approved drawing (T-438), in the order the owner confirmed 2026-09-06 — what the app is and who it is open to, the tables, data connections, the interface, how often it runs, analysis and prompts, **check and open** (the publish act: working copy → published copy, stamped, ADR-0056 addendum ruling 2) — with the agent in its own pane beside them (ruling 5): tables — with the agent asking **whether each holds contractual data and so needs an acceptance step** (ADR-0056 §2a–§2b); interfaces and who may open each (narrow-only); schedule (stored, not yet honoured); analysis and prompts; connection *requirements* (declared, unfillable until deployment). The agent generates interface code that **runs in the viewer's browser and calls the typed API as the viewer**, holds no secret and makes no outward call — and, on the T-430 posture, **the generator has no code path that emits one, pinned by a test** rather than filtered afterwards. Generated screens are stored on `apps.definition` (the working copy) with a version, and reach the app's people only when published. **Done when:** the owner can define the returns app's tables, interfaces and schedule through the steps; the agent's questions about contractual data and about who opens each interface appear in the flow; and a test proves generated code cannot reference a credential or reach a URL outside the API. **Deps:** T-441. ✅ **Built 2026-09-07.**
  **As built. *Plainly: a person can now build an app step by step — saying what it is, what tables it holds, what screens it offers and who may open each — with an agent beside the steps that asks the two questions nobody should be able to skip and draws the screens. What the agent draws is not program code: it is a short list of parts from a fixed menu, so there is nowhere in a screen to put a web address or a password.***

  **The seven steps** are [`apps/web/src/screens/app-builder.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/app-builder.tsx), in the order the owner confirmed on 2026-09-06: what the app is and who it is open to → the tables → data connections → the interface → how often it runs → analysis and prompts → **check and open**, which is the publish act itself and not a summary before one. Steps 1–2 write to the stores that already exist (the app row, scope grants, `app_tables`); steps 3–6 write the definition JSON through T-440's `PATCH /apps/:appId/definition`; step 7 is T-440's publish. The agent sits in its own pane beside them (the addendum's ruling 5), the conversation is continuous across the steps, and **every choice lands in the form** — closing the pane loses nothing, which is the sentence that ruling turns on.

  **The two required questions are computed in code, not remembered by a model** (ADR-0056 §2b, and ruling 6's reasoning carried one step further). `pendingBuilderQuestions` in [`packages/contracts/src/app-builder.ts`](../../packages/contracts/src/app-builder.ts) derives them from the state of the definition — *does this table hold contractual data?* and *who may open this screen?* — and they are marked on the step rail and listed in the pane. The addendum declined a chat that fills the steps in because *"a chat can skip a question, a form cannot"*; a pane beside the steps is still a chat, so what asks is the form. A new field, `answeredQuestions`, records which have been answered: `hasAcceptance: false` and `openToOrganisationIds: []` are each both a real answer and what an untouched field looks like, so without it the agent would either nag forever or count a default as a decision.

  **🔒 The generated-screen mechanism — Claude's, for the ADR's ruled posture, and flagged for the owner's veto.** ADR-0056 §11 fixes the *posture* (a generated screen runs in the viewer's browser, calls the typed API as the viewer, holds no secret, reaches no outside system) and T-442 adds T-430's: *the generator has no code path that emits one, pinned by a test, rather than filtered afterwards.* The record does not say what a screen **is**. Two mechanisms could carry that posture — freeform JavaScript inspected after generation, or a closed grammar the platform interprets — and **the grammar is chosen**, because with it the guarantee is true by construction rather than as good as the inspector. A screen is `{version: 1, blocks: […]}` over six block shapes (`heading`, `paragraph`, `rowForm`, `rowTable`, `total`, `count`), **none of which has a field that could hold a URL, an endpoint, a key or a token**, and none of which can name a row, an organisation or a person — a block names COLUMNS of one declared table, and which rows appear is `canReadAppRow`'s answer over the ordinary row route. `parseAppScreen` **refuses rather than sanitises**: an invented block, an extra field on a known one, or a column the table never declared fails the whole screen, because keeping the good parts and dropping the bad one is exactly the filtering the posture rules out. What the model is asked for is a choice from that menu; what it says is never program code and is never run.

  **The pinning test the done-when names, in three places.** (1) [`packages/contracts/src/app-screen.test.ts`](../../packages/contracts/src/app-screen.test.ts), 12 tests — the grammar's field names are walked **from the schema itself** and checked against a list of every word a screen would need to reach outward or carry a secret, so a seventh block introducing one fails rather than slipping in; the closed block list is pinned literally. (2) **Rule 4 of [`scripts/source-rules.mjs`](../../scripts/source-rules.mjs)**, which runs inside `pnpm run check` on the same footing as the grounding-index fence: the one module that renders a generated screen ([`apps/web/src/screens/app-screen.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/app-screen.tsx)) may contain no `fetch`, no socket, no `href=`/`src=`, nothing that evaluates text as code — 5 fixture tests prove the guard fails on each. (3) [`apps/api/src/app-builder.test.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-builder.test.ts), 16 tests, where a **hostile router** answers with a screen carrying a fetch block, an endpoint, an API key and a script: nothing lands, through the parser and through the route, and a hostile screen `PATCH`ed straight at the definition is refused 400 at the boundary. A web test also proves the last mile — a heading whose text *is* `https://exfiltrate.example?key=…` renders as characters, in no attribute and no link.

  **A viewer opening a published screen receives only what the read predicate allows, proved as the other party.** The screens a person is *offered* are assembled server-side (`openableInterfaces` in [`apps/api/src/apps.ts`](../../apps/api/src/apps.ts)) — an interface narrowed to the client's firm is **absent** from what a peer firm receives, never present-and-disabled (T-269's rule). And being offered a screen widens nothing: in the e2e, the client's dashboard block asks for every column and every organisation, and Redgate Ecology still reads only its own row while Trentmoor Energy reads both firms'. **No permission is computed in any screen**, generated or otherwise — the review note left for this ticket was to watch that when generated screens arrived, and the answer is that a generated screen computes nothing at all: it draws the rows it was handed and sums them.

  **The rest of the steps, honestly labelled.** The schedule is stored and the surface says *"Saved, but not running yet"* with the reason (ADR-0056 §13d). A connection requirement is described and carries a `Cannot be connected yet` badge, with the screen saying plainly that there is nowhere to type a password on purpose. The analysis prompt is stored and marked *"Saved, and not yet used"* — T-443 gives it work.

  **Verified:** 16 API tests ([app-builder.test.ts](../../apps/api/src/app-builder.test.ts)), 12 contract tests ([app-screen.test.ts](../../packages/contracts/src/app-screen.test.ts)), 5 guard tests ([source-rules.test.mjs](../../scripts/source-rules.test.mjs)), 6 surface tests in [render.test.tsx](../../apps/web/src/render.test.tsx), and an end-to-end walk of all seven steps on the seeded world across three organisations ([app-builder.spec.ts](../../e2e/tests/app-builder.spec.ts)), with Owen Vance — the seeded Calder & Hale participant whose firm has not given him the right to build — refused the builder as a real negative.

  **Deviations, stated loudly.**

  **(1) The generated-screen mechanism is Claude's choice and wants the owner's veto.** ADR-0056 §11 ruled the posture, not the representation. Choosing a closed grammar buys the guarantee by construction and costs expressiveness: an app's screen can be a heading, a paragraph, a form, a table, a total and a count, and nothing else — no chart, no map, no file upload. The lands app ADR-0056 imagines (*"a land register on a map"*) cannot be drawn in this vocabulary today. The alternative — freeform code, inspected — buys expressiveness and pays for it with a guarantee only as strong as the inspector, which is the lane the record declines for servers and leaves open for browsers. **If the owner would rather have the wider vocabulary, this is the decision to reopen**, and the closed list is pinned by a test precisely so that widening it is a deliberate act.

  **(2) `apps.definition` is now validated at the boundary, which it was not.** `patchAppDefinitionBody` took `z.unknown()`, so the header of `packages/contracts/src/app-builder.ts` — *"a definition that does not conform is refused at the boundary rather than at the first read"* — was aspiration. It is now `appDefinitionSchema`, a strict shape. Anything already stored that does not conform would be refused on its next edit; nothing in the seed or the tests was in that position, and the definition has only existed since T-440.

  **(3) A new route, `PATCH /app-tables/:appTableId`, changes one field and only while the table is empty.** The agent's first required question has to be answerable *when it is asked*, including about a table declared before anybody asked — and `hasAcceptance` had no way to change. It is gated by `canBuildApp` and refused 409 the moment a row exists, because whether a table holds contractual data is what decides whether its rows change hands (§2a): flipping it under existing rows would retrospectively make a contractor's figure into the client's record, or take one back.

  **(4) The builder's conversation is not stored.** It lives in the component and nowhere else, so no new record about a named person was created and [personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md) needed no new row. The addendum's ruling 5 is what makes that safe rather than lossy: every choice is recorded in the form, so a refreshed page starts a fresh conversation over a definition that already carries every answer. If the owner wants the conversation kept, that is a store, a register row and a deletion path — a ticket, not a tweak.

  **(5) The screens follow the approved mockup's behaviour, not its layout** — T-441's precedent, applied again. `app-builder-stepped-flow.html` draws a three-column frame with a step rail, a step body and the agent's pane; what is built is the same seven steps in the same order, the same two moments the agent asks, the pane in the same place, and the seventh step as the publish act, in the plain kit. The drawing's live screen previews are rendered by the real renderer over the builder's own readable rows rather than as sketches. The mockup stays in `docs/design/mockups/` until T-447 captures it.

  **(6) Nothing from the deferred register was built.** Connections remain declared text with no field that could hold a credential; the schedule is stored and unhonoured; the analysis prompt is stored and unused. No migration was needed and none was written.

  **Gates:** `pnpm run check` with its exit code read directly; a wiped volume, migrate and seed; `eval:smoke`; the e2e suite twice on one clean seed.

- **T-443 — Runs and insights.** *Plainly:* an app can be run by hand and produce a written insight over its rows, kept as a record with what it covered and when; the monthly schedule is saved so it starts working the day there is a server that stays on. An app run is an ADR-0028 Run (`app_runs` links to it); trigger `manual` now, `scheduled` when a clock exists; the run acts as the clicker — or, for a schedule, the owner — **narrowed to the app's declared tables**; the insight lands as a row in the app's insight table stamped with that person's organisation, with `definitions_version` and `rows_covered`; the number computed in code, the model writing only the sentence (the landscape's one trusted pattern). The schedule is stored from this ticket and marked unhonoured in the UI. *(Widened 2026-09-07, two items from the T-442/T-444 review and its rulings: **(a)** the stepped builder's table step gains the `insight` table kind — T-442 built `data` only, and this ticket's insight has to land somewhere a builder can declare; **(b)** the screen grammar gains **chart blocks** — a bar chart, a line chart with a trend line, a pie chart, drawn by Infora over the rows the viewer may read exactly as the table block is — so the owner's T-446 walk can judge whether blocks draw the screens they want before ruling on agent-written code (ADR-0056's second addendum, ruling 5).)* **Done when:** a run produces an insight row readable by the running organisation and the owner and not by a peer; a run by a person who cannot see a shared table's rows covers only their own; a run on a closed app is refused; and a published screen can show a chart block over the viewer's own readable rows. **Deps:** T-442. ✅ **Built 2026-09-07.**

  **As built. *Plainly: pressing Run now does something. Infora reads the rows the person running is allowed to read, works out the numbers itself, asks the model for one sentence about those numbers, and keeps that sentence as a row in the app's own insight table — stamped with that person's firm, with how many rows it covered and which opened version it ran against. Screens can now also draw a bar chart, a line chart with a trend line and a pie chart over the rows the person looking at them can read. The monthly schedule is still only saved, and still says so.***

  **What is where.** The run itself is a new file, [`apps/api/src/app-runs.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-runs.ts) — the two run routes moved out of `apps.ts` unchanged, because a run reads rows and rows are reached through `app-rows.ts`, which already imports from `apps.ts`; leaving them together would have made two files import each other, and `app-exports.ts` (T-444) sits in exactly that position for exactly that reason.
