The arithmetic and the one model call are [`apps/api/src/app-insight.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-insight.ts). The three chart blocks are in the grammar, [`packages/contracts/src/app-builder.ts`](../../packages/contracts/src/app-builder.ts), and drawn in the one fenced renderer, [`apps/web/src/screens/app-screen.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/app-screen.tsx). The table step's new **insight** kind is in [`apps/web/src/screens/app-builder.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/app-builder.tsx).

  **🔒 The run reads through the rows screen's own resolution and nowhere else.** It calls `reachTable` and `listRows` in [`app-rows.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-rows.ts), which call `canReadAppRow` in `@infora/governance` — the same two functions the rows screen and the export use, and no query of its own. That is why the ticket's hardest negative is a consequence rather than a promise: *a run by a person who cannot see a shared table's rows covers only their own*, because those are the only rows the run was ever handed. The e2e drives it three ways on one app — Calder & Hale's run covers one return, Trentmoor's covers two, and Redgate's covers one, then two the moment the client shares the table, then one again when the share is revoked.

  **🔒 The numbers are computed in code and the model writes only the sentence** (ADR-0056 §3, and the landscape's one trusted pattern). `figuresFor` totals, averages and takes the extremes of every **number** column, counts rows per organisation, and counts states where the table has an acceptance step. What the model receives is that arithmetic as text plus the builder's own analysis prompt — **no row, and no value of any non-number column**, so a land register's landowner names cannot leave through an insight. A unit test asserts exactly that with a name planted in a free-text column. An empty answer from the model writes **no insight at all**: a row with a date and a rows-covered count and nothing in it would read as a finding that there was nothing to find.

  **🔒 The insight's words are on the ROW and never on the run record.** The run list is read by everyone who may open the app; an insight is stamped with the organisation of the person the run acted as and is read by that organisation and the project owner alone. So `AppRunRecord` carries `insightRowId` (an identifier — reading the row behind it goes through `canReadAppRow` like any row) and an `outcome` that is one of two fixed phrases Infora writes. The e2e reads the whole run list as the peer firm and asserts the other firm's figure does not appear in it.

  **An insight table's columns are Infora's, not the builder's** — Claude's mechanism for ADR-0056 §3, which fixes that the insight *is a row in a declared insights table* and does not say who names the columns. A run has to know where the sentence goes; a builder who called the text column `notes` would have got a table that silently took nothing. So `POST /apps/:appId/tables` replaces the columns of any `insight` table with `INSIGHT_TABLE_COLUMNS` (`as_at`, `insight`, `rows_covered`, `definitions_version`) and forces its acceptance step off — an insight is written by a run and submitted to nobody, and the route that sets an acceptance step answers 404 for such a table. The stepped builder shows those four columns rather than asking for them.

  **The charts, and why they are blocks.** `barChart`, `lineChart` (with `showTrend`) and `pieChart` join the closed grammar, taking the pinned block list from six kinds to nine — **edited in the same commit as the test that pins it**, which is the act that line exists to force. They carry `categoryColumn` and `valueColumn` and nothing else: no colour, no size, no picture, no link. The declared-column walk in `parseAppScreen` was rewritten as one exhaustive `columnsNamedBy` switch, because it used to work by looking for a field *named* `columnKey`/`columnKeys` and a block shaped differently would have slipped past it. The forbidden-word test gained `image`, `embed`, `iframe` and `link`, since a chart is exactly where somebody would later reach for a picture. **They are drawn as SVG shapes computed from the rows the viewer already received** — no image tag, no external chart library, nothing added to `package.json`; `scripts/source-rules.mjs` rule 4 still passes over the renderer. The trend line is a least-squares fit through the points, drawn dashed, with a sentence on the screen saying it is Infora's line through those rows and **not a forecast**.

  **The schedule is untouched and still labelled.** Step 5's *"Saved, but not running yet"* badge and its paragraph are exactly as T-442 built them, and the e2e asserts a stored `monthly` survives publication. What changed at step 6 is honest rather than cosmetic: the analysis prompt now says whether it has anywhere to land, and warns in words when the app has declared no insight table.

  **Proof.** `packages/contracts/src/app-screen.test.ts` — three new cases on the charts (the three parse and round-trip; a chart naming an undeclared column fails the *whole* screen; an extra field and a non-boolean `showTrend` are refused), plus the pinned nine-kind list and the widened forbidden-word list. `apps/api/src/app-insight.test.ts` — seven cases on the arithmetic and the model call, including the planted-name one. `apps/api/src/apps.test.ts` — five new cases driven as four parties: the fixed insight columns and the 404 on setting acceptance; an insight readable by the running firm and the project owner and not by the peer; the covering-only-your-own-rows narrowing and what a share changes; a run on an app with no insight table recording that it had nowhere to write; and a closed app refusing to run with nothing written. `apps/web/src/render.test.tsx` — six new cases reading the drawn markup (bars with each viewer's own figures on them, the trend line and its sentence, the pie legend, the nothing-to-draw state, the grouping, the fit). `e2e/tests/app-insight.spec.ts` — two tests: the whole run story across the three seeded organisations, and a browser test that opens a published dashboard as Calder & Hale and reads the chart, with Redgate's 30 tonnes absent from it.

  **Deviations, stated loudly.** **(1) The two run routes moved out of `apps.ts` into `app-runs.ts`.** The ticket did not ask for a move; the alternative was `apps.ts` and `app-rows.ts` importing each other, which works in ESM and is a trap for the next person. The routes, their paths and their behaviour are otherwise as they were. **(2) `tables_covered` now records the tables the run actually read, not every declared table.** T-440 wrote every non-retired table id into it; a run does not read its own insight table, and a run by somebody who cannot reach a table does not cover it, so the field now says what happened rather than what exists. Nothing depended on the old value. **(3) The quick "declare a table" form on the app page still declares `data` tables only.** The ticket names the *stepped builder's* table step, which is where the insight kind is offered with its fixed columns shown; the quick form carries a comment pointing at step 2 rather than a second, thinner version of the same choice. **(4) The `reference` table kind is still not offered anywhere.** It belongs to playbooks (T-445) and nothing needs it yet; it is named in the builder's listing so an existing one would read correctly. **(5) No insight is shown on the app page's own screen except through its table.** An insight is a row, and the rows screen already draws rows; a second place rendering the same row would be a second thing to keep in step. A builder who wants it on a dashboard puts a `rowTable` block over the insight table. **(6) A defect outside this ticket was found and fixed: the whole app-builder surface could not be opened in a browser.** `apps/web/vite.config.ts` proxies a fixed list of API namespaces to the API, and `/apps`, `/app-tables` and `/app-rows` were never added when T-440 → T-444 built them. The failure was the silent one that file's own `/lenses` note warns about — the browser's fetch got `index.html` back, the JSON parse failed, and the app page sat on *"Loading…"* forever with nothing in any log. No unit or API test could have seen it, because every app test so far drove the API directly; this ticket's browser test for the chart opened an app page for the first time and found it. The three prefixes are added in this commit. **(7) T-444's Word-export test was edited**, because it declared an insight table with a column of its own and entered a row into it: with an insight table's columns now fixed, it enters the row under the platform's own keys and asserts the replacement happened.

  **Not done, and not attempted.** No scheduler and no clock — `scheduled` remains a stored intention (ADR-0056 §13d), and the only trigger a caller may ask for is still `manual`. No connections (ADR-0057, deferred to deployment). No migration: `app_runs` already carried `rows_covered`, `insight_row_id`, `finished_at` and `outcome` from T-439, and an insight table is an `app_tables` row of an existing kind. Nothing was added to the personal-data register: the insight row is an `app_rows` row with an `entered_by_participant_id` and an `organisation_id`, which the register's existing app-rows entry covers, and the run's actor is covered by its `app_runs` entry — no new fact about a named person is stored.

  **Gates, with exit codes read directly.** `pnpm run check` → 0. `docker compose down -v` and back up, `migrate` and `seed` → clean. `eval:smoke` → 7 cases, 0 fail. The e2e suite twice on that one seed → 70 passed both times (68 before this ticket, plus its two). **One honesty note on the gates:** the first `check` run of the session failed on three cases — one real (T-444's export test, fixed above) and two in `sessions.test.ts` about clock timing and the session sweep, which passed on the very next run, pass in isolation, and pass on the unmodified base. They look like load-related flakes rather than anything this ticket did, and they are recorded here rather than left for somebody to rediscover.

- **T-444 — Export to a file with the provenance stamp.** *Plainly:* a person downloads the app's data as a spreadsheet, containing only what they may see, with a note of what data it came from and when — and nothing saying an agent made it. Excel (and Word for an insight) via the existing `file_ref` path; `app_exports` row with `data_as_of`, `tables_covered`, `rows_covered`; **no producer column and no agent-drafted marking** (ADR-0056 §8). The file is the person's to edit, transpose and put through the normal review cycles; this ticket ends at the download. **Done when:** an export by a contractor contains only its organisation's rows, an export by the owner contains all, and the file's stamp shows data-and-time only. **Deps:** T-441. ✅ **Built 2026-09-07.**
  **As built. *Plainly: a person can now download an app's data as a spreadsheet, or one insight as a Word file. It contains only the rows that person can see on screen — a contractor gets its own, the client gets everybody's. The file carries a short note saying what it came from and when, and nothing else: nothing on it says an agent made it, because it is the person's file to edit and send on.***

  Routes in [`apps/api/src/app-exports.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-exports.ts), the button and the export history on [`apps/web/src/screens/apps.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/apps.tsx), and a per-row *Download as Word* on an insight table in [`apps/web/src/screens/app-rows.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/app-rows.tsx).

  **🔒 The export reads through the rows screen's own resolution and nowhere else.** `reachTable` and `listRows` in [`app-rows.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-rows.ts) were exported for this and are called unchanged; they call `canReadAppRow` in `@infora/governance`. There is no query in the export file, no filter, and no second statement of who may see a row — which is what makes *"an export by a contractor contains only its organisation's rows"* a consequence rather than a promise. A draft is absent from the project owner's spreadsheet exactly as it is absent from the owner's dashboard.

  **🔒 The stamp is provenance, not authorship** (ADR-0056 §8, and the ADR-0021 addendum's companion rule). The spreadsheet's `Provenance` sheet is three lines and stops: *Produced from* (the app), *Tables*, *Data as of* (an ISO timestamp). The Word file's last two lines say the same. **Who exported is on the `app_exports` ROW and not in the FILE** — the record is an audit answer, and a person who edits a spreadsheet and sends it to their client should not be handing over a claim about authorship they did not make. A test asserts the absence directly: the exporter's name, *produced by*, *prepared by*, *author*, *agent*, *drafted*, *generated by* appear nowhere in the bytes.

  **No new dependency.** The spreadsheet is built with `buildXlsx` (T-358's minimal writer) and the Word file with `textToDocx` (the renditions path), both already in the tree; the blob lands through `putBlob`, which is ADR-0056 §13b's *"wherever `file_ref` points on the day"* and becomes S3 once deployed (ADR-0047 §3). The workbook is read back in the tests with `parseXlsxSheets`, the reader that already existed.

  **The record.** One `app_exports` row per export, append-only as drawn: `data_as_of`, `tables_covered`, `rows_covered`, and who took it. `GET /apps/:appId/exports` renders it, narrowed on the row predicate's own shape — **your own organisation's exports, and the project owner sees them all** — because a rival firm learning that another firm exported twelve rows last Tuesday learns something about the project it was never given, which is the same reasoning that keeps a table's shares from a third organisation.

  **Verified:** 13 API tests ([app-exports.test.ts](../../apps/api/src/app-exports.test.ts)) on a three-organisation fixture, reading the produced workbook back sheet by sheet; and an end-to-end export taken by both parties over one app on the seeded world ([app-builder.spec.ts](../../e2e/tests/app-builder.spec.ts)) — Calder & Hale's file holds 41.5 and not Redgate's 7.25, Trentmoor Energy's holds both, and the client's file names neither Rachel Bowen nor Eleanor Price.

  **Deviations, stated loudly.**

  **(1) No person's name is written into the file — only the organisation's.** A row's `entered_by_participant_id` is registered personal data whose deletion path runs through the entering organisation ([personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md), drawer 9's row); a copy inside a downloaded spreadsheet would sit outside that path, and nobody has ruled on that. The organisation stamp stays, because it is what the wall keys on and what makes the project owner's export readable at all. If the owner wants *entered by* in the file, it is a line of code and a register question.

  **(2) The export is one act, not a link.** `POST /apps/:appId/exports` builds the file, stores the blob, writes the record and returns the bytes in the same response; there is no `GET /app-exports/:id/file`. An export is a snapshot of ONE person's read at ONE moment, and a link to somebody else's snapshot would be a second door into rows the predicate had already decided about. The browser fetches rather than navigates (T-358's reason, already in `api.ts`).

  **(3) The Word export is offered on an insight table only.** ADR-0056 §8 says *"Excel, Word"* without saying which for what; a Word file of one monthly return would be a worse spreadsheet, where a Word file of an insight is the thing a person actually sends on. Insight rows are written by hand until T-443 gives runs something to write; the route is indifferent to how the row got there.

  **(4) An app with no readable table still exports a file.** It is a stamp with nothing under it, which is honest — an error would leave the person guessing whether they were refused or there is nothing there. An app they cannot open answers 404 as everything else does.

  **Gates:** `pnpm run check` with its exit code read directly; a wiped volume, migrate and seed; `eval:smoke`; the e2e suite twice on one clean seed. **No migration** — `app_exports` has existed since T-439.

- **T-445 — Playbooks: save to the workspace, deploy as a copy.** *Plainly:* a firm keeps an app as a template in its own workspace with all the client's rows stripped out, and can deploy that template into the next project. Save-as-playbook from an instance: the definition and table declarations travel and **no rows of any origin do** — the owner struck the reference-row softening on 2026-09-06 ("by reference tables i meant the database structure for an app - not the content from within it"), and T-439's `playbooks_carry_no_rows` trigger enforces it; the saver stamped. The workspace's playbook shelf (org-private; Infora-supplied ones on the same shelf, `supplied_by_infora`). Deploy: a copy into a project as a new instance naming `playbook_id` + `playbook_version`; **no live link** — changing the playbook changes no instance. **Done when:** saving the returns app from Client A's project produces a playbook with zero rows of any kind; deploying it into Client B's project produces an empty instance with the same steps; and editing the playbook leaves A's instance untouched. **Deps:** T-442. ✅ **Built 2026-09-07.**
  **As built. *Plainly: a firm can now keep an app it has built as a template on its own shelf, and put a copy of that template into the next project. The template holds the shape of the work — the tables and their columns, whether each needs signing off, the screens, how often it runs, what the analysis asks — and not one row of anybody's data, including the lookup rows the firm typed in itself. Deploying makes a brand-new app with the same steps and empty tables. After that the two never speak: the firm can change its template a dozen times and nothing it has already put into a client's project moves.***

  Routes in [`apps/api/src/playbooks.ts`](../../apps/api/src/playbooks.ts) (a new file — `GET /organisation/playbooks`, `POST /apps/:appId/playbook`, `POST /projects/:projectId/apps/deployments`), the two predicates in [`packages/governance/src/playbook.ts`](../../packages/governance/src/playbook.ts) (also new), the types in [`packages/contracts/src/app-builder.ts`](../../packages/contracts/src/app-builder.ts), and the three surfaces in [`apps/web/src/screens/playbooks.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/playbooks.tsx) — the shelf in the workspace beside the firm's manuals and saved outlines, the *Keep this as a template* card on an app, and a *from a template* picker in a project's Apps section. **No migration**: T-439 built the `playbooks` table and its trigger, and neither was touched.

  **🔒 No rows travel, and it is true three times over.** Nothing in the route file reads `app_rows` on either path — there is no query for it. `PlaybookTableDeclaration` is `{name, columns, kind, hasAcceptance}` and has nowhere a row could sit. And T-439's `playbooks_carry_no_rows` trigger refuses a `rows` key anywhere in either JSON column, which is the guard that survives the file being rewritten by somebody who has not read it. The owner's clarification is honoured exactly: a **reference** table's definition travels, its rows do not, and a deployed instance starts every table empty.

  **🔒 No live link, and it is structural rather than policed.** Saving again writes a NEW `playbooks` row with the next version number, and a playbook row is never updated after it is written. So a deployed instance's `playbook_id` points at a row that *cannot* change — there is no shared record for either side to edit, and "editing the playbook leaves the first instance untouched" is a consequence rather than a rule anybody has to keep. The instance names the version on its own page (`AppRecord.deployedFrom`), so the client reads a number that cannot move under them.

  **🔒 A deployed instance is an ordinary app.** T-440's creation body was lifted unchanged into [`apps/api/src/app-instance.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-instance.ts) and both paths call it, so a deployed app gets the same owner, creator and definition stamps, the same starting scope and the same rules as one built from nothing. There is no second statement of how an app comes into existence.

  **Who may do what, and where each line came from.** **Saving** is `canBuildApp` and nothing wider — the record's own answer for who edits and publishes an app (§12's per-person toggle, and the app's own firm). So the client whose project the app lives in cannot take a copy of its consultant's template, and neither can a peer consultancy inside the app's scope; both are driven as those parties in the tests. **Deploying** needs the same toggle plus a live seat on the target project — the toggle because deploying must not be an easier way to get an app than making one, and the seat because it is the ordinary entitlement question, answered by `resolveSlice` rather than restated. **Reading the shelf** is the toggle alone, and *that line is Claude's, not the record's* — see the deviations.

  **What is deliberately left behind when a template travels.** A screen keeps the **name** of the table it was over rather than its id (an id belongs to the instance it was declared in), and loses `openToOrganisationIds` entirely — an organisation id from Client A's project means nothing in Client B's, so who may open each screen is asked again by the deploying firm in front of somebody who knows who is on that project. `answeredQuestions` does not travel either; the acceptance answers are re-recorded against the tables the deployment makes, and the who-may-open questions come back unanswered on purpose (§2b). Everything else does travel: schedule, analysis prompt, connection *requirements* (text, never a credential — ADR-0057 is not built) and the screens themselves.

  **Verified:** 12 API tests ([playbooks.test.ts](../../apps/api/src/playbooks.test.ts)) on a fixture of one consultancy acting for two clients, every negative driven as the other party over HTTP; 4 predicate tests ([playbook.test.ts](../../packages/governance/src/playbook.test.ts)); and one end-to-end test ([playbooks.spec.ts](../../e2e/tests/playbooks.spec.ts)) that walks the ticket's own "done when" on the seeded world — Eleanor Price builds the returns app in Trentmoor's Wrenfield scheme, keeps it, deploys it into Marchwood's Quarry Rail Link, and then changes the template and finds Marchwood's app unmoved. The strongest assertion is the cheapest: after a save the stored row is read back **raw** and searched for every value anybody typed, in both tables, and for the string `"rows"`.

  **Deviations, stated loudly.**

  **(1) Who may READ the shelf is a line Claude drew.** ADR-0056 fixes who may build (§12) and says a playbook is org-private, but says nothing about who inside a firm may look at its shelf. The build gates the shelf on `may_build_apps` — the population that can actually do anything with a template — which means **an org admin who is not allowed to build apps sees no shelf at all**. The alternative (every person in the firm reads it, only builders act) is one line away. The owner should say which they want.

  **(2) A closed app cannot be kept as a template.** Saving is `canBuildApp`, and that predicate refuses a closed app. §10's reverse path does not mention closure either way. So a firm that closes an app at the end of a job can no longer keep it — the template has to be taken before the app is closed. If that is wrong it is a one-line widening, but it is a real behaviour and not an oversight.

  **(3) The PUBLISHED definition is what travels, falling back to the working copy when nothing has been published.** §10 calls a playbook *"the finished definition of its steps"*, and half-edited work in progress is not what a colleague deploying it next month is asking for. That is a reading of the words, not a quotation of them.

  **(4) The shelf withholds the source project's NAME from a colleague who is not on that project.** Who saved it and which app it came from are always shown; the client's name is shown only to somebody entitled to that project. The record does not ask for this — it is Claude's, on ADR-0046's internal walls: a firm may hold a wall over a pair of clients, and a shelf that named every template's client to every builder would leak through it.

  **(5) The deployed instance's scope is the deploying firm's own organisation, and nothing else.** "Empty scope" is read as *nothing inherits the source project's scope*, not as *no grant at all* — an app nobody can open, including the person who just deployed it, is T-440's stated bug rather than a strict default. Widening is then a deliberate act on the app's own page. The e2e proves the target project's own client cannot see the app until the deployer opens it to them.

  **(6) Two live tables sharing a name refuse the save.** A screen travels by its table's name, so two same-named tables would be a template whose screens could re-attach to the wrong one. `app_tables` does not forbid a duplicate name (a name is a label, not a key), so the save refuses with a worded 409 rather than the deployment guessing.

  **(7) Infora-supplied templates are carried but not exercised end to end.** The shelf query and both predicates handle `supplied_by_infora`, and the predicate tests cover it; nothing seeds one, so no test deploys a supplied template through HTTP. Infora's own pre-built apps are §11's *afterwards*, and this ticket did not mint one.

  **(8) A playbook cannot be retired or deleted.** The column exists and `canDeployPlaybook` honours it, but no route sets it, so a shelf only grows. The ticket did not ask for it; if the owner wants a template taken off the shelf, that is a ticket.

  **Gates:** `pnpm run check` with its exit code read directly (never through a pipe); the container wiped and recreated, then migrate and seed clean; `eval:smoke` — 7 cases, 0 fail; and the e2e suite twice on that one seed, 69 tests green both times. Run on an isolated Postgres on port 5433, in a worktree, because T-443 was building in parallel on the shared database.

- **T-448 — The publish gate: no app opens with a required question unanswered.** *Plainly:* the platform itself refuses to publish an app until the builder has answered, for every table, "does this hold contractual data?" and, for every screen, "who may open it?" — however the app was built, by hand, by the agent, or straight at the API. ADR-0056's third addendum (2026-10-18), ruling 1 — the re-housing of the first addendum's ruling 6, whose reason was that a chat can skip a question: now nothing can, because `POST /apps/:appId/publish` computes the required questions server-side (the same facts `pendingBuilderQuestions` reads, moved where no surface can route around them) and refuses with a worded answer naming each question still open. **Done when:** a publish with an unanswered table or interface question is refused 409 naming it, driven as the builder over HTTP and again with a hand-built definition PATCHed directly; answering through the ordinary acts clears it; and an app with no tables and no screens still publishes (nothing was asked). **Deps:** none — it lands first and alone, so the gate exists before the agent that must be unable to skip it. ✅ **Built 2026-10-18.**
  **As built. *Plainly: Infora itself now refuses to open an app to its people while either required question is unanswered — "does this table hold contractual data?" for every table, "who may open this screen?" for every screen — and it says which questions, by name, in a sentence. It does not matter how the app was built: through the building screen, by the agent, or by somebody writing the whole definition straight at the API. The builder sees the same sentence before pressing the button.***

  **Where the gate is.** [`apps/api/src/apps.ts`](../../apps/api/src/apps.ts) — `publishGateFor` reads the STORED working copy (`apps.definition`, whose `answeredQuestions` records each answer) and the LIVE declared tables in `app_tables`, and hands them to the same `pendingBuilderQuestions` the building screen has used since T-442 ([`packages/contracts/src/app-builder.ts`](../../packages/contracts/src/app-builder.ts)). `POST /apps/:appId/publish` calls it on every attempt and answers **409** with `PublishRefusedResponse` — `detail` is the sentence, `questions` the same list as data — while any question stands. The sentence comes from one function, `publishGateOf`, which the record for a builder also carries as `GetAppResponse.publishGate`, so the words before the click and the words of the refusal are one computation and cannot drift apart. An insight table is never asked (a run writes it, nobody submits it); a retired table is not asked; **a reference table IS asked**, because the brief's rule is "every live non-insight table".

  **What counts as answering, and what does not.** Two ordinary acts now record the table answer themselves, server-side, rather than trusting a surface to record it afterwards: declaring a table **with an explicit** `hasAcceptance` (`POST /apps/:appId/tables`), and setting it on an empty table (`PATCH /app-tables/:appTableId`). The declaration body defaults `hasAcceptance` to false, and **the default is not an answer** — a table declared without the field stays an open question at the gate (the third addendum: the wall questions are never defaulted). The screen answer is recorded the way it always was: `answeredQuestions` on the definition, written through `PATCH /apps/:appId/definition`. The recording write is one SQL statement that only appends to the list, so an edit landing between a read and a write is never overwritten by a stale copy.

  **Verified.** [`apps/api/src/app-publish-gate.test.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-publish-gate.test.ts), 9 tests, three firms on one project: an app with no tables and no screens publishes; an unanswered table is refused 409 with its exact sentence and nothing is published; setting the acceptance choice clears it; an explicit choice at declaration counts and an insight table is never asked; **a hand-built definition PATCHed straight at the API** with two screens (one narrowed to the client) is refused naming all three questions, then one, then opens; a republish is refused when a late screen arrives unanswered and the people keep the copy they had; a retired table is not asked; the gate's words ride the record for the builder and are null for the client and the peer; and their publish stays the same 404. End to end, [`e2e/tests/app-publish-gate.spec.ts`](../../e2e/tests/app-publish-gate.spec.ts) on the seeded world: Calder & Hale refused in words, Trentmoor still unable to see the app, **Owen Vance refused 404**, the same sentence on the app page in a browser after clicking *Check and open*, answering through the acceptance act, a screen written straight at the API refused by name, and then opened and read by Trentmoor.

  **Deviations, stated loudly.** **(1) Six existing tests had to answer their questions before publishing** — two in `apps/api/src/app-builder.test.ts`, one in `apps/api/src/playbooks.test.ts`, both tests in `e2e/tests/app-insight.spec.ts`, and the one test in `e2e/tests/playbooks.spec.ts` (two hand-written definitions inside it). Each had written a whole definition by hand with `answeredQuestions: []`, or deployed a playbook (whose screens' who-may-open is asked again by design, ADR-0056 §10) and published straight after. That is exactly the route the gate exists to close, so the tests now carry their answers; none of them was testing the absence of a gate. **(2) The stepped surface's publish buttons now show the refusal's own words** (`apps/web/src/screens/app-builder.tsx`, `apps/web/src/screens/apps.tsx`) instead of *"That could not be opened."* — a small surface change in a ticket that is otherwise the server's, because a refusal nobody can read is not a refusal in words. T-450 replaces the stepped surface. **(3) No migration**, as the entry said.

  **Gates:** `pnpm run check` with its exit code read directly; the container recreated empty, migrate and seed clean; `eval:smoke` 7 cases, 0 fail; the e2e suite twice on one seed.

- **T-449 — The agent-led build conversation.** *Plainly:* you tell the agent what app you want; it asks what it needs — the two wall questions always, in its own words, never assumed — and builds the working copy in front of you: declaring tables, writing screens, setting the schedule and prompts. The conversation is kept, so you can come back tomorrow and continue. ADR-0056's third addendum, rulings 2, 3 and 5. The agent acts through the SAME typed acts a person has (the existing routes drive table declarations, definition writes, screen generation), as the builder's own entitlement — and it may propose but never perform a scope grant, a share, a publish, a reassignment or a closure (§4, §6, §7: nothing the agent does widens access). Draft-then-confirm: it drafts freely on the builders-only working copy and asks before anything destructive (retiring a table); the contractual-data and who-may-open questions it must ASK and record, never default. The conversation is stored against the app, builders-of-this-app private, deleted with the app — **registered in [personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md) at ruling; this ticket keeps the row true, never re-adds it.** The screen grammar is untouched (blocks-versus-code stays with T-446). **Done when:** "build me a monthly sustainability returns app for three contractors" ends, over one stored conversation with the agent's questions in it, in a working copy with a declared acceptance table, a contractor screen and a client screen with answered who-may-open, a schedule and an analysis prompt — and the same conversation resumed in a fresh session continues with its memory; a test proves the agent's tool-calls cannot grant scope, share, publish or close. **Deps:** T-448. ✅ **Built 2026-10-18.**
  **As built. *Plainly: a builder can now describe the app they want to the agent in plain words — "build me a monthly sustainability returns app for three contractors" — and the agent builds the working copy: the tables, a form for the contractors, a dashboard for the client, a monthly schedule and an analysis prompt. It then asks the two questions it is never allowed to answer for them — does this table hold contractual data, and who may open each screen — and records their answers only after they give them. The conversation is kept with the app, so it can be picked up the next day, and only the people allowed to build the app can read it. Nothing the agent can do opens the app to anyone, shares a table, hands the app over or closes it: those stay a person's buttons.***

  **The conversation and its store.** `POST /apps/:appId/builder/conversation` (one thing the builder says; the agent's reply and the app as it now stands come back) and `GET /apps/:appId/builder/conversation` (the stored turns, oldest first), both in [`apps/api/src/apps.ts`](../../apps/api/src/apps.ts) and both `canBuildApp` — everybody else, the client and the app's own users included, gets the same 404 as for an app that does not exist. The turns are **`app_build_turns`, migration [0068](../../packages/db/migrations/0068_app-build-conversation.sql)**, drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) Drawer 9 before it was written and reduced to narrative in this commit (the state rule): who spoke (on an agent turn, the builder it answered — the agent acts as that person), what was said, and on the agent's turn what it **asked**, **did** and **proposed**; a `CHECK` keeps those three off a person's turn; UPDATE is refused, DELETE is not (it is the deletion path); `ON DELETE CASCADE` from `apps`. The personal-data register's row, written at ruling, was **amended, not re-added**: it now names the table and its two columns and says plainly how deletion works today (see deviation 3).

  **🔒 How the agent's tool set is bounded.** The model is not given tools to call; it is asked to answer in JSON choosing from a **closed menu of ten acts** — `BUILDER_AGENT_ACT_KINDS` in [`packages/contracts/src/app-builder.ts`](../../packages/contracts/src/app-builder.ts): describe the app, declare a table, write a screen, remove a screen, set the schedule, set the analysis prompt, add or remove a connection requirement, and record a person's answer to either wall question. The answer is parsed with `builderAgentAnswerSchema`, **strict everywhere**: an act not on the menu, or one extra field on an act that is (such as `hasAcceptance` on a table), fails the WHOLE answer and nothing of it is performed — the screen grammar's "refuse, don't filter" posture (T-442) applied to acts. Each act is performed through **[`apps/api/src/app-builder-acts.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-builder-acts.ts)** — `declareTableAct`, `writeDefinitionAct`, `setTableAcceptanceAct`, `recordAnsweredQuestion` — the same functions a person's own routes now call, so an agent's table and a person's meet the same checks and the same stamps. That file and the agent's contain **no reference to anything that publishes, grants scope, shares, reassigns or closes**, and a test reads both files' source to keep it so.

  **🔒 The two wall questions: asked by the agent, answered by the person, never defaulted.** The agent's `declareTable` has **no field** for whether a table holds contractual data, so every table it declares arrives with that question open; a screen it writes arrives open to everyone and **unanswered**. It may record an answer only to a question an **earlier** stored turn asked (checked against that turn's `asked`), so asking and answering in one breath is refused and turned into the question. Any required question still open after its acts that no turn has yet asked is **added to the agent's own turn in code** — a model that forgets to ask cannot leave one unasked. Narrowing a screen is accepted only to organisations the app is already open to. And T-448's gate refuses a publish past any of it.

  **Draft, then confirm; read before writing.** The agent drafts freely on the working copy. **Removing a screen or a connection requirement** is proposed first and performed only if the agent's previous turn proposed exactly that and the person has spoken since; a removal attempted cold becomes a proposal. Each act re-reads the working copy and changes only the one thing it names; if that thing differs from what the model was shown — somebody edited it by hand while the model was answering — the act is skipped and the turn says so. The model is shown the app fresh every turn, hand edits included, as a state block.

  **Verified.** [`apps/api/src/app-builder-agent.test.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-builder-agent.test.ts), **16 tests**: the returns app built by conversation end to end (draft → three questions asked in the agent's own turn → the gate refuses → the person answers → acceptance on, the dashboard narrowed to the client, the gate open → the PERSON publishes, the client offered both screens and the peer one); an answer given in the same breath as its question refused; a forgotten question asked in code; a narrowing to an organisation outside the app's scope refused; **the pinned ten-kind list, with the schema's own kinds walked and none naming publish, scope, grant, share, reassign, owner or close**; **the source of `app-builder-agent.ts` and `app-builder-acts.ts` read for fifteen forbidden references**; **a hostile model asking to publish, grant scope, share, reassign and close — plus one ordinary act — performing nothing at all**, checked in the database (no publication, no new grant, no share, same owner, not closed, schedule unchanged); a table declared with an acceptance answer refused whole; a removal proposed then performed on "yes"; a cold removal turned into a proposal; a hand edit made while the model was answering kept; the conversation readable by the builder and 404 to the client, the peer and the colleague who may not build — each of whom CAN open the published app; **a fresh login resuming with the earlier turns in what the model is shown**; the turns append-only, a person's turn refused acts, and the cascade from `apps`; an unreachable model leaving a stored turn and nothing changed; and the gate's refusal naming what the agent left open. End to end, [`e2e/tests/app-agent-builder.spec.ts`](../../e2e/tests/app-agent-builder.spec.ts) on the seeded world: Eleanor Price builds the returns app by conversation, **Owen Vance, Rachel Bowen and Nadia Okonjo are each refused the conversation — reading it and speaking into it — before publication, and reading it after**, Eleanor answers and publishes, Trentmoor is offered both screens and Redgate one, Redgate's submitted return reaches Trentmoor to decide, and a fresh login reads all four turns. The e2e substrate's agent is a scripted stand-in ([`apps/api/src/fake-builder-agent.ts`](../../apps/api/src/fake-builder-agent.ts)) that answers in the same closed menu, so every server guard is exercised by it.

  **Deviations, stated loudly.**

  **(1) "Tool-calls" are a closed JSON menu, not the model provider's native tool use.** Infora's model router carries text in and text out and has no tool-calling seam; the menu, parsed strictly, is the same guarantee by construction and is what the grammar already does for screens. Claude's mechanism, for the owner's veto with the rest of Session AC's list.

  **(2) There is no "retire a table" act, for the agent or anyone.** The entry names retiring a table as the destructive act to ask before; no person has that act on any route today, so the agent has none either. The destructive acts the agent has — removing a screen, removing a connection requirement — are the ones held to propose-then-confirm.

  **(3) "Deleted with the app" is a mechanism waiting for a path.** The turns cascade from `apps` and refuse UPDATE but not DELETE — proved on an app row written without scope grants. **No route deletes an app today, and an app's scope grants refuse DELETE as append-only intervals (T-439)**, so no real app can be deleted at the moment, its conversation included. The register row now says exactly that rather than implying a working deletion. Nothing here makes the position worse than the app's other tables; it is the same gap.

  **(4) The agent's acts are not separately audited as agent-performed, and have no undo.** The receipt is the agent's own turn; the working copy's "last changed by" names the builder the agent acted for; no `agent_acts` row (T-370) and no Run is written. ADR-0027's 2026-08-11 amendment asks for both on direct administrative acts; the third addendum asks for drafting "without ceremony" on a builders-only copy. **Raised as `Q-053`** rather than ruled here. (The T-442 pane wrote no Run either.)

  **(5) The real model's conduct is untested.** Every test, the e2e included, drives the scripted stand-in or a hostile script; the system prompt has never been answered by a real model in this build, and no eval case covers the builder's agent. What is proved is that the SERVER holds the line whatever the model says — which is the part the addendum rests on — not that a real model drafts well.

  **(6) The old pane route `POST /apps/:appId/builder/ask` is still there**, superseded; T-450 removes it with the stepped surface it served.

  **(7) The model is shown the last forty turns**, the rest stored and readable but not sent, so one call stays bounded.

  **Gates:** `pnpm run check` with its exit code read directly; the container recreated empty, migrate (0068 included) and seed clean; `eval:smoke` 7 cases, 0 fail; the e2e suite twice on one seed.

- **T-450 — The builder's surface: conversation first, the state of the app beside it.** *Plainly:* the building screen becomes a conversation with the agent, with a panel beside it showing everything decided so far — tables, screens and who may open each, schedule, prompts, connection requirements — and what is still open; the panel is directly editable, so you can fix a label without asking. ADR-0056's third addendum, rulings 2 and 4: the seven steps die as navigation and live on as the panel's sections; the agent reads before writing and respects manual edits; what is still unanswered is marked, and the publish act shows T-448's gate state in words before you click. With it, ADR-0058 decision 2's navigation: **apps leave the Tools shelf** for their own section of the project, and the Tools section keeps what you run. **Done when:** the returns app can be built end-to-end through the conversation with the panel live-updating; a manual panel edit survives the agent's next turn; an unanswered question is visible in the panel and blocks publish in words; and the project navigation shows Apps beside Tools, each holding its own. **Deps:** T-449. ✅ **Built 2026-10-18.**
  **As built. *Plainly: the screen where an app is built is now a conversation with the agent on the left and, on the right, a panel showing everything decided so far — who the app is open to, its tables, its screens and who may open each, the connections it would need, how often it runs, what its analysis says — with every question still unanswered marked where it lives. Anything in the panel can be changed by hand, and the agent's next turn leaves a hand change alone. The button that opens the app says, before anyone clicks it, whether it can be opened and if not which questions remain. And apps now have their own place in each project, "Apps", beside "Tools", instead of sitting at the foot of the Tools page.***

  **The building screen** is [`apps/web/src/screens/app-builder.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/app-builder.tsx), rewritten: `BuilderConversation` (the stored turns, the agent's receipt — *what it did* and *it suggests* — drawn from the turn's data rather than its prose, and the box you type into) beside `AppStatePanel`, whose seven sections are the seven old steps' concerns in the owner's confirmed order: what the app is and who it is open to; tables; screens and who may open each; data connections; how often it runs; what each run's analysis says; open it to its people. **The step rail, Next and Back are gone.** Every panel edit goes through the routes it always did (`PATCH /definition`, the table routes, the scope routes); the agent's acts go through the same functions on the server (T-449), so neither can do something the other cannot see.

  **What is still open is the server's answer.** The panel reads `publishGate` (T-448) and marks each question on the thing it is about — *Still to answer* on the table, *Still to answer — who may open "…"?* on the screen, an *N to answer* count on each section's head. The open act shows `publishGate.words` — the same sentence a refused publish carries — and its button stays shut while the gate does; the server refuses past it regardless.

  **The agent reads before writing and respects manual edits** — built server-side at T-449 and driven here through the browser: the panel's rename of a screen made between two turns survives the agent's next turn, which redraws a different screen and records three answers in the same breath.

  **The navigation split (ADR-0058 decision 2).** The project rail gains **Apps** beside **Tools** ([`apps/web/src/screens/project.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/project.tsx)). The Apps section is `AppsScreen` at `/projects/:id/apps`; an app is at `/projects/:id/apps/:appId` and its building screen at `…/build` ([`apps/web/src/main.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/main.tsx)). The Tools page no longer lists apps ([`apps/web/src/screens/tools.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/tools.tsx)). The old `tools/apps/…` addresses redirect to the new ones, so a saved link still lands. Words changed only where the navigation did: the app page's button now reads *Build it with the agent*, and component 8's two rail sentences name Apps ([component-8-surfaces.md](../architecture/components/component-8-surfaces.md)). The walkthrough and the record fold stay T-447's.

One API test was added to [`app-builder-agent.test.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-builder-agent.test.ts) for the bug below. Rendered with headless Chrome at 1440px and read by eye before committing.

  **Deviations, stated loudly.**

The turn now carries one state across its acts, updated after each of the agent's own writes ([`apps/api/src/app-builder-agent.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-builder-agent.ts)); the new API test *lets its own acts in one turn build on each other* pins it. A hand edit made while the model is answering is still kept, as T-449's test proves.

No mockup was drawn for this surface; the third addendum describes it (a conversation, a panel beside it, sections in the old step order, questions marked, the gate's words before the click) and the styles are the kit's tokens ([`packages/ui/src/styles.css`](../../packages/ui/src/styles.css), the stepped builder's rules replaced by the two-column ones). - **T-451 — The file source: an app table fed from a spreadsheet the project holds.** *Plainly:* the substrate that lets an app table point at a spreadsheet — a sandbox document or a library record — and refill itself from every new version of that file, so a contractor updating their cost report in Excel is feeding the dashboard without retyping anything. [ADR-0059](../architecture/adr/0059-the-file-source.md), drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) drawer 9 (migration **0069**, the drawing is the spec). The attach/import/refresh-now acts in one shared act file (the app-builder-acts pattern); the import triggered by the version landing (the replace-file act, T-220's route) and by refresh-now, never a poll; each import supersedes the last import's rows; rows stamped with **the file version's uploader** and their organisation (ADR-0059 decision 2 — the register's app-rows entry carries the dated clarification); `submitted` on an acceptance table, stateless otherwise; the .xlsx reader built in-tree first (values, never formulas), a dependency only if that fails, flagged loudly. Attaching needs `canBuildApp` AND read access to the document, resolved at attach. **Done when:** replacing a source file's spreadsheet refills the table as the uploader's submitted rows and supersedes the prior import, driven as each party over HTTP; a vanished region or unmappable column fails the import loudly in the stored receipt, changing no rows; detaching stops imports and deletes nothing; and a table without a source behaves exactly as before. **Deps:** none (the substrate exists). ✅ **Built 2026-10-18.**
  **As built. *Plainly: an app table can now be pointed at a spreadsheet the project already holds — an uploaded workbook in a firm's sandbox, or a workbook record in the library. The builder picks the block of cells under a header row and says which heading feeds which column; the rows land at once. From then on, each time the spreadsheet's owner uploads a new version, the table refills by itself: the new rows are entered in the name of the person who uploaded that version (never the builder), they arrive waiting for the client's acceptance where the table has an acceptance step, and the previous month's rows step aside. If this month's file does not fit — a heading renamed, "TBC" where a number should be — nothing changes and the table's receipt says exactly what was wrong. Detaching stops the feed and deletes nothing. There is no screen for it yet; that is T-452.***

  **The store.** `app_table_sources`, **migration [0069](../../packages/db/migrations/0069_file-source.sql)**, drawn in [data-model.md](data-model.md) Drawer 9 before it was written and reduced to narrative in this commit (the state rule): one source per table (`app_table_id` unique), exactly one of a sandbox document or a library record (the drawing's one `CHECK`, `app_table_sources_exactly_one_document`), the sheet, the region's header row, the heading → column mapping, the configuring builder, the receipt, and `detached_at`. **Two columns and two cascades beyond the drawing** — deviation 1. Registered in [personal-data.md](../architecture/personal-data.md) as "The file source's configuration"; the app-rows entry's 2026-10-18 clarification was already true and is untouched.

  **The acts, once.** [`apps/api/src/app-table-source.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-table-source.ts): `attachSourceAct`, `importSourceAct`, `detachSourceAct` and `importOnVersionLanding`, with five builders-only routes — `GET /apps/:appId/source-documents` (the workbooks this builder can open), `GET /apps/:appId/source-documents/regions` (the table-shaped regions in one of them), and `GET`/`POST /app-tables/:appTableId/source`, `POST …/source/refresh`, `POST …/source/detachment`. Everyone without `canBuildApp` gets the 404 an absent app gets. **The version-landing hooks:** the replace-file route ([`upload.ts`](../../apps/api/src/upload.ts), T-220's `POST /sandbox-documents/:id/file`) calls `importOnVersionLanding` after the new ambient version is written, and promotion into the library ([`cycle.ts`](../../apps/api/src/cycle.ts)) calls it after the new revision's renditions — deviation 3. Never a poll; a failed import never fails the upload.

  **🔒 Who the rows name.** For a sandbox document, the person who saved its newest version — the upload or the replace-file that put the current file there. For a library record, the producing organisation's person who **issued** the current revision (the sender of the transmittal carrying it, or of the newest earlier one for a contractual C revision, which re-issues the accepted P's file) — deviation 2. The builder is stamped on the configuration only. No request body can name an enterer.

  **The import.** Everything is read and checked first — the table still live and the app open, the mapping still fitting the table's declared columns, the document's current file, the region re-found by its mapped headings, every cell converted to its column's type and then put through `checkValues`, the same check a typed row meets (now exported from [`app-rows.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-rows.ts)). A failure writes only the receipt, naming up to three problems by Excel row number and heading. A success, in one transaction holding the source row's lock, supersedes **exactly the previous import's rows by id**: submitted or accepted → `superseded` (an accepted row keeps its decider, 0067's carve-out), stateless → retired by the new version's person, rejected → left as decided (flipping it would erase its required reason; the corrected file is its correction). Rows typed by a person into the same table are never touched. Imported rows land `submitted` on an acceptance table, stateless otherwise.

  **The reader — in-tree, no dependency.** [`apps/api/src/xlsx.ts`](../../apps/api/src/xlsx.ts) gains `readXlsxCells`: the existing sheet walk, typed — text, number, boolean, error, empty, and **`uncalculated`** for a formula with no stored result. A formula's **cached result** is read and the formula itself never is (ADR-0059 decision 5). `usesDate1904` reads the workbook's date origin. The two string readers (`parseXlsxSheets`, `parseXlsx`) now run through the same typed walk and return what they returned before. **The region finder** (`findRegions`): a header row is a run of two or more adjacent text cells; the region runs down to the first row blank across those columns; a cell already inside a region is never another's header; a short label row sitting directly on a wider header row is skipped. **Re-finding** takes the first row carrying every mapped heading (case and spacing ignored), so a block that moved or gained a column survives and one whose heading vanished fails naming it; a heading appearing twice on that row fails asking for a rename. **Conversion never guesses**: a number may carry thousands commas or a currency sign and nothing else; a date is an Excel date or an ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` and `31/10/2026` is refused; booleans read yes/no/true/false/1/0; an error cell or an uncalculated formula is refused naming the cell.

  **Verified.** [`apps/api/src/app-table-source.test.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-table-source.test.ts), **21 tests**, over HTTP as each party on a three-firm fixture (a contractor builder, a colleague who may not build and keeps the spreadsheet, the project owner, a peer firm): the reader's formula results, uncalculated formulas, error cells, row numbering and booleans; 1900 and 1904 dates and a refused text date; regions under a title line, side by side, and under a label row; a region re-found after moving and refused after a rename; **the colleague's file attached by the builder lands as the colleague's submitted rows, the owner accepts one, the colleague replaces the file and the table refills with the prior import superseded (the accepted row keeping its decider), the owner reads the new rows and the peer firm none**; stateless rows retired by the new version's person; a typed row untouched by an import; **a vanished heading and a "TBC" plus an uncalculated formula each failing in the receipt with the rows unchanged**; refresh-now after a fix; detach keeping rows and ignoring the next version; a purge of the source document deleting the configuration and keeping the rows; a table without a source untouched by an unrelated replace; a non-builder refused (404) on every source route; a peer firm's spreadsheet unattachable and unlisted; a required column left unfed refused in words; the database refusing a source naming both documents; a library record's rows naming its issuer and refilling when the next revision lands; and a never-issued library record refused at attach. [`apps/api/src/app-builder-agent.test.ts`](../../apps/api/src/app-builder-agent.test.ts)'s source-reading pin gains `appTableSources`, `app-table-source` and `attachSourceAct`: neither the agent nor its acts file can reach the file source. End to end, [`e2e/tests/file-source.spec.ts`](../../e2e/tests/file-source.spec.ts), **2 tests** over HTTP on the seeded world: **Owen Vance — who may not build — uploads and replaces the cost report Eleanor Price attached**; every row names Owen; Rachel Bowen accepts October and it is superseded keeping her name when Owen's November file lands; Owen gets 404 on the source; Nadia Okonjo reads nothing; and a "TBC" month fails in the receipt with every party's rows unchanged.

  **Deviations, stated loudly.**

  **(1) Two columns and two cascades beyond the drawing.** `last_import_succeeded` (a receipt's success must not be parsed out of its sentence) and `last_import_row_ids` (superseding "the previous import's rows" needs to know which rows those were, and anything looser would sweep up a row a person typed). Both pointers `ON DELETE CASCADE`: purge deletes sandbox documents and library records, a plain foreign key would have made a sourced document unpurgeable, and the configuration quotes the file's headings. All recorded on the drawing.

  **(2) A library record's "uploader" is its issuer.** Library versions store no creator, so the person named is the producing organisation's sender of the transmittal that issued the revision. Bulk-loaded reference material has no issuer and is **refused at attach** in words, rather than attached to fail forever. Claude's mechanism for ADR-0059 decision 2; on the owner's veto with the rest.

  **(3) The library's landing hook is promotion only, and is exercised through `importOnVersionLanding` rather than a real promotion.** Acceptance's contractual C revision is not hooked: it carries the same file as the P it accepts, and re-importing it would supersede rows the client had just accepted with identical submitted copies. The test calls the hook the promotion route calls; no test drives a full review cycle to a promoted spreadsheet.

  **(4) Re-importing re-submits figures the client already accepted.** Each import supersedes the last, as decision 1 says, so an unchanged October in November's file comes back for acceptance again. Raised as **[Q-054](../grill-sessions/grill-questions.md)** with a recommendation (carry acceptance on unchanged rows); built as ruled until then.

  **(5) Small choices the drawing left open:** a file with no rows under its headings is a failed import, not an empty one (a cleared sheet must not quietly empty a dashboard); at most 5,000 rows per import; imported rows' `entered_at` step by one microsecond in file order, because one transaction is one `now()` and the rows screen orders by it; attach refuses (400) a document that can never import, but saves the source and records a failed receipt when it is the file's *values* that fail. The reader's cell pattern also changed from greedy to lazy, which fixes a latent bug in the string readers: a self-closing empty cell could swallow the cell after it.

  **(6) Not done here, by the brief:** the panel (T-452); no sentence was added to the builder agent's prompt.

  **Gates:** `pnpm run check` with its exit code read directly; the container recreated empty, migrate and seed clean; `eval:smoke` 7 cases, 0 fail; the e2e suite twice on one seed.

- **T-452 — Pointing at the cells: the source on the builder's panel.** *Plainly:* in the builder, a table's panel section gains a Source: pick a spreadsheet from the project, Infora shows the table-shaped regions it found in it (header-topped blocks, the Power BI lesson — never loose cells), you pick one and confirm what each column means, and from then on the panel shows what version the table reflects and a refresh-now button beside a last-import receipt that states failures in words. The agent gets NO source act this round (ADR-0059 decision 4) — attaching is a person's panel act; the agent may TALK about sources (its prompt may name that the panel does this) but cannot perform one. **Done when:** the cost-reporting dashboard is buildable end to end — upload the spreadsheet, attach it to a declared table from the panel, see the rows land, chart them — and a second person replacing the file as its uploader updates the dashboard without touching the app. **Deps:** T-451. ✅ **Built 2026-10-18.**
  **As built. *Plainly: in the app builder, every table that people fill in now has a Source line in the panel. "Feed this table from a spreadsheet" lets the builder choose a spreadsheet they can open — or upload one there and then — and Infora lists the tables it found in it: a row of headings with the rows beneath, each shown with its sheet, its row, its headings and how many rows it holds. The builder picks one, Infora matches the headings to the table's columns for them to confirm, and the rows land. From then on the panel says which spreadsheet the table is fed from, which version of it the table reflects, and what the last import did — or, in words, why it did nothing — with buttons to refresh from the file now, change the cells, or stop. When a colleague uploads next month's spreadsheet, the dashboard redraws without anyone touching the app, and its chart and totals show next month's figures once each rather than piling them on top of last month's.***

  **The panel.** [`apps/web/src/screens/app-builder.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/app-builder.tsx): `TableSource`, under each non-insight table in the Tables section, and `SourcePicker`. Every value on it is the server's: the documents offered are `GET /apps/:appId/source-documents` (only what this builder can open), the regions are `GET …/source-documents/regions` (T-451's `findRegions`), the receipt and the version the table reflects are `AppTableSourceRecord`, and "the file is now at v0.3" is shown only when the two differ. The heading → column match is a **suggestion the builder confirms** — a heading reading as the column's label, ignoring case, spacing and a bracketed unit, so "Cost (£)" is offered for Cost — and nothing is attached until every required column has a heading. "Change the cells" is offered only while `mayReconfigure` (the builder can still open the document, ADR-0059 decision 4). A document the builder can no longer open is named *"a spreadsheet you can no longer open"*. Upload goes through the existing `POST /projects/:projectId/sandbox-uploads`, into the builder's own sandbox. Client methods in [`apps/web/src/api.ts`](../../apps/web/src/api.ts); a few lines of `.builder-source` styling in [`packages/ui/src/styles.css`](../../packages/ui/src/styles.css).

  **🔒 No source act for the agent.** The builder agent's prompt gains one sentence saying a table can be fed from a spreadsheet and that pointing it at one is the person's, from the panel; its act menu is unchanged and T-451's source-reading pin stands.

  **A fix the walk needed: figures from current rows only.** [`apps/web/src/screens/app-screen.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/screens/app-screen.tsx)'s count, total and chart blocks summed **every row the viewer received, superseded and retired included** — rare while corrections were rare, and every month once a table refills from a file: November's superseded 120 drew as a bar beside its replacement and the total counted both reports. They now draw from `isCurrentRow` (neither retired nor superseded); the table block still lists every row with its state. Not an access change — every row had already passed `canReadAppRow`.

  **Verified.** [`e2e/tests/file-source-panel.spec.ts`](../../e2e/tests/file-source-panel.spec.ts), **2 tests**, in a browser on the seeded world: **(1)** Eleanor Price opens the builder for a published cost dashboard (a total and a bar chart over a declared table), uploads the cost report from the table's Source, sees the one region under the title line offered, finds Month and "Cost (£)" already matched, feeds the table and reads *"Imported 2 rows from v0.1."*; **Owen Vance, who may not build, replaces the spreadsheet over HTTP and nobody touches the app**; the rows name Owen; **Rachel Bowen opens the dashboard and reads a total of 315 (not 535) and a chart with December and 125 and no 120**; Eleanor's panel then reads *"The table reflects v0.2."* and the import receipt. **(2)** a "TBC" month shows *"Last import failed"* and the reason in words, the table still reflecting v0.1 with the file at v0.2; after Owen's fix, refresh-now lands v0.3. [`apps/web/src/render.test.tsx`](../../apps/web/src/render.test.tsx) gains one test: a total, a count and a bar chart over a superseded and a retired row beside two current ones draw the current figures, while the table block still shows *Superseded*.

  **Deviations, stated loudly.**

  **(1) The dashboard fix above is outside the ticket's text** and changes T-443's chart, count and total blocks for typed rows too: a corrected or retired figure no longer counts. The table block is unchanged. A **rejected** row still counts in a figure, as before — whether a client's dashboard should total a rejected figure is a product question this ticket did not take.

  **(2) No mockup was drawn.** T-441's and T-450's precedent: the acts and the states in the plain kit. The panel was not photographed for the walkthrough — that is T-447's fold, as for T-450.

  **(3) Upload from the panel** is an addition the ticket did not name, using the sandbox's existing upload route; the spreadsheet lands in the builder's own sandbox and is from then on an ordinary sandbox document.

  **Gates:** `pnpm run check` with its exit code read directly; the container recreated empty, migrate and seed clean; `eval:smoke` 7 cases, 0 fail; the e2e suite **three times on one seed — 79 passed, then 78 with one failure, then 79**. The failure was `app-builder.spec.ts:284` (T-444's export walk), which asserts the contractor's workbook bytes do not contain `7.25`: the export's own *Data as of* time was `…:27.250Z`, which does. A clock coincidence in an existing test, not touched here and reported rather than edited.

*Review note, 2026-10-18 (the co-captain pass on the file-source branch, T-451 and T-452 — built in parallel with office-editing and reconciled with it here). The verification pass confirmed the substance — the reader, the region re-finding, the guarded routes, the uploader stamp, the supersession, the records — and found what follows; every fix is in the review commit, with a test where one could exist.* **(1) Anyone with sandbox access could become the named enterer.** The enterer was the creator of the NEWEST version row, and a plain text edit or a restore also writes a version row without touching the file — so a stray note typed by a colleague would have put their name, and their firm's stamp, on the next import's figures. The enterer is now the creator of the version that LANDED the current file, with a test that drives the drift and finds the uploader still named. The library side had the matching flaw — a current revision with no transmittal of its own borrowed an EARLIER revision's issuer — and now refuses instead, as its own receipt already claimed it did. **(2) Rejected imported rows counted forever.** A re-import superseded submitted and accepted rows and left rejected ones standing, so a rejected figure and its correction both fed every total and chart — the exact double-count T-452's own dashboard fix was built to end. A rejected row is now RETIRED by the next import, its state and required reason intact on the retired row, because the corrected file version IS the answer to the rejection; the build's recorded reasoning for leaving them was honest and is answered here rather than deleted. **(3) A client's decision racing an import aborted the whole import.** The supersession read states and then wrote them; a reject landing between the two violated the rejection-reason CHECK and rolled everything back into a "stopped unexpectedly" receipt. The writes are now state-guarded at write time, so a mid-flight decision changes which path a row takes and never detonates the import. **(4) A slow import of an older version could overwrite a newer one's rows.** The file is read outside the transaction by design; the import now carries a freshness token and walks away inside the lock, touching nothing — not even the receipt — when a newer version has landed. **(5) Receipts quoted cell contents.** "Reads «TBC»" put the offending cell's text in a receipt every builder in the firm can read — and the register's claim that the receipt names nobody was therefore false the day it was written. Receipts are now content-free by construction (the row and the heading, never the value), and the register says what is now true, dated. **(6) The reconciliation with office-editing:** migration 0069 takes journal seat 69 and 0070 moves to seat 70 with its snapshot regenerated to chain through 0069 (a wiped database walks the whole journal clean); the version-landing hook moved to where the replace logic now lives and the EDITOR'S SAVES fire it too — a co-authored spreadsheet feeds its table with no extra wiring, fired after the save's transaction commits, never inside it; and the question both sessions minted as Q-054 is resolved by seniority — office-editing's sandbox-grants question keeps Q-054, this branch's re-acceptance question is renumbered **Q-055**. **(7) Corrections to the records' own words:** six source routes, not five (contracts note corrected; the moved record's "every source route" negative was also wider than the tests, and the review added the missing three — refresh, detachment, regions — driven as the non-builder and the peer); the no-rows failure and the 5,000-row ceiling, stated as behaviour, now have the tests the statements implied (the ceiling at exactly 5,001); the refresh-now uploader stamp, claimed, is now pinned; and T-444's export test asserts its figure as a CELL (`>7.25<`), ending the clock-coincidence flake the builder correctly reported rather than papering over. **(8) Recorded, deliberately not fixed:** a typed correction of an imported row survives re-imports (a person's correction is theirs — the next import does not supersede what it did not write); date cells mapped to text columns import the serial digits (map dates to date columns); shared-string workbooks are covered by the older reader tests only; the panel's receipt wording and header texts remain readable to the app's builders after document access is revoked (structure, not contents, since fix 5); and `findRegions` shows a 5,000-row preview for a larger table that will then fail at import, which is honest if unglamorous. The self-closing `<row/>` twin of the builder's cell fix was closed in passing.*

*Review note, 2026-10-18 (the co-captain pass on the agent-led builder, T-448–T-450). The verification pass failed three of the build's claims and its probes found two real holes; everything below was fixed in the review commit, each fix with a test.* **(1) The agent could WIDEN access through an act on its own list** — the one thing the addendum's ruling 3 forbids. Once a who-may-open question had ever been asked, any later turn could re-answer it, lifting a person's "client only" back to "everyone the app is open to", stamped as that person; the contractual-data answer could likewise be flipped on an empty table. Fixed: **a settled answer is settled for the agent** — re-answering is refused with the person told the change is theirs to make from the panel; tests drive both. **(2) The build's own concurrency fix created the clobber it claimed to prevent.** After each act the agent re-read the store into its baseline, absorbing a person's mid-turn edit — so a turn with two acts would overwrite, say, a schedule the person had just changed, and the claim "a hand edit survives the agent's turn" was false for every multi-act turn. Fixed with an own-writes ledger: the baseline never absorbs the store; the agent builds on its own acts and skips anything a person changed meanwhile — pinned by a test that lands a hand edit deterministically BETWEEN two acts of one turn, which no earlier test could do. **(3) The gate accepted answers that answered nothing.** Any string could sit in `answeredQuestions` — a typo, a nonexistent table, a screen not yet made (pre-answering it for later) — and the panel's stale whole-definition save could silently UN-answer a question just recorded, reopening the gate behind the person's back. Fixed at the one boundary: a key must name a live non-insight table or a screen in that very definition, refused otherwise never trimmed; and the stored answers fold into every save, so a stale copy cannot un-answer (removing a screen still removes its question — its key stops naming anything). One T-448 test had encoded the old dropping behaviour as intended; it now asserts the survival. **(4) Two bounds added:** a build conversation has a worded ceiling (500 turns — each person turn is a model call and two stored rows, and nothing else bounded them), and turns on one app QUEUE behind each other in-process (two builders' interleaved turns let the asked-set and baseline go stale under each other; the queue is honest about the one-process deployment we have, and is the thing to revisit when that changes). **(5) Kept, not fixed — recorded so nobody reads the proofs optimistically:** the server cannot verify that the person's reply MEANT yes — any next message after the agent asks (or proposes a removal) lets the model record an answer or perform the removal, stamped as the person; the stored turn is the audit of what was actually said, `Q-053` (whether agent acts need their own audit rows) is the open question this belongs to, and the working-copy-only blast radius plus the human publish act are why it is tolerable meanwhile. Likewise recorded: other builders' turn text and scope-grant organisation names reach the model's prompt (injected text can steer a turn — the strict act schema, the closed menu and the gate bound what steering can reach); the e2e "hand edit survives" check uses a screen the scripted agent never touches, so the API test above is the real proof; the publish-gate e2e checks the sentence after the click, not before, despite its comment; and "drawn first then reduced" for migration 0068 cannot be verified from git — the drawing and its reduction landed in one commit, so the data-model discipline was honoured in spirit at best. **(6) Report gaps, for the record:** T-450's removal of `POST /builder/ask` also deleted one test and retargeted two others, which the report's "only added answers" claim missed; declaring a table with an explicit acceptance choice now bumps the definition version and stamps the actor (unreported but right); the playbook deploy response gained `publishGate`; and the old stepped-builder styles were removed. The verifier confirmed everything else as claimed, including the strict act schema, the hostile-model tests checking the database, the cascade, the register row amended in place, and all four record moves char-for-char.

*Review note, 2026-09-07 (the co-captain pass on the stepped builder, T-442 and T-444). The build's claims held better than most; what follows was found by the review's verification pass and fixed or recorded in the review commit.* **(1) A behaviour the build's own report flagged was missing from this record:** on the PUBLISHED copy, an interface narrowed to named organisations is withheld from **the building firm's own people too** — the working copy the builders edit still carries every screen, but once published, a screen open to the client alone is the client's alone, and the builder opens the app like anyone else in its scope. The e2e pins it; the review judges it correct (the published copy is what the app's people open, and narrowing that did not bind its own author would not be narrowing) and puts it to the owner. **(2) The stored export file joined the personal-data register.** The build kept a copy of every exported file behind `app_exports.file_ref` and registered the exporter, but not the file's **contents** — a snapshot of app-table rows, which the register holds as potentially naming outside people.
